en: The Kṛtyakalpataru composed by Śrī Lakṣmīdhara:
The Section on the Religious Student (Brahmacārikāṇḍa)
[Prayer] [Viṣṇu]:
O God, manifesting that very infinite Fish-incarnation of Your majesty...

May that great ocean of consciousness, whose wondrous glory was proclaimed through his births as the Tortoise and others, who consists of the bubbles of the cosmic egg, and whose fragments of radiance flash forth— may he dispel your illusion. 1.

I know that even a single line of flame from the eye on the forehead of the Lord Śiva becomes like the moon for the seed of the world, which is the very essence of the prosperity of the Goddess of Fortune.

That great light, the abode within the heart of Hara, which dispels the vast darkness residing in the lotus-heart of the yogis who have attained mastery over the movement of the vital breaths—may that [light] grant me great joy. || 2 ||
May Manu,
who is well-disposed toward his friends and who acts as a swan to separate the milk of merit from the water of demerit, purify you by entering your minds. 3.
[2] [Praise of the King:
Victorious is that illustrious Govindacandra, the Indra among men.
The kings were rendered motionless with fear by the thundering roar of Gauḍa, which he had provoked in play;

since even his own self was conquered by him— who, fearing that the mere echo of his vow to conquer all the lords of the earth might cause the sky to contract— I imagine that others, once he has attained tranquility, are nothing at all.
This Govindacandra, the sole abode of wisdom and prowess, shines brilliantly on all sides, dyed red by the arrows of both Kandarpa and his enemies;
he who, by his own will, utterly destroys even the illusory circle of sovereign kings.
By which skillful person non-duality was established for himself in just a few days. || 5 ||

In his exertion, terrified by the resonance of the deep kettledrums at the commencement of unequalled battles, they abandoned their treasuries in their homes, their elephants and horses on the road, their kinsmen halfway along the path, and their inner apartments in the mountain fastnesses. They fled as he marched forth.
The enemies' ranks were shaken by glances that caused a fever in the ears with the sound "bhāṃ," making them tremble with agitation.
Who would not pay homage to him, who is like a garland of rays that seizes away the splendor of the entire constellation of proud kṣatriyas,
and who is insatiably devoted to the abundant victories of unequalled battles among the heroic?
By whom the hero Hammīra was limited in battle, limit by limit.
[The Author’s Praise:

There is a preeminent lord of ministers named Śrī Lakṣmīdhara, the best among the foremost of Brahmins and a supreme tree for the playful vine of knowledge; he possesses inconceivable majesty and belongs to Vīra.
By him, for the sake of the sport of the pair of ruddy geese that are the feet of the Lord of the Earth,
a river consisting of the light from the jewels in the crowns of many kings was brought forth.
Having offered a hundred thousand lotus-like heads of enemy kings into the fire of his valor while conquering the ocean-girt earth,
how many of cruel intent have not been brought to their end by this most excellent achiever, the illustrious Lord of Devakāśī?
They were entreated by one who was devoted to the vow of battle and seeking the dissolution [of his enemies] for the sake of knowledge.

[The Praise of the Work] Therefore, this work has the Vedas as its root, possesses a trunk composed of a collection of Smṛtis, has branches developed from the array of Purāṇas, and is formidable with a multitude of sections and a dense mass of chapters.

This wish-fulfilling tree is now being unfolded: its leaves are blossoming words, it is beautiful with the radiance of most lucid knowledge as its flowers, and it bestows the nectar-like fruits of glorious virtue, wealth, and pleasure. (10)

In some places he employed ancient expressions that were not artificially composed, while in others, Gopāla— the companion of those [ancient sages]— fashioned his own compositions in the form of sentences.
This work shall be made to captivate the minds of the wise with the essence of the Śruti, Smṛti, and other scriptures.
Now, this composition is not extensive, yet it is a vast expanse of discourse whose meanings are refined by Mīmāṃsā. || 11 ||
Upon whose rising the Fortune of the great ocean no longer remains steadfast, and beneath whom the wish-fulfilling cow Kāmadhenu is said to dwell in sleep—
that [king] shall extend delight to the gods and the twice-born.
Is he not indeed a sprout from the wish-fulfilling tree? || 12 ||
What concern is there for following the great ocean? What longing for the wish-fulfilling cow? In whose heart do those petty things such as strings of jewels manifest?
By the power of the sprinkling of the nectar of the intellectual majesty of the illustrious Lakṣmīdhara—this...
By which he becomes, right here, a wish-fulfilling tree for the benefit of the three worlds. || 13 ||
Among words with the same meaning, one has been accepted at times while another has also been adopted due to its utility;

that which is rooted in ignorance, though it persists, has been discarded, whereas that which is rooted in true knowledge has been embraced by the learned, stated, and clarified when its meaning was obscure.
Where an apparent contradiction manifests, a systematic resolution has been formulated by him for that case.
[4] This work was indeed churned from the ocean of the words of the foremost sages by Lakṣmīdhara, using the mountain of logic as a churning-stick,
and extracted in fourteen sections with wonderful arrangements of chapters.
Whose desire does the wish-fulfilling tree not bear fruit? || 15 ||
[The opening verse and vow for the section on the life of a religious student:

Terrified, turned away from pleasures of the senses, sleeping upon the bare ground, subsisting on the alms-gathering lifestyle, their bodies covered only by their skins and wearing nothing but a loincloth;
Lakṣmīdhara, by whom those enemies of the lord of Kāśī were brought to the highest state of celibacy, inaugurates at the outset this first hermitage of fame in this section. 16.
In this first section of the Kṛtyakalpataru, the determination of the religious duties of the student (brahmacārin) is established according to their essential nature, results, measures, and causes.
Next, the technical definitions, the formative rites, as well as the ceremony of initiation; then the rule for sipping water, and likewise the occasion and the purification itself.

The twilight rituals, the fire-rites, salutation, and clasping the feet; the designations "teacher" (ācārya) and "preceptor" (guru) and so forth for those worthy of honor, and the sequence for honoring them.
Obedience to the guru and teacher, following the conduct of a son toward his wife,
and restraint of the senses are the observances for those practicing celibacy.
The procedure for teaching may be performed on days other than those for one's own Vedic study;
likewise, the rules for the four stages of life and the duties of the lifelong student are to be studied.
Regarding the teacher’s fee and the ritual bath, twenty-two stages are set forth in detail according to their respective divisions.

Determination of Dharma. Now follows the definition of dharma, which is conducive to its practice, by way of its essential nature, result, means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), and cause (*nimitta*). In that regard, in response to the inquiry "What is dharma?", there is the definition of dharma, conducive to its practice, by way of its essential nature, result, means of valid cognition, and cause. Manu [2.1]:
Learn that dharma which is practiced by the wise and the virtuous who are ever free from hatred and passion, and which is approved by the heart.

[This is] served—that is, constantly practiced—by the wise, those who know the meaning of the Vedas; [it is] always unblamable by the virtuous; [it is] approved by the heart—that is, accepted as something to be done without hesitation—by those free from hatred and passion, whose attachment and aversion have been eliminated through scriptural injunctions. Viśvāmitra:
"For when it is performed, those who know the scriptures praise its purpose."
That which they censure is dharma; that which they praise, they declare to be adharma.

[6] Āpastamba [1.10.6–7]: Dharma and Adharma do not walk about saying, "We are here. Neither the gods, nor the Gandharvas, nor the ancestors declare, "This is dharma" or "This is adharma. Rather, that which the noble ones (*āryas*) praise when it is being performed is dharma; that which they censure is adharma.

The meaning is this: speaking thus before the eyes of all the world that "we two are engaged in a wager regarding dharma and adharma" for the purpose of declaring the truth, they do not speak falsely.
As stated in the *Bhaviṣya Purāṇa*:
"Dharma is declared to be the highest good; the highest good is characterized by worldly prosperity (*abhyudaya*)."

"Dharma is the highest good" (dharmaḥ śreyaḥ) means that "the highest good" (śreyaḥ) refers to the means of attaining it by way of dharma. However, the primary highest good is of the nature of worldly prosperity (abhyudaya). Thus he says: "The highest good is characterized by worldly prosperity. Now, regarding the specific types of dharma, Hārīta states:

Now, regarding the stages of life (*āśrama*), there is the distinct duty (*pṛthagdharma*), the specific duty (*viśeṣadharma*), the common duty (*samānadharma*), and the complete duty (*kṛtsnadharma*). The distinct duty arises from the performance of the individual stages of life, such as the duties of the four social classes (*cāturvarṇya*). The specific duty arises from the performance of the particular requirements of one's own stage of life, such as those of the lifelong student (*naiṣṭhika*), the householder (*yāyāvara*), the forest-dweller (*anujñāyin*), and those perfected through all four stages (*cāturāśramyasiddha*). That which is common to all is the common duty. The lifelong student’s practice is the complete duty.

The *naiṣṭhika* is a specific type of forest-dweller (*vānaprastha*). The remainder [of the definition] is that this is established by the four stages of life (*cāturāśramya*). Regarding the term *naiṣṭhika*: "niṣṭhā" means the finality of *saṃsāra*; it refers to the performance of obligatory and occasional rites (*nitya-naimittika*) by one who possesses self-knowledge (*ātmajñāna*) for the sake of avoiding transgression. Thus, it is that which has that as its purpose—a *naiṣṭhika*. This occurs in the *Bhaviṣya Purāṇa* following the word "dharma":
"That eternal dharma, rooted in the Vedas, is said to be fivefold."

The duty of the social classes (varṇadharma) alone is traditionally taught first; after that comes the duty of the stages of life (āśramadharma); and thirdly, the duties of both class and stage (varṇāśramadharma), which are further categorized as secondary (gauṇa) and occasional (naimittika).
O King, that duty which proceeds by relying upon a single caste is called the duty of caste (varṇadharma),
just like the initiation ceremony (upanayana).
But that which, having taken recourse to a stage of life (āśrama), proceeds as a specific qualification—
that indeed is the duty of that stage, such as the alms-bowl, the staff, and so forth.
That which operates with reference to both caste and stage of life is the dharma of caste and stage (varṇāśramadharma), just as the girdle made of muñja grass is [the specific mark] for the student.
That which proceeds by virtue of a quality is called a "quality-dharma," just as the massaging of the subjects by one who has been consecrated as a head-anointed king.
Whatever phenomenon proceeds by depending upon a single cause should be understood as "caused," just like the rule for penance.
In this context, dharma is the subject matter.
As stated in the Kālikāpurāṇa: "Dharma is traditionally held to consist of iṣṭa and pūrta; it is indeed recorded in the Śruti and approved by the learned."
Of these two, *pūrta*—characterized by works such as sacrificial rites (*iṣṭa*) and public works—is the foundation;
*pūrta* bestows worldly enjoyment and liberation, while *iṣṭa* is the means for achieving the objects of enjoyment.

"Pratiṣṭhādyam" refers to the consecration of deities, the dedication of reservoirs of water, and so forth. Between those two—namely, *iṣṭa* (sacrificial rites) and *pūrta* (charitable works)—it is stated in the Śrī Mahābhārata: "The single-fire ritual is the oblation performed in the *ekāgni*; where it is offered in the *tretā*..."
And that gift which is offered within the sacrificial altar (antarvedi) is now described.
O noble ones, the wise declare that the construction of ponds, wells, and tanks, temples for the deities, the gift of food, and groves constitutes *pūrta* (meritorious works of public utility).

The rite of offering into a single fire (*ekāgnikarma*) is an act consisting of oblations (*homa*) performed in a single fire, such as the *āvasathya*. In the *tretā* state, it refers to the three fires.
Manu [1.88–91] states:
"Teaching, studying, sacrificing for oneself, and likewise sacrificing for others..."
He ordained both the giving and the receiving of gifts for the Brāhmaṇas.
He prescribed for the Kṣatriya the protection of subjects, as well as giving, sacrifice, and study, along with non-attachment to sense objects.
The protection of cattle, giving, sacrifice, study, trade,
money-lending, and agriculture are the duties of the Vaiśya.
But the Lord ordained only one duty for the Śūdra:
to serve these very classes without malice.
Non-attachment to sense objects is the conquest of the senses. Trade is commerce. Usury is the lending of money for the sake of interest.
In the Mahābhārata:
"Of Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras, O scorcher of foes..."
Actions are divided according to the qualities born of their own nature.
Tranquility, self-control, austerity, purity, forbearance, and uprightness;
as well as knowledge, realization, and faith in the Vedas—these are the duties of a Brahmin, born of his own nature.
Skill in performing sacrifices and other rites is consciousness; valor, splendor, fortitude, dexterity, not fleeing in battle, generosity,
and lordliness are the duties of a kṣatriya, born of his own nature.

Valor is the disposition toward martial action; majesty is a specific quality characterized by being unassailable; dexterity is enthusiasm; and lordship is sovereignty. Agriculture, cattle-rearing, and trade are born from the inherent nature of the duties of the Vaiśya.
Service is the duty of the Śūdra, born likewise from his inherent nature.
Gorakṣa is the protection of cattle.
A man who is devoted to his own respective duty attains perfection;
thus [it is said in 18.47].
One's own duty, though deficient, is better than the duty of another well-performed;
death in one's own duty is better, for the duty of another brings fear.
One's own duty (*svadharma*) is the duty of one's own caste and stage of life (*varṇāśramadharma*).
As stated in the *Mahābhārata*: "Compassion, non-violence, vigilance, and sharing."
The performance of ancestral rites, hospitality toward guests, truthfulness, and freedom from anger.
Contentment with one's own wife, purity through constant conformity [to duty],
self-knowledge, and forbearance— these, O King, are the common duties for all.
Compassion is the absence of cruelty. Knowledge of the Self is the knowledge of its eternal nature. Forbearance is patience.
Likewise, Viṣṇu is the common dharma [of all these]. [2.16–17]
Forgiveness, truthfulness, self-restraint, purity, generosity, control of the senses, non-violence, service to the teacher, and likewise visiting sacred fords.
[11] Straightforwardness, freedom from greed, worship of the gods and Brahmins,
and likewise freedom from malice— this is called the common dharma.
Common to all four castes is that which Bṛhaspati [in the Saṃskāra section,
verse 489] states: compassion, forbearance, freedom from envy, purity, lack of exertion, and auspiciousness.
Freedom from miserliness, lack of covetousness, and that which is common to all beings.
In the Śrī Mahābhārata: Truth, self-restraint, austerity, purity, contentment, modesty, forgiveness, straightforwardness,
knowledge, tranquility, compassion, and generosity— this is the eternal dharma.
Devala said: Purity, charity, austerity, faith, service to the guru, forbearance, compassion, discernment, humility, and truth— this is the compendium of dharma.
Yājñavalkya [1.8]:
Among the acts of sacrifice, conduct, compassion, non-violence, charity, and the study of sacred texts, this is the supreme dharma: the perception of the Self through yoga.
Toward others, toward one's circle of kinsmen, toward a friend, or even toward an enemy, one must always protect them when they are in distress; this is proclaimed as compassion.
Whether external or internal suffering arises anywhere,
one who neither becomes angry nor retaliates— that is proclaimed as patience (kṣamā).
She does not destroy the virtues of the virtuous, she praises even those of meager merit, and she takes no delight in the faults of others; this is proclaimed as being free from envy (anasūyā).
Abstaining from forbidden food, associating with those who are blameless,
and remaining steadfast in one’s own duty— this is proclaimed as purity.
Whatever action, even if most auspicious, causes the body to suffer, that should not be done at all; that is called "effortlessness."
The constant practice of what is commendable and the avoidance of what is uncommendable—
this indeed is declared to be auspiciousness by the seers who perceive the truth.
For one should give even from a small amount with an undepressed inner self;
whatever is given day after day, however little it may be, that is remembered as being free from miserliness.
One should indeed be content with whatever object has arisen;
not considering the wealth of another, that state is proclaimed as being free from desire.
In the Mahābhārata: Truth is said to be that which is beneficial to living beings; self-restraint is the taming of the mind;
austerity is the practice of one's own duty; and purity is the avoidance of mixing [with those of other classes].
Contentment, renunciation of sense objects, modesty, desisting from what should not be done,
forbearance, endurance of dualities, straightforwardness, and equanimity of mind.
Knowledge is the perfect awakening to the meaning of reality; tranquility is the clarity of the mind;
compassion is the desire for the welfare of living beings; and meditation is the mind free from objective referents.
Devala says: Austerity is the heating of the body through vows, fasts, and observances.
Likewise:
"Confidence is likewise proclaimed as faith regarding the activities of the Dharma;
for one who lacks faith, there is no purpose in the activities of the Dharma."
In the Devīpurāṇa: "Subtle Dharma is not attained through many bodily hardships, nor even by heaps of wealth, by those devoid of faith— even if they were gods."
Devala says:
Forgiveness (kṣamā) is the endurance of the faults arising from another's anger— namely, contempt, transgression, insult, injury, affliction, and physical violence.
Likewise, the sages have said that compassion toward the sufferings of others, as if toward one's own, and benevolence toward living beings, is called *dayā* (pity) and *anukrośa* (sympathy).
Furthermore, the retention of all sciences, both Vedic and worldly, in their entirety, is proclaimed as "higher knowledge" (vijñāna).
They say that discipline (vinaya) is twofold: constant self-restraint and tranquility;
tranquility is the stilling of the body, while knowledge arises from the clarity of wisdom.
Listen to the essence of all dharma, and having heard it, let it be firmly grasped:
one should not do unto others that which is disagreeable to oneself.
Dakṣa said: One who desires happiness should regard another exactly as one regards oneself;
just as with oneself, so too with others, should joys and sorrows be regarded as equal.
Now follows the definition of Dharma by way of its results; regarding this, Manu (2.9) says:
"For a human being who practices the Dharma proclaimed in the Śruti and Smṛti..."
In this world one attains freedom from distress, and after death, unsurpassed happiness.
"Supreme happiness" is intended as an indication of each respective fruit attained according to one's practice.

Members of the various classes (*varṇa*) and stages of life (*āśrama*), being devoted to their own respective duties, after death experience the fruits of their actions; then, by the remainder [of that merit], they obtain a birth distinguished by [excellent] country, caste, family, form, lifespan, learning, conduct, wealth, happiness, and intelligence. Those who act contrary to this perish like poison.

[15] Regarding the phrase "then by the remainder" (*tataḥ śeṣeṇa*), the Master [Bhartṛmitra] holds that it refers to the remainder of that very same karma. The Bhaṭṭapādas, however, maintain that it refers to a different remaining karma. As they state in the *Gautamīya*: "And that remainder [is determined] from that [previous karma], depending upon the mind and so forth. The word *medhasaḥ* ends in *s* and denotes vigor (*vīrya*). "Moving in all directions" (*viṣvañcaḥ*) means going everywhere; that is to say, acting according to their own will. "The contrary ones" perish after experiencing the fruit of evil in hell and other such realms; having taken birth in hostile lands and the like, they become devoted to sin. Āpastamba [2.2.2–5].

For all social classes (*varṇas*), there is supreme and immeasurable happiness in the performance of their own specific duties (*svadharma*). Upon transmigration, by the remainder of the fruits of their actions, they obtain birth, appearance, class, strength, intelligence, wisdom, wealth, and the performance of duty. This wheel revolves for their benefit in both worlds. Just as the growth of fruit from the seed of medicinal plants and trees increases according to the specific nature of the field and the action performed, so too is the increase of the fruits of defects explained by this.

"Supreme" means most excellent. "Immeasurable" means lasting for a long time. "Reversion" (parivṛtti) means recurrence. "By the remainder of the fruit of action" means by the remainder of the means for producing the fruit of action; this is the meaning. And this is a different kind of fruit specifically for obligatory (*nitya*) rites—so says the *Kapardibhāṣya*. [16] Therefore, he exists in happiness alone, not in suffering. Just as there is an increase in the fruit of a seed sown in a field—growth in every respect, in magnitude, in vigor, and so forth—so it is for the person who performs the necessary rites.
Thus says Manu [4.153]:
For through right conduct one obtains long life; through right conduct, desired offspring;
through right conduct, imperishable wealth; and right conduct destroys inauspicious marks.

*Ācāra* refers to obligatory duty (*āvaśyaka-karma*). *Akṣayya* means exceedingly abundant. *Alakṣaṇa* refers to bodily marks indicative of inauspiciousness, such as moles or dark spots on the shoulders and so forth; the meaning is that it destroys the demerit indicated by those marks which has not yet begun to bear fruit.
As Manu, Vasiṣṭha, and Yama state:
"Even if a man is devoid of all auspicious marks, if he possesses good conduct..."
One who is faithful and free from malice lives for a hundred years.
Hārīta [Vasiṣṭha 6.1]:
Those who know the Veda understand that right conduct is the highest dharma;
for the wise do not declare that those who lack right conduct attain the higher worlds.
Likewise:
some, having attained worlds through sacrifices, gifts, and austerities performed for the sake of desire, return again to birth.
Those who are liberated from desires, whose sacrifice is truth, who are liberal givers,
and who are devoted to austerity, go to imperishable worlds.
[17] By this, it has been shown that the difference in results is based on the presence or absence of desire. In the *Bhaviṣya Purāṇa*:
"The performance of obligatory rites (*nitya*) is clearly intended even without a result."
But for the sake of the fruits of optional rites, and indeed for the sake of destroying defects.
The performance of occasional rites is said by some to be the threefold fruit of actions;
others declare it to be the exhaustion of accumulated demerit.
Likewise, others consider the non-occurrence of transgression [to be the result];
and others hold that the scriptural injunction regarding obligatory rites has a concomitant fruit.
On this point, Bṛhaspati [Saṃskāra 11.229] says:
"The Śruti and Smṛti are the two eyes of the twice-born for the path of justice;
those devoid of them are deluded regarding the way, and having fallen from the path, they wander."
On the path of justice, for the sake of justice—that is to say, for *dharma*—here [are the views of] Manu and Vasiṣṭha (Manu 4.157; Vasiṣṭha 6.6):
"For a man of evil conduct becomes censured in the world."
And he will constantly share in suffering, being diseased and short-lived.
One of evil conduct is one whose conduct is censured.
Āpastamba [1.12.11–12]:
"But where activity proceeds from the perception of pleasure and there is no scriptural injunction for it, one who follows such [activity] prepares himself for hell."

[18] Regarding the phrase "because of the perception of joy": when one acts based on the knowledge that something is a means to joy according to worldly authority (*laukikapramāṇa*), the operation of the treatise (*śāstra*) does not apply there. One "strives for hell" (*narakaṃ rādhyati*) means one comes under the power of hell; for the author of the *Nirukta* states [Nirukta 6.32]: "The root *radh* signifies coming under the power [of another]. Aṅgiras says:
"Whatever action is performed out of one's own personal intention, if it is devoid of [correct] knowledge..."
And all that pertains to the play of children is entirely without purpose.
"Devoid of knowledge" means devoid of scriptural knowledge.
Āpastamba [1.20.1–2]:
"One should not practice dharma while placing worldly interests before oneself; for such acts become fruitless in regard to spiritual prosperity."
Having placed this—wealth, fame, and so forth—in the foreground, that is, with reference to them, regarding prosperity, which concerns the results prescribed by the scriptures; Manu [4.242] says:
"Therefore, one should always gradually accumulate merit for the sake of assistance."
For with dharma as one's companion, one crosses over unbearable darkness.

Darkness is evil. Thus [4.171]: "Even if one is suffering on account of dharma, one should not turn the mind away from dharma, seeing that the wicked who act contrary to dharma swiftly meet with their downfall."

[19] For those who are unrighteous, failing to perform what is ordained, and for the wicked who do what is forbidden—“quickly” (āśu) is used here for the sake of emphasizing the intensity of the censure. As stated in the *Mahābhārata*: “He whose mind does not deviate from that which follows the path of Dharma...”
Of him they say, "He is a doer of meritorious deeds, not to be grieved for by friends and kinsmen."
Having attained this human state, which is difficult to find and serves as a staircase to heaven,
one should so compose oneself that one does not fall away from it again.
Likewise: "Those men who, possessed by delusion of intellect, harbor malice toward the Dharma—
even a follower of those traveling on the wrong path perishes."
And here, my dear, I tell you this further word, which bestows merit and is most distinguished:
never, out of desire, nor out of fear, nor out of greed—
One should abandon even the Dharma for the sake of one's life.
On this very point, the Taittirīya Śruti states:

"Dharma is the foundation of the entire world; in this world, people approach one who is most righteous. By means of dharma they dispel evil; everything is established in dharma; therefore, they call dharma supreme. [20]
Now, regarding the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), Manu [2.6] states:
"The entire Veda is the root of Dharma, as are the tradition (*smṛti*) and conduct (*śīla*) of those who know it."
The conduct of the virtuous and the satisfaction of one's own self as well.

"Entire" (*akhila*) means consisting of injunctions, prohibitions, and so forth. The word "dharma" (righteousness), through the figure of *ajahatsvārthalakṣaṇā* (retaining its own primary meaning while indicating another), refers here to [the Vedas] as well, because the Veda is the root source for the cognition of dharma. This is a restatement (*anuvāda*) intended to establish, by means of that [Veda], that the Smṛtis and other texts are rooted in the Veda. "Conduct" (*śīla*) consists of non-malice and so forth. Thus it is said in the Mahābhārata:
"Non-malice toward all beings in action, thought, and speech, as well as benevolence and charity—this, the wise know, is conduct."
Hārīta says:

Reverence for Brahmins, devotion to the gods and ancestors, gentleness, not causing pain to others, freedom from envy, mildness, absence of harshness, friendliness, pleasant speech, gratitude, providing refuge, and humility—these constitute the thirteenfold ethical conduct (*śīla*). In this matter, those who possess proper conduct are the authority.

"Of those who know that"—meaning those who know the meaning of the Vedas. "Conduct" (*ācāra*) refers to the performance of rites such as tying the marriage bracelet during weddings and other ceremonies. "Self-satisfaction" (*ātmatuṣṭi*) is the mental contentment of virtuous persons whose inner faculties have been refined by Vedic sacraments when a doubt arises regarding what is *adharma*. As stated by the venerable Bhaṭṭa:
"By this, for the sake of establishing *dharma*, the authority of self-satisfaction is established for those whose souls have been refined by the cognition of various Vedic duties. [21]
Yājñavalkya [1.7]: Revelation (śruti), tradition (smṛti), the conduct of the virtuous (sadācāra), and what is pleasing to one's own self—
desire born of right resolve (samyaksaṃkalpaja)— this is remembered as the root of dharma.

By the word *priya* (dear), affection (*prīti*) is indicated. It is the root of one’s own dharma, not that of everyone. "Born of right resolve" (*samyaksaṃkalpaja*) means produced from right resolve. Viśvarūpa explains that desire (*kāma*) refers to a purpose not contrary to the scriptures, such as: "I must not drink water except with food. Alternatively, from "right resolve"—that is, a resolve free from passion and the like—there arises what is born of knowledge, such as the desire to benefit a Brahmin; that which was described by Manu as "good character" (*śīla*) is precisely what is expressed here by the phrase "born of right resolve. Thus [it is said in 1.3]:
The Purāṇas, Nyāya, Mīmāṃsā, the Dharmaśāstras, and the Vedāṅgas— these,
together with the Vedas, are the fourteen seats of knowledge and of dharma.
[22] The foundations of the sciences (*vidyā*), which consist of the knowledge of human goals, and of *dharma*, are the factors that establish them by means of making them known.
As stated in the *Śrī Viṣṇupurāṇa* [3.6.28–29]:
"The auxiliary limbs (*aṅga*), the four Vedas, Mīmāṃsā, and the extensive system of Nyāya..."
The Dharmaśāstra and the Purāṇa—these indeed are the fourteen branches of knowledge.
Āyurveda, Dhanurveda, and Gāndharvaveda— these three,
together with Arthaśāstra as the fourth, constitute those eighteen branches of knowledge.

Fourteen factors are primary with respect to the determination of Dharma. Furthermore, four among them—being primarily based on perception—are authoritative even regarding Dharma when they establish some extraordinary matter. Sumantu says: "The Vedas, the Vedāṅgas, the Itihāsas and Purāṇas, Logic (Tarka), Mīmāṃsā, and the Dharmaśāstras are the authorities that establish the regulations for the duties of families, groups, regions, castes, and classes, as well as for heretics, stages of life, and those learned in the Vedas."

The first term, *dharma*, is connected individually with each of the preceding items ending in *varṇa*. *Kuladharma* refers to the customs of a family, such as the time for the tonsure ceremony (*cūḍākaraṇa*) and so forth. The *gaṇadharas* will be explained later. *Deśadharma*s are specific practices of regions, such as the particular ways women arrange their clothing. *Jātidharma*s are the duties of castes, such as charioteering for horses by those born of the *sūta* caste and others. *Varṇadharma*s include the initiatory rites (*upanayana*) and so forth. *Pākhaṇḍas* and the like are those outside the Vedic fold. *Āśramadharma*s include the begging of alms, carrying a staff, and so forth. A *śrotriya* is one who has studied the Vedic meters; his *dharmas* include eating only on the ground while studying the *kārīrī* sacrifice and other such rules. The repetition of the word *dharma* is for the purpose of excluding any connection with the heretical (*pākhaṇḍa*) practices.
Pāraskara states:
"The Veda consists of six limbs: injunction (vidhi), that which is to be enjoined (vidheya), and reasoning (tarka).
Injunction is that portion of the Veda which makes known what was previously unknown; the vidheya is the mantra; and reasoning is Mīmāṃsā."
Devala: The Vedas consist of the Ṛg, Yajur, Sāman, and Atharva [Vedas].
Śaṅkha and Likhita: [The same].

*Smṛti* refers to the treatises on Dharma (*dharmaśāstra*). Their authors are Manu, Viṣṇu, Yama, Dakṣa, Aṅgiras, Atri, Bṛhaspati, Uśanas, Āpastamba, Vasiṣṭha, Kātyāyana, Parāśara, Vyāsa, Śaṅkha, Likhita, Saṃvarta, Gautama, Śātātapa, Hārīta, Yājñavalkya, Prācetasa, and others.
Yama says: "Manu, Yama, Vasiṣṭha, Atri, Dakṣa, Viṣṇu, and likewise Aṅgiras..."
Uśanas, Vākpati, Vyāsa, Āpastamba, and then Gautama;
Kātyāyana, Nārada, Yājñavalkya, Parāśara, Saṃvarta, Śaṅkha, Hārīta, and likewise Likhita.
[24] Those treatises on Dharma which were indeed composed by these [sages] in ancient times— those very works are most excellent and must not be refuted by means of logical arguments.

In the treatises of Śaṅkha and Likhita: these are the ones included by the word "etcetera"—Budha, Devala, Soma, Jamadagni, Viśvāmitra, Parāśara, Vasiṣṭha, Vṛddha-Śātātapa, Sumantu, Paiṭhīnasi, Pitāmaha, Baudhāyana, Chāgaleya, Jābāli, Cyavana, Marīci, and Kāśyapa.
And likewise in the Bhaviṣya Purāṇa:
"O son, whatever statements are found in the eighteen Purāṇas..."
Having examined those, O mighty-armed one, as well as in other Smṛtis, [one should act].
As for those thirty-six Smṛtis proclaimed by Manu and others,
I shall speak to you after having examined their statements in due order.
Thus, in the words of the Lord addressed to Guha:

"The Smṛtis of Manu and others are fulfilled by those very [Smṛtis] just mentioned, which are accepted by all. As for the works of Vṛddha-Śātātapa, Yogiyājñavalkya, Vṛddha-Vasiṣṭha, Vṛddha-Manu, Laghu-Hārīta, and so forth, they have authors included within the well-known thirty-six [Smṛtis], being composed by those very same authors according to different circumstances.
And so it has been stated by Yājñavalkya: "And that which is called the Yoga-śāstra... Likewise:

"O sinless one, that which was previously mentioned by you regarding bathing with mantras whose deities are the waters. As for those works such as the *Gṛhya-sūtras* and their *Pariśiṣṭas*, they belong to a distinct category and are authoritative just like the Purāṇas, because they are designated separately in the phrase "and likewise in other Smṛtis. Furthermore, those works such as the *Viṣṇudharma*, the *Śivadharma*, the *Mahābhārata*, and the *Rāmāyaṇa* are also included by that very same expression, "and likewise in other Smṛtis. Thus it is stated in the *Bhaviṣyapurāṇa*:
"The eighteen Purāṇas, as well as the life-story of Rāma..."

The Viṣṇudharma and other scriptures, O Bhārata, as well as the Śivadharma, the Kārṣṇa— which is remembered as the fifth Veda, namely the Mahābhārata— and the Saura-dharmas, O Indra among kings, were spoken by Manu, O lord of the earth.
The wise proclaim that the name of these [texts] is *Jaya*.

As for the statement of authoritative persons here in this verse, taking it to be *smṛti*, that too is authoritative because it is accepted by the great multitude (*mahājana*). It should be understood as being included by the very phrase, "and likewise in other *smṛtis* [26]. Furthermore, authority is derived from the *Vijñāna* [text], which is accepted by some, such as the *Ṣaṭtriṃśanmata* and others. Śaṅkha and Likhita [state]:
"Because of the authority of the sacred tradition (āmnāya), proper conduct (ācāra) is taught to all by the teachers"— this is the meaning. [As stated] in the Viṣṇupurāṇa (3.11.3).
The virtuous, however, are those whose defects have been destroyed; the word "sat" (good/true) denotes them. That which is their conduct is called "sadācāra" (the conduct of the virtuous).
Vasiṣṭha [1.4–5]:
Dharma is that which is prescribed by the Śruti and the Smṛti; in the absence of those, the conduct of the learned (śiṣṭācāra) is the authority. Baudhāyana and Yama [Baudhāyana 1.1.5–6].

The cultured (śiṣṭas) are indeed free from envy, devoid of egoism, possessing only enough grain in a single jar, and lacking greed; they are bereft of hypocrisy, pride, covetousness, delusion, and anger.

Their Veda, along with its supplements, has been acquired through righteous means. The cultured are those who infer [the truth] from that [Veda], for whom scripture and direct perception are the means of knowledge.

* Matsara* is the inability to endure the excellence of others. *Nirahaṃkāraḥ* means those free from pride. *Kumbhīdhānyāḥ* refers to those who are content with little. *Alolupāḥ* means those who are not greedy for sense objects. *Dambhaḥ* is the performance of religious duty for the sake of reputation. "Study according to the Dharma" means study accompanied by the prescribed ritual procedure (*itikartavyatā*). "With its supplements" (*saparibṛṃhaṇaḥ*) means together with the *Itihāsas* and *Purāṇas* as its auxiliary limbs (*aṅga*). "Knowing inference regarding that" means being skilled in the process of reasoning (*ūhāpoha*) concerning the Veda. "The Śruti is the Veda"—those for whom the Śruti, which is perceptible and graspable by the organ of hearing, is the cause or means for the knowledge of Dharma, are described as such. [Thus spoke] Vasiṣṭha (6.43).
Those for whom the Veda, along with its supplements, has been handed down through an unbroken lineage,
are to be known as cultured Brahmins, who are the authorities for both scripture and direct perception.
Hārīta says: The learned (śiṣṭas) are those who abide in what is ordained by the Śruti and Smṛti; they are to be followed as authorities.
"Abiding" means being established in knowledge and its practical application.
Āpastamba [2.29.16]:
"Some say that one should learn the remaining rules of dharma from women and from all social classes (*varṇa*).

These "some" are those who were previously mentioned by Āpastamba as teaching that the *Atharvaveda* is the supplement (*śeṣa*) for women and Śūdras. To prevent an over-extension regarding the authority of the conduct of the learned (*śiṣṭācāra*), Āpastamba says [2.13.7–8]:

Transgressions of the Dharma and acts of violence were seen even among the ancients; however, due to their extraordinary spiritual power (*tejas*), no karmic hindrance (*pratyavāya*) accrued to them. Observing this, one who is inferior and weak incurs sin by employing such [transgressive] means.

*Vyatikrama* is acting out of passion with deliberate intent, such as Indra’s approach to Ahalyā. *Sāhasa* is acting without reflection due to anger and the like, such as Vasiṣṭha’s entry into the water. *Abalaḥ* means one who is without luster; that is to say, one who does not know Brahman. *Avarajaḥ* means one of the present day. *Tejaḥ* is the knowledge of Brahman; its specific realization is what is meant. As it is said: "Just as water does not cling to a lotus leaf, even so evil action does not cling to one who knows thus"—for this scriptural passage teaches that only the knower of Brahman is not tainted by sins.
Śaṅkha and Likhita state:
"Even in times of extreme distress, one should never desire the property of another;
one should not eat anything that is forbidden to eat, nor should one perform an act previously practiced [as wrong]."
The former and the new sense-faculties are composed of light;
they are not defiled by sins, just as a lotus leaf is not wetted by water.
The gods drink that liquor which is undrinkable by the twice-born;
they seize the wealth of the perfected ones (siddhas), which does not exist for those who have not attained perfection.
The former deeds are intended as merely prohibited. They consist of light and are dominated by knowledge. As stated in the Mahābhārata:
"Whatever deeds were performed by the gods and likewise by the sages..."
A righteous person should neither practice those things nor, having heard of them, should he condemn them.
— Baudhāyana [1.2.1–9].

There are five types of deviation, both to the south and likewise to the north. We shall explain those that occur to the south: namely, eating together with one who has not been initiated (*anupanīta*), eating together with a woman, eating food that has stood overnight, and marrying the daughter of a maternal uncle or a paternal aunt. Now, as for the north: selling wool, drinking *sīdhu* liquor, trading with people of both classes of teeth (i.e., with foreigners), serving as soldiers, and sea-voyaging. One commits an offense by practicing what is forbidden in one region in another; in each case, the local custom of the country would be the authority. Gautama says this is false. However, one should not respect either of these two, because they are seen to contradict the tradition of the learned (*śiṣṭa*).

*Misconduct* (*vipratipatti*) is conduct contrary to the *Dharmaśāstras*. Regarding this, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that local custom alone should be authoritative. The remainder is easy to understand.
Here, the definition of a *Purāṇa* is stated in the *Matsyapurāṇa* (53.65):
Primary creation, secondary creation, genealogy, the periods of the Manvantaras,
and the accounts of the dynasties— thus the Purāṇa has five characteristics.
Pratisarga is the re-absorption (saṃhāra).
In the Viṣṇupurāṇa [3.6.20–24]:
"Those who know the Purāṇas declare that there are eighteen Purāṇas."
The Brāhma, the Pādma, the Vaiṣṇava, the Śaiva, and likewise the Bhāgavata.
Likewise, another is the Nāradīya, and the Mārkaṇḍeya is the seventh;
the Āgneya is the eighth, and the Bhaviṣya is remembered as the ninth.
The tenth is the Brahmavaivarta, and the eleventh is remembered as the Liṅga;
the twelfth is the Vārāha, and the thirteenth here is the Skānda.
The fourteenth is the Vāmana, and the Kaurma is remembered as the fifteenth;
then follow the Mātsya, the Gāruḍa, and after that, the Brahmāṇḍa.
O great sage, these indeed are the eighteen Mahāpurāṇas.
In the Matsya Purāṇa [53.60–64]:
"That description of Narasiṃha which was proclaimed in the Padma Purāṇa,
consisting of eighteen thousand verses, is here called the Nārasiṃha."
That Purāṇa in which the greatness of Nandā is described by Kārttikeya is called the Nandīpurāṇa, and it is celebrated by people as the one named after Nandā.
However, that narrative which shall take place with Sāmba placed at its forefront is further called "The Sāmba" in the world, O you who observe the vows of sages.
"In this way, the notion of the Sun is also fully explained therein;
however, as for that Purāṇa which is seen as distinct from the eighteen [canonical ones],"
"Understand, O best of the twice-born, that this has emerged from them.
"Emergent" means arisen, as in the case of the *Kālikāpurāṇa* and others. Devala says:

The Vedāṅgas are phonetics (śikṣā), grammar (vyākaraṇa), etymology (nirukta), prosody (chandas), ritual (kalpa), and astronomy (jyotiṣa). Likewise, the Itihāsas are the ancient accounts composed by seers (ārṣa) based on past events, which have realization as their fruit. "Composed by seers" means authored by ṛṣis. In the Bhaviṣya [Purāṇa]:
Some Smṛti has its purpose visible in this world, while another has its purpose invisible;
yet another consists of both visible and invisible purposes, and others are rooted in logic (nyāya).
But another, the fifth, is observed by the learned as "recollection based on tradition" (anuvādasmṛti);
all these are rooted in the Veda, provided that their purpose is not already perceived [in other sources].
Likewise:
The application of the employment of the sixfold policy (ṣāḍguṇya) according to the scope of the task,
and the conjunction of the means (upāyas), beginning with conciliation (sāma), both in detail and in summary.
The deposition of officials and the investigation of thorns—
this Smṛti has been declared by the sages, O elder brother of Garuḍa, for the sake of visible worldly ends.
The twilight worship (sandhyopāsti) must always be performed, and one must not eat the flesh of a dog;
this Smṛti has been proclaimed by the seers who are experts in knowledge for the sake of an unseen purpose (adṛṣṭārtha).
The wise know that one should carry a staff made of *pālāśa* wood for both purposes;
however, when there is full understanding, there may be an option, as in the case of the Vedic injunctions regarding recitation (*japa*) and burnt offerings (*homa*).
If what is seen in the Śruti is not likewise fully realized in the Smṛti, then that [Smṛti] speaks what was not said; such is the case regarding renunciation from the household.

The sixfold policy (*ṣāḍguṇya*), consisting of peace, war, and so forth, will be explained later. The meaning is that, due to the gravity of the task at hand, the sixfold policy itself must be applied both in detail and in summary. The meaning is also that, due to the gravity of the task, the application of conciliation (*sāman*) and the other means must likewise be performed both in detail and in summary. Regarding the phrase "recitation, oblation, and sacred study": just as the recitation of the *Sāvitrī* until sunrise pertains to the oblation offered before sunrise; and just as Manu [6.38] speaks of one who "speaks what has not been said" (*anuditavādinī*), meaning one who speaks what has not yet occurred—just as he says, "Having renounced the desire for sons, the desire for wealth, and the desire for worlds, they wander about as mendicants according to their lot"—by this [verse], Manu restates what was previously mentioned: "One should go forth from the house of Brahman. This is the meaning.
Manu [12.105–06]: One who desires purity in dharma should thoroughly understand the triad of direct perception, inference, and verbal testimony consisting of various scriptures.
He who examines the instruction on Dharma given by the seers with reasoning that does not contradict the Vedas and the Shastras knows Dharma, and no other.

[Verbal testimony] is the cognition of an object not present [to the senses] arising from the knowledge of a word. "Based on various scriptures" (*vividhāgamam*) means that the instrument of this knowledge is various scriptures (*āgama*) consisting of the various forms of *Śruti*, *Smṛti*, *Itihāsa*, and *Purāṇa*. "Sages' [knowledge]" (*ārṣam*) refers to Vedic [knowledge]. "[By means of] reasoning" (*tarkeṇa*) refers to Mīmāṃsā and so forth. And this is intended as an illustration for all means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Thus, since there is application of *dharma* through presumption (*arthāpatti*), comparison (*upamāna*), and non-existence (*abhāva*), the application of comparison is thereby stated.
Vyāsa says: "By those desiring the purification of substances, nothing other than the Veda is sought."
[33] The cause of Dharma is declared to be pure; the other is proclaimed as mixed.
Therefore, that dharma which is understood from the Veda is supreme;
however, that which resides in the Purāṇas and other such texts should be known as inferior.
Know that whatever else besides these might express the Dharma is a marvelous word; delusion is considered its basis.
One should diligently practice that which was ordained of old by the sages, the foremost knowers of the meaning of the Vedas,
and one should avoid that which is forbidden by them.
For those who know the true essence of the meaning of the Vedas have prescribed that Dharma for the welfare of the worlds;
one should not deviate from that Dharma.
Even if there might be ignorance regarding that meaning of the Veda which one has understood by oneself,
what doubt could there be for the wise concerning that which has been determined by the seers?
Śaṅkha and Likhita state:
For those consumed by the fires of passion and hatred and drinking the poison of ignorance,
the treatises on Dharma are the remedy, just as medicine is for diseases.
By a portion of passion and hatred, that delusive cognition which is rooted in them is indicated.
Yama says:
Just as a vessel made of clay, once defiled, is purified even after hundreds of years by being fired again, so too is a twice-born man purified according to the treatises on Dharma.
Hārīta: For those blinded by the darkness of ignorance and led astray by false views,
this lamp of the Dharma-śāstra should be upheld as a guide for the path.
[34] By those with wrong views and wrong perspectives, such as the Buddhists and others;
Yama says: "The Vedas are authoritative; the Smṛtis are authoritative."
Speech endowed with Dharma and meaning is authoritative. For one whose own speech is not authoritative,
who would take their words as authoritative?
For him, neither the Vedas, nor the treatises on Dharma,
nor the words of the elders shall be authoritative; that evil-souled man, whose vision is destroyed, is a doer of unrighteousness.
Even the self would not be a means of valid cognition for it in this world.

The singular number in the phrase "the Vedas are the authority" (*vedāḥ pramāṇam*) is intended to express that the collection as a whole is the source of valid knowledge. Furthermore, the expression "speech endowed with dharma and artha" refers to true speech. The meaning of the phrase "he who would not accept that which is the authority" is that he does not acknowledge the aforementioned authorities, such as the Vedas. Regarding this, Vasiṣṭha [1.16] states:
"That which those who know dharma declare to be dharma, as do the elders learned in the three Vedas..."
In both falling and purifying, that is indeed the dharma; there is no doubt in this matter.

The term *trividyā* means "threefold knowledge"; the suffix *-aṇ* is used in the sense of "one who knows that. However, the author of the *Mahābhāṣya-ṭīkā* notes that if it were formed as *tisro vidyā vedeti*, the rule *dvigor luk* (Pāṇini 4.1.88) would require the elision of the suffix. Alternatively, *traividya* refers to those who are elders (*vṛddha*) or possessors of knowledge regarding all three branches of learning (*tisṛṣv api vidyāsu*). Here, the suffix *-aṇ* is used in its own primary sense (*svārthe*). Regarding the sin that causes one to fall (*patane patananimitte pāpe*) and the purifying acts such as ritual bathing (*pāvane snānādau*), whatever dharma they may declare is the true dharma. As Manu says (12.108, 110): "If it should be asked how one should act regarding dharmas that are not known..."
Whatever learned Brahmins may declare, that shall be the Dharma, free from doubt.
Whatever Dharma an assembly of at least ten members may determine,
or even one of at least three who are established in virtuous conduct, one should not deviate from that Dharma.

"Having at least ten" means that assembly in which there are at least ten; by this, he permits [an assembly of] eleven or more. When a matter is not known, it should be decided by at least ten learned men who are experts in *ūha* (logical reasoning), free from greed, and praiseworthy. "Not known" means either unperceived or doubtful. Śaṅkha and Likhita state:

"In case of conflict with the *Śruti*, the decision among assemblies of those possessing the threefold knowledge (*trividya*) shall rest upon those having at least ten members. The mention of *Śruti* is intended to include all sources of Dharma, such as *Smṛti*, custom (*ācāra*), and the authoritative testimony of the distressed (*mārtā*).
Now, regarding the characteristics of the assembly, Manu and Pārāśara state [Manu 12.11]:
"One learned in the three Vedas, a logician, a dialectician, an etymologist, and a reciter of the Dharma."
[36] And the three who belong to the previous stages of life shall constitute the assembly; it should consist of at least ten members.
In this context, *hetuka* refers to one who employs inference not contrary to the Vedas; *tarka* is the conceptual deliberation (*vikalpa*) to be described hereafter. Vasiṣṭha and Baudhāyana state:
"One learned in the four Vedas, a conceptualizer, one who knows the auxiliary sciences (*aṅga*), and a reciter of the Dharma."
The three principal stages of life constitute this assembly, which consists of at least ten members.
The principal [members] shall be at least ten:
Yama says, "A Chāndoga, a Bahvṛca, an Adhvaryu, or else a reciter of the Dharma."
In the same way, this assembly of those belonging to the [four] stages of life consists of at least ten members.
Purified by the Vedas, steadfast in their vows, and sanctifiers of the assembly— whatever those high-souled Brahmins declare is authoritative, without a doubt.

[37] Śaṅkha and Likhita state: A group of at least ten persons consists of those who know the Ṛgveda, Yajurveda, Sāmaveda, and Atharvaveda along with their six auxiliary sciences (ṣaḍaṅga), those who subsist by gleaning (uñchavṛtti), lifelong celibates (naiṣṭhika-brahmacārī), and those who maintain the five sacred fires (pañcāgni). Legal proceedings regarding dharma are to be conducted in such an assembly.
The inclusion of the term "lifelong celibate" is for the purpose of excluding the temporary student (upakurvāṇa).
Paiṭhīnasi states: "For those who are free from greed, free from hypocrisy, authors of the Dharmaśāstras, free from envy, and masters of the Vedas—these ten indeed determine that Dharma.

Here, "authors" (praṇetāraḥ) means "promulgators" (pravartayitāraḥ). In this context, the particle *iti* indicates a reason; therefore, the masters of the Vedas determine the Dharma for this reason. The word "ten" refers to persons. It does not mean "those possessing excellence" (guṇavatpara) by way of a distinction of qualities, because qualities—whether few or many—are mentioned here and there [in various contexts].
Śaṅkha and Likhita state:

"Four who are knowers of the Vedas and one who is a knower of the Dharmaśāstra [constitute a court]. Some say five at minimum. In cases involving ten or more, they should deliberate on the legal proceedings according to their conviction and in accordance with the scriptures; that is the law. "According to their conviction" means according to the perceived fault.
Paiṭhīnasi: Whether four or even three expounders of Dharma should declare something, or even a single person who has mastered the Vedas— if they say it, that is an authority beyond doubt.
Yājñavalkya [1.9]:

"A council (parṣad) consists of four who know the Vedas and the Dharma, or even those possessing the threefold knowledge; what they declare shall be the Dharma, or else one who is the most excellent among those who know the supreme self."
Vasiṣṭha, who had directly realized the reality of Brahman, said:
"That which even four or three persons who have reached the further shore of Dharma might declare..."
That alone is to be known as the Dharma, and not that of thousands of others.
Aṅgiras: Four or even three Brahmins who are learned in the Vedas and maintain the sacred fire, when assembled together, are designated as an assembly (parṣad).
But those who have not maintained the sacred fires, yet have mastered the Vedas alone—
these five, who are knowers of the Vedic scriptures, are declared to be what is termed an "assembly" (parṣad).
Those Brahmins who know the Dharma, who are discerning in what ought and ought not to be done,
and who are formulators of penances— these seven are proclaimed [as authorities].
One should appoint as members of the assembly twenty-one persons who have mastered the Mīmāṃsā and the Vedas, as well as those skilled in the Vedāṅgas.
Even a single member of those ascetics who possess true austerity, who know theoretical and practical knowledge,
and who have performed the ritual bath after the head-vow, may constitute an assembly.
But those three whom I previously mentioned, who abide on the path of the wandering mendicant, should be known as an assembly that removes all sins.
This [penance], however, is for minor offenses and middling ones;
but for those requiring expiation for mortal sins (mahāpātaka), it must be performed a hundred times or even more.
But beyond this, those Brahmins who possess only the knowledge of names do not have the status of an assembly, even if they are multiplied by a thousand.

"Abiding in the assembly" means gathered together. "Knowers of the Veda and the Śāstras": the *śāstra* is the auxiliary to the Veda, namely Mīmāṃsā; they are those who know the truth regarding what is prescribed and what is forbidden therein. [39] Due to the reduction of qualities (*guṇa*), there is a number of twenty-one. "Knowledge" (*jñāna*) is the understanding of the meaning of reality. "Higher knowledge" (*vijñāna*) is the retention of worldly and Vedic sciences. "The head-vow" (*śirovrata*) is the vow of all branches of learning at the completion of Vedic study. "It should be an assembly" means it should be like an assembly. Although favoring others is prohibited by them according to the rule, "one who does not undertake acts of injury or favor," nevertheless—because of statements such as "for those who are distressed and seeking [help]" and because of the scriptural hearing of fault in failing to grant expiation to one who has approached—it is understood that this [rule] also intends to prohibit favoring others in a manner not sanctioned by the scriptures, as was previously seen in the verse beginning with "those possessing the Veda, performers of the Agnihotra. "Yāyāvaras" are those whose livelihood consists of gleaning ears of grain and the like, who are devoted to their vows and maintain the Agnihotra. "In minor cases" refers to small sins. In cases requiring expiation for great crimes, there is something else for the purification of great crimes.

Hārīta says: "Those who know the four Vedas, those who know the auxiliary sciences (*aṅga*), those who know the *dharma*, and those belonging to the three stages of life (*āśrama*)—these they call an assembly (*pariṣad*) of at least ten members. Among them, the first four are superior.
Gautama [28.50–52] says:

Four who have mastered the four Vedas, three of the highest [orders], and three ascetics who each know their respective duties—these ten, at minimum, are called an assembly (*pariṣad*). In the absence of these, however, one who is learned in the Vedas (*śrotriya*), a knower of the Veda, and an established authority (*śiṣṭa*) is [the arbiter] when there is disagreement; for from him comes the power over all beings. The "highest" are those who have renounced the world (*pravrajita*). Regarding the phrase "when there is disagreement," the ellipsis is "then that [decision] must be carried out. By the word "this," the Veda is referred to by virtue of its suitability; it is "without origin" (*aprabhava*), meaning it is not of human authorship (*apauruṣeya*).
Manu, Vasiṣṭha, Yama, Parāśara, Baudhāyana, and Paiṭhīnasi are the authorities in the first [category].
There is no status as an assembly for even thousands gathered together who are devoid of vows, devoid of mantras, and subsist merely by their caste.
Whatever those who have become like darkness, the fools who do not know the Dharma, proclaim—
that sin becomes tenfold and follows after those speakers.
Aṅgiras:

Those who have mastered all four social classes and are the best among the twice-born are traditionally known as "Cāturvidya" (possessors of the fourfold knowledge), even if they lack the Vedic auxiliary sciences (*aṅga*).
A learned Brahmin who knows the authority of these three— the Dharma, this very assembly, and the sequence of penance— shall be the one to make the legal decision.
One should be well-versed in grammar, Vedic meter, ritual procedure, and phonetics; likewise, one should be a knower of the auxiliary sciences regarding the movements of the luminaries and etymology.
One who has completed the ceremonial bath after studying the Vedas and their branches, who is true to his word, has conquered his senses,
and is learned in many treatises on dharma, is called a reciter of dharma (dharmapāṭhaka).
After the stage of the student (brahmacarya), the three elder orders of life shall declare to him the dharma that has been proclaimed by me.
Likewise, [Aṅgirā 3.16]:
"The assembly for Brāhmaṇas is prescribed as such; for kings, it is remembered as being double that;
and for Vaiśyas, it is triple. And the vow is remembered to be in accordance with the assembly."

"In the *jyotiṣām ayana*, that is, in the science of astrology (*jyotiṣaśāstra*); and in the *sanirukta*, that is, together with the *Nirukta*. This doubling and so forth applies to those to be purified, such as Kṣatriyas and others. As for the doubling [of the penance] prescribed in the context of a vow (*vrata*), that has been stated in the *Bhaviṣya Purāṇa* regarding the killing of a person of a higher caste by one of a lower caste, sexual intercourse with their women, and other such acts; and the procedure for the assembly (*parṣad*) has been declared right here by Aṅgiras."
For Kṣatriyas it is remembered as double, and for Vaiśyas it is threefold.

An assembly of four high-souled Śūdras has been declared for those of great soul; and the penance prescribed by such an assembly is proclaimed for the purification of those who have committed sinful deeds.
O Hero, by this [act], one is born [as an outcast] except when it concerns the highest caste;
however, O Guha, in the case of killing a superior among the lowest castes,
the fault is to be known as even more grave for those such as Kṣatriyas— of this there is no doubt.
Then Manu (2.14–15):
"But where there may be a conflict between two Vedic texts, both are traditionally held to be Dharma;
for both of those have been correctly declared as Dharma by the wise."
Whether the sun has risen, has not yet risen, or is at the time of twilight, the sacrifice is performed in every way; such is the Vedic revelation.
"At the time when the day has dawned" means at the hour of dawn.
Gautama [1.6]:
"When there is a conflict between two rules of equal force, there is an option."
Jābāla says:
"In the case of a conflict between Śruti and Smṛti, the Śruti alone is more authoritative;
when there is no conflict, the Smārta [practice] should always be performed just like the Vaidika."
Śaṅkha says:

When there is a conflict between equally authoritative scriptural texts (*śruti*), the scriptures are to be treated as optional alternatives (*vikalpa*). For scripture is indeed more weighty; it is the sacred tradition (*āmnāya*).
By virtue of being the sacred tradition, its independence has been declared.
Bṛhaspati [Sanskrit 13]:
"Because it is based upon the meaning of the Vedas, the authority of Manu's Smṛti is recognized;
however, that Smṛti which contradicts the meaning of Manu is not praised."

That whose composition is based upon the meaning of the Vedas is "vedārthopanibandhaḥ. It is called an *upanibandha* because it is composed (*upanibadhyate*) by means of this; that is, a treatise (*grantha*). And the Veda states: "Whatever Manu has spoken is indeed medicine, for the sake of its medicinal efficacy.
[43] Gautama says: "The customs (*dharma*) of regions, castes, and families, when not in conflict with the sacred traditions (*āmnāya*), are authoritative."
By the *āmnāyas*, such as the Vedas and so forth, including the *śruti* and *smṛti*;
in the *Smṛtyanuvṛtti* section of the *Bhaviṣya Purāṇa*:
"But when there is a conflict with the *śruti*, [the *smṛti*] is sublated, except in its specific domain."
In other cases, investigators should act in accordance with established rules without contradiction.
When there is a conflict with the purpose of the *Smṛti*, the treatise on worldly affairs (*Arthaśāstra*) is set aside;
however, when there is a mutual conflict between two *Smṛtis*, that which is consistent with logic is authoritative.
But when a conceptual construction regarding an unseen purpose is possible within a fixed rule, it is a conceptual construction of a scriptural injunction;
however, when there is a fulfillment of expectancy, it is a conceptual construction of a traditional teaching.

The meaning is that when there is no conflict, the scope for application (*vyavasthā*) should be established elsewhere. "By the purpose of the *smṛti*" means by the purpose of the *Dharmaśāstra*. "Of the *Arthaśāstra*" refers specifically to that composed by Manu and others, such as the science of royal polity (*rājanīti*). When a fixed rule (*vyavasthā*) is possible—that is, in the absence of a fixed rule—there is an option (*vikalpa*) between two [texts] whose purposes are transcendental (*adṛṣṭārtha*). By this, the fulfillment of expectancy is indicated; through this state of mutual expectancy, the combination (*samuccaya*) of the *smṛtis* and other sources is suggested. Now, Aṅgiras says: "The authorities (*pramāṇas*) must be diligently protected by those who know the authorities."
For means of valid cognition collapse when they themselves are not established by other means of valid cognition.
Whatever is accompanied by valid means of knowledge is all easily understood;
for that which lacks a valid means of knowledge, its comprehension occurs with great difficulty.

Now, regarding the causal factors (*nimitta*), Śaṅkha and Likhita state that the characteristics of dharma therein are: place, time, means, substance, faith, recipient, and renunciation. When all these are present, there is the arising of dharma; this is the common rule, whereas otherwise it is the opposite. Dharma, when perfected by faith and a worthy recipient, depends upon time. The production of the substance [of the gift] through faith is "time," and place is rooted in that.

Place (*deśa*) refers to Brahmāvarta and so forth; time (*kāla*) refers to the solstice (*saṃkrānti*) and so forth; means (*upāya*) refers to the procedure (*itikartavyatā*); [substance (*dravya*) refers to cows and so forth]; faith (*śraddhā*) is firm conviction in the meaning of the scriptures. Faith is the production of a firm substance—this is time. This too, like the solstice and so forth, is the time for the practice of dharma such as giving. Place is rooted in that. The meaning is that when such a perfection of time occurs, place also becomes dharma.
As stated in the *Viṣṇupurāṇa* (2.3.1): "That which lies north of the ocean and south of the Himālayas..."
That region is named Bhārata, where the descendants of Bharata dwell in continuous succession.
Likewise [2.3.23–25]:
"In this regard, O best of beings, even after thousands of thousands of births,
a living being may perhaps obtain a human birth through the accumulation of merit."
The gods indeed sing these songs:
"Blessed are those who dwell in the region of the land of Bhārata,
which serves as the path to the abode of heaven and liberation."
Men become even more so because of their state as gods.
Having attained that infinite realm of action within the true Viṣṇu, who has become the Supreme Self, [one performs] actions whose fruits have not been intentionally sought.
But those who are stainless attain dissolution in that.
In the Bhaviṣya Purāṇa: "Brahmāvarta is the supreme region; next is the land of the sages (Ṛṣideśa);
inferior to that is Madhyadeśa, and next is Āryāvarta."
*Anantara* means slightly less. The negative particle (*nañ*) is used here in the sense of "slight," as in the expression "rice gruel that is not salty" (*alavaṇā yavāgū*).
That which lies between the two divine rivers, the Sarasvatī and the Dṛṣadvatī...
They declare that region created by the gods to be Brahmāvarta.
Whatever custom has been handed down by tradition in that region is called the right conduct (sadācāra) for the social classes (varṇas), including those of intermediate status.
Kurukṣetra, the Matsyas, the Pañcālas, and the Sūrasenas—
this is indeed the land of the Brahman-sages, immediately following Brahmāvarta.
From the presence of a twice-born man born in this region,
all human beings on earth should learn their respective duties.
That region which lies between the Himavat and Vindhya mountains, to the east of Vinaśana and to the west of Prayāga, is celebrated as Madhyadeśa.
From the eastern ocean to the western ocean,
and between those very two mountains, they declare the region to be Āryāvarta.
Where the black antelope roams by its own nature, that land should be known as fit for sacrifice; beyond that is the land of the Mlecchas.
The twice-born should diligently seek refuge in these countries;
however, a Śūdra, when distressed for a livelihood, may dwell in any place whatsoever.

The intermediate *saṃkara* castes are those born from mixed unions. Words such as "Matsya" and others, ending in the plural, refer to regions: Matsya is the Virāṭa region; Pāñcāla refers to the Kānyakubja and other regions; Śūrasena refers to the Mathurā and other regions. "Agrajanman" means a Brāhmaṇa. "Vinaśana" is the place where the river Sarasvatī disappears. "By nature" means by way of food, drink, and so forth. "Fit for sacrifice" (*yajñiya*) means worthy of sacrifice. A "mleccha country" is one unfit for sacrifice and the like. "Livelihood" (*vṛtti*) is the means of acquiring wealth suitable for maintaining one's own family. "Distressed by its absence" means afflicted or oppressed by its lack. [Vasiṣṭha 1.8–15]

Dharma exists in Āryāvarta—the region to the east of where the Sarasvatī disappears, to the west of Kālakavana, to the north of Pāriyātra, to the south of the Himavat, and to the north of the Vindhya range. Whatever laws and whatever customs exist in that land, all of them are to be accepted; for others do not possess the qualities of the *pratiloma* (inverse) skin. This they call Āryāvarta. Some say it is the area between the Gaṅgā and Yamunā. Others say that as far as the black antelope roams, so far extends the realm of spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*). Furthermore, the Bhāllavins cite this verse in their Nidāna:
[48] Behind lies the Sindhu, the Vitaraṇī, and before one, the rising of the sun;
as long as Kṛṣṇa hastens forward, so long indeed does the splendor of sacred knowledge (brahmavarcasa) endure.

[Those who possess the *kakṣa* dharma] are contrary [to the norm] and have an indistinct nature. The word *kakṣa* is used here to demonstrate an etymological designation (*anvarthasaṃjñā*). It refers to that in which the three noble castes (*āryās trayo varṇāḥ*) revolve; therefore, the noble ones must dwell in this very place. The *brahmavacas* is the perfection of conduct and Vedic study. The *Bhāllavins* are followers of the *Chandoga* branch [of the Sāmaveda]. The *Nidāna* is a *sūtra* of the *Chandogas*. The *Sindhu* is a particular river. The *Vataraṇī* is well-known among the local people as having been created by Paraśurāma near the Janaka mountain in the Mālava country, after he pierced a pool with the tip of his bow.
Śaṅkha and Likhita state:

"The land of the Āryas is that which lies east of the sunset [mountain] and west of the sunrise [mountain], as far as the high mountains and as far as the holy rivers; because it was established first, this land is eternal and auspicious. Or, as far as the black antelope roams, so far shall be the sphere of proper conduct (*ācāra*). To the east of Sindhu-Sauvīra, to the south of the Himavat, to the west of Kāmpilya, and to the north of Pāriyātra—within these limits, the spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*) of all is irreproachable. Beyond these, the lineages (*anvaya*) of those born in other lands, castes, and families are [not so].
'Irreproachable' means unimpaired. 'Lineages' means descendants. The ellipsis is to be supplied with 'are to be accepted'."

Paiṭhīnasi: From the Himavat to Kumārī, the Sindhu and Vaitaraṇī rivers, the rising of the sun in the east, or as far as the black antelope roams—therein Dharma moves with its four feet. [49] Saṃvarta:
That place where the black antelope, that ever-roaming deer, naturally comes to rest should be known as a region for the practice of dharma, a means for the twice-born to accomplish righteousness.
One should not perform a *śrāddha* in a barbarian (*mleccha*) territory, nor should one go to a barbarian territory. By drinking water in foreign lands, one attains equality with them.
That country in which the established order of the four castes (*cāturvarṇya*) is not seen...
One should know that region as the land of the Mlecchas; beyond this is Āryāvarta.
Baudhāyana [1.2.14]: The Ānartakas, Aṅgas, Magadhas, Surāṣṭras, those from the Deccan (Dakṣiṇāpatha),
the Upāvṛts, Sindhus, and Sauvīras— these are of mixed origin.
Having gone to the Āraṭṭas, Kāraskaras, Puṇḍras, Sauvīras, Vaṅgas, Kaliṅgas, and Prāsūnas, one should sacrifice with the Punastoma or with the Sarvapṛṣṭhā. Furthermore, they cite this:
"He who enters the Kaliṅgas commits a sin with his feet;
the seers have declared the Vaiśvānara oblation to be the atonement for him."
Ānartaka is the region in which Dvārakā is located; Aṅga is the region of Campā.
Now, regarding the general definition,
it is stated in the Bhaviṣya Purāṇa:
"An action must be performed by an authorized person through its complete accomplishment."
O hero, one who is free from desire always [attains the goal], whereas one possessed by desire attains only that which is desired.
One who is endowed with right conduct, possessed of faith, a knower of the Vedas, the best among those who know the supreme self,
and who possesses wealth acquired by righteous means, attains the fruit of his actions.

This is the meaning: "accomplishment" (*saṃsādhana*) refers to performing the rite according to the prescribed means. It must be performed correctly—according to one's capacity—by an eligible person who is desirous of the result, learned, and capable, following the primary ritual procedure (*prathamakalpa*) and so forth. In rites for specific desires (*kāmya*), the presence of that desire is the distinguishing feature. "Conduct" (*ācāra*) refers to the honoring of guests and other duties as taught by Manu and others. "The best knower of the inner self" (*adhyātmavittamaḥ*) is one who possesses firm conviction regarding the self as partaking in the world beyond. "Wealth acquired by righteous means" (*nyāyārjitadhanaḥ*) refers to wealth earned through one’s own lawful occupation (*svavṛtti*) which serves as a requisite for the performance of the rite. The word "complete" (*sampūrṇam*) refers to the fruit; this is the ellipsis (*śeṣaḥ*). Thus says Āpastamba [2.29.1–2].

The instigator, the consenter, and the doer are sharers in the fruits of heaven and hell; among them, he who undertakes more [of the action] receives a greater portion of the fruit. Yogi-Yājñavalkya says:
"And whatever rite prescribed by rule one performs, but in a manner contrary to the rule..."
[51] He obtains no fruit at all; rather, that for him is merely affliction.
"Seen in the injunctions" means as prescribed. Manu [11.31]:
"He who, though capable of following the primary rule, proceeds by way of the secondary rule..."
For that person of evil intellect, there exists no fruit pertaining to the future life.
"Prabhuḥ" means capable. "Sāmparāyikam" means pertaining to the next world.
Kātyāyana in the *Chandogapariśiṣṭa* [1.3.1–3] states:
"The learned have declared that the non-performance of rites by those who ought to perform them is of three kinds."
Non-action, that which is spoken by others, and thirdly, improper action.
That fool who, abandoning what is based on his own branch of scripture, desires to perform what is based on another's branch, finds that whatever he has done is in vain.
That which is not mentioned in one's own Vedic branch, but is stated elsewhere and does not contradict [the core doctrine],
should be adopted by the learned, just like the Agnihotra and other such rites.

"Spoken by another" means spoken in another Vedic branch (*śākhā*). "Improper performance" is the execution of a rite in a manner other than that which is prescribed; for example, the *agnihotra* is prescribed in the branches of the Yajurveda, yet it is performed by the *chandoga*s (Sāmavedins) and others in a different way. Since it might follow from the principle of the section on different branches (*śākhāntarādhikaraṇa*) that all *smṛti*s are to be followed according to one's own conviction even regarding the *gṛhya* rites, the author of the *Gṛhyapariśiṣṭa* states this exception: "Whether much or little has been proclaimed in one's own *gṛhya*, to that extent it is declared for him."
When that much of the meaning of the treatise has been accomplished by him, everything will have been accomplished.
As Kātyāyana states in the *Chandogapariśiṣṭa* (1.3.4–6):
"If one should perform a rite that has begun otherwise due to some delusion,
one should complete it from the very point at which it became otherwise."
If, upon completion, one should realize that this has been performed incorrectly, one should perform it again at that very moment; there is no repetition of the entire ritual procedure.

Where there is a non-performance of the primary act, that rite together with its subsidiaries must be performed again; however, in the case of the non-performance of a subsidiary, there is neither a repetition of the whole nor a performance of that specific subsidiary alone.

"Commenced" means begun. "Otherwise" means in a contrary manner. The meaning is that while performing that rite, if there is a deviation from the sequence and so forth—starting from whichever constituent element (*padārtha*) the rite was performed incorrectly—one should perform it again starting from that very same element in the manner previously described. Regarding the phrase "when completed": when the rite has been completed and the knowledge of the incorrect performance arises, one should perform again only that specific constituent element whose incorrect performance was recognized, and not the subsequent elements as well. This concerns the subject of incorrect performance. However, the passage beginning with "of the primary," etc., concerns the subject of non-performance. Where there is non-performance of the primary rite, that must be performed again together with its subsidiaries (*sāṅga*). But if there is non-performance of a subsidiary (*aṅga*), there is neither a repetition of the primary along with its subsidiaries, nor the performance of only that much of the subsidiary; rather, only an expiation (*prāyaścitta*) is to be performed.

Hārīta: The upper line of the thumb is the *brāhma* tīrtha; that behind the little finger is the *prājāpatya*; that at the tips of the fingers is the *daiva*; that between the thumb and the forefinger is the *pitrya*; and that in the middle is the *āgneya*.
Vasiṣṭha [3.66]: [The same].
Human [beings] are on the tips of the fingers;
