the conch [is at the base of the ring finger]; the sacred site (tīrtha) of the twice-born is said to be at the base of the little finger.
And likewise, at the base of the thumb, the Prājāpatya [tīrtha] is proclaimed.
Regarding the meaning "Which Brahmā is his deity for this body?", [the suffix] *aṇ* is applied according to the rule "kasyet," and there is the substitution of *it*. [Thus:
Yogi-Yājñavalkya.
The gentle one is established in the middle.
"In the middle" means in the middle of the palm. Baudhāyana [1.8.12–13]:
"At the base of the fingers is the *brāhma* *tīrtha*; at the tip of the thumb is the *pitrya*; at the tips of the fingers is the *daiva*; and at the base of the fingers is the *ārṣa*."
Śaṅkha and Likhita state:

"To the north of the base of the thumb, along the line running toward the east, is the *brāhma* tīrtha; between the forefinger and the thumb is the *pitrya*; the space between the little finger and the palm is the *prājāpatya*; and the joints of the fingers toward the front are the *daiva*."

And thus it is stated that the root of the little finger is designated as the *prājāpatya*, *kāya*, and *daiva* tīrthas; the middle of the hand is designated as the *āgneya*, *saumya*, and *brāhma* tīrthas; the tips of the fingers are designated as the *daiva*, *mānuṣa*, and *ārṣa* tīrthas; the base of the thumb is designated as the *prājāpatya* and *brāhma* tīrthas; the line above that is designated as the *brahma* tīrtha; and the space between the index finger and the thumb is designated as the *pitṛ* tīrtha. Manu [2.58] says:
"A Brahmin should always perform the ritual sipping (*upaspṛśet*) with the *brāhma* tīrtha."
Or [one may eat] with those who follow the thirteen-fold ritual for the body, but never with one who follows the ancestral (pitrya) rite.
The *daiva* [pavitra] consists of twelve [strands].
Hārīta says:

one should perform the ritual sipping (*upasparśana*), rinsing (*ācamana*), oblation (*homa*), and libation (*tarpaṇa*) with the *brāhma* [pavitra]; the sprinkling (*mārjana*), worship (*arcana*), offering of bali (*balikarman*), and eating (*bhojana*) with the *daiva*; rites for the ancestors (*pitrya*) with the *pitrya*; and one should accept a gift (*pratigraha*) with the *āgneya*.
In the Bhaviṣya Purāṇa: "O King of kings, a wise man should always perform the ritual touching of the water-pot and the consumption of curd at Soma-tīrtha."

In the *Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa* (34.109): A wise man should perform the offering of rice-balls (*piṇḍa*) and water for the *Nāndīmukha* ancestors using the *prājāpatya* tīrtha, as well as whatever else belongs to Prajāpati.
In the *Brahma Purāṇa*: "The *prājāpatya* great tirtha is situated between the root line, the mouth, the thumb, and the wrist; therefore, O Brahmin, one should always perform *ācamana* with it."
The Soma-tīrtha is indeed located in the middle of the lines for wealth, longevity, and wife;
there, the offering of oblations and likewise the shaving of the head should be performed.
Shaving refers to the pouring out of rice and other grains. [Chāgaleya says:
That which is in the middle of the hand is the *brahmatīrtha*, as is that used for receiving the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*).
In the continuation of the discussion on the syllable *oṃ*, Āpastamba [1.13.8–9] states:
"And at sacrifices, these and others are the *prasavas*.
The *prasavas*, such as *praṇaya*, are sentences of authorization.

And in the world, in rites for prosperity (*bhūtikarma*), there would be such sentences as these, namely: "An auspicious day! Well-being! Prosperity! In rites for prosperity, such as the taking of the hand in marriage and others, there should be such utterances beginning with *oṃ* and including words such as "well-being" (*svasti*).
[56] (From the *Mahābhārata*)
Therefore, having uttered "Om," the acts of sacrifice, charity, and austerity,
as prescribed by the rules, are constantly performed by those who discourse on Brahman.
Likewise:
"A duration of three *mātrās* should be employed in all undertakings of ritual action;
however, those who contemplate all goals should perform them with three and a half *mātrās*."
At the times of meditating upon the deity, one should perform the prolated vowel (pluta), without a doubt.
Yama states: "The recitation for the declaration of an auspicious day (puṇyāhavācana) is prescribed for a Brāhmaṇa in rites for the gods;
one should perform this very same rite without the syllable Om for Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas."
Viṣṇu [64.40]: One who has bathed becomes qualified for rites dedicated to the gods and the ancestors,
as well as for the recitation of purifiers (pavitra) and for giving according to the prescribed rule.

Of purifying mantras, such as the *pāvamānī* verses and others—according to the statement of the author of the *Nirukta*: "A mantra is called a purifier" (*mantraḥ pavitram ity ucyate*) [5.6]. In the *Vāyupurāṇa*:
"He who performs the ritual action in the fire-oblation (*homa*) should wear washed garments."
Adorned, pure, silent, and with senses subdued, one should perform the śrāddha and other rites.
Baudhāyana says:
Whatever recitations, burnt offerings, or ritual acceptances one performs while wearing saffron-colored garments—
neither those nor the sacrificial offerings for gods or ancestors reach the deities, nor does the oblation itself.
"Clad in ochre garments" means wearing clothes dyed with tree decoctions and the like.
Vyāsa states: "But he who, while wearing wet clothes, performs the undertaking of recitation (*japa*) or fire-oblations (*homa*),"
One should know all that which is performed outside the knees to be demonic.
Yogiyājñavalkya says:
A garment whose inner fold is tied outside the waistband is indeed "demonic" (āsurī);
it should be diligently avoided by the wise in all religious rites.
"Bahiḥkakṣā" means having gone outside. As stated in the Viṣṇupurāṇa (3.12.20):
"But in rites such as the fire-oblation and the worship of the gods, as well as in the ritual sipping of water (ācamana)..."
One should not engage in the recitation for Brahmins or in silent chanting while wearing only a single garment.
Regarding the recitation by Brahmins, such as the *svastivācana* (invocation of blessings) for Brahmins,
Śātātapa states:
"When the garment has slipped from the left shoulder and is held at the waist..."
One should know that he who wears but a single garment is unfit for rites for the gods or the ancestors; one should avoid him.
Śāṭyāyana says:
One should not perform giving, sipping water, fire-offerings, eating, worship of the deities, Vedic study, or libations to the ancestors while sitting with one's feet outstretched.
One who has placed his feet upon a seat, with his thighs and calves likewise [supported],
and has performed the *avasakthika* posture, is called *prauḍhapāda*.
In the Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa:
"Without the rising of the sun, rites such as ritual bathing and giving of gifts do not take place;
nor does the establishment of the sacred fire occur, and thus no sacrifice is observed."

The phrase "without the rising of the sun" indicates by the word *sūryodaya* that the time of dawn (*uṣaḥkāla*) is meant. The intended meaning is that rites such as bathing and giving gifts should not be performed at night, apart from that [dawn]. Dakṣa says: "Rites for the gods should be performed in the forenoon, but those for humans in the midday."
And it is the settled rule that the rites for the ancestors should be performed in the afternoon.
Kātyāyana in the *Chandogapariśiṣṭa* [1.1.6–8]:
"In cases where an action is prescribed but the specific limb of the performer is not mentioned,
the right hand should be understood as the one that brings the ritual acts to completion."

[59] Where no restriction of direction exists for rites such as recitation (japa) and fire-oblation (homa), three directions are to be known there: namely, the eastern (aindrī), the northern (saumyā), and the unconquered (aparājitā).
Whether sitting, standing, or bowing, where no such rule is specified,
that [rite] should be performed while sitting, and not while bowing or standing.
The north is auspicious, the northeast is invincible.
Yogi-Yājñavalkya says:
"The seer, the meter, the deity, and likewise the application."
This should be understood with diligent effort, especially by a Brahmin.
But he who performs officiating at sacrifices, teaching, as well as fire-offerings, immersion in water, and so forth, without knowing [the rules], his fruit shall be meager.
The "antarjalādi" (and so forth within the water) refers to rites such as the *aghamarṣaṇa* performed in the midst of water.
Likewise: "And he who knows according to reality the seer (*ārṣa*), the meter (*chandas*), and the deity (*daivata*)."
The application, the Brāhmaṇa, the meaning of the mantra, and the knowledge and ritual action.

Action whose nature is knowledge is "knowledge-action" (*jñānakarma*); that is to say, its purpose is the recollection of the matters to be performed. Even for each individual seer (*ṛṣi*), he should indeed be honored like a guest;
and there is no doubt that one attains union (*sāyujya*) with the deity in this regard.
Sāyujya means the state of being joined together.
[60] That twice-born one who knows the seers (ṛṣis) and so forth in the manner previously described shall possess the qualification for the secret rites and others.

In the *Rahasyas* and other such texts, regarding the secret recitations (*rahasyajapa*) and so forth: by whichever seer (*ṛṣi*) a mantra was seen and by whom its accomplishment (*siddhi*) was attained, that mantra is declared to belong to him; that is the "seer-nature" (*ārṣaka*) of the seer.
Desire is taught to be so called because it covers, like two garments over a form;
in ancient times, the Self was indeed covered by the gods out of fear of death.
By the Ādityas, Vasus, and Rudras, those very meters were indeed [established]. Of whatever mantra there is a deity specified, that belongs to its particular form— that is, its bodily configuration.
"Its divinity consists in having that form; it is called a deity.

Whichever deity of whichever mantra is designated and primarily propounded in the form of Indra or others—that very form constitutes the divinity of that mantra. The word "its" (*tasya*)—though separated by intervening words—is to be construed with "of the mantra" (*mantrasya*). By this, the following is stated: "That indeed is the deity of that particular mantra.
(Yogiyājñavalkya)
Mantras arose in ancient kalpas solely for the sake of ritual action;
that which specifies "this must be performed by means of this" is called *viniyoga*.
That in which the etymology of a mantra, its application, its purpose,
its foundation, and its praise are set forth is here called the Brāhmaṇa.

[61] *Pratiṣṭhāna* is application (*viniyoga*). Others, however, say that *pratiṣṭhāna* means the substratum (*āśraya*). As it is said in the *Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa*: "Of the verses for the leading forth of Agni and Soma, this sun is the twenty-first, the final *pratiṣṭhā*.
Likewise: "In this way, one should indeed recollect the fivefold yoga at the time of recitation."
At home, within water, during yoga, in private study, and likewise in officiating at a sacrifice.

*Yoga* refers to the connection with the *ṛṣis* and other [components of mantras]. *Antarjale* means within water, such as during bathing and similar rites; *yoge* means during yoga practices such as the recitation (*japa*) of the *praṇava*, which is a limb of yoga. Kātyāyana states in the *Chandogapariśiṣṭa*:
"One should always wear the sacred thread (*upavīta*) and always have one's topknot tied."
Whatever one does without the sacred thread or without the upper garment is as if not done at all.
Āpastamba [1.15.1]:

"In the presence of gurus, elders, and guests; during the performance of the *homa* and *ijyā* rites; while eating; while sipping water (*ācamana*); and while reciting the Veda (*svādhyāya*), one should wear the sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*).
[Nigama-Parishiṣṭa].

Wearing the sacrificial cord over the left shoulder (*yajñopavītin*) is for rites dedicated to the gods; worn otherwise, with the right shoulder over the left (*prācīnāvīta*), it is for the sacrifice to the ancestors (*pitṛyajña*). For malevolent magic (*abhicāra*), it is suspended from the navel with two loops around the neck (*dvikaṇṭhāvasakta*); for common worldly acts (*grāmyadharma*), it is worn as a *nivīta*, hanging down from the back.
Otherwise, it is on the right shoulder. "Suspended with two loops" means hanging from both sides of the neck. [62] Baudhāyana [1.8.5–8].

Having placed the sacrificial cord over the right arm down to the navel, one should cover the head; for the ancestors, it is the reverse. When suspended from the neck, it is *nivīta*; when suspended below [the arms], it is *adhovīta*.
Thus say Manu, Baudhāyana, and Paiṭhīnasi.
[One should also wear it] in the fire-sanctuary, in a cow-pen, and in the presence of Brāhmaṇas.
During Vedic recitation and while eating, one should indeed raise the right hand.

Āpastamba says: [One should not speak harshly] in a temple, likewise at a śrāddha, in a cow-pen, at a sacrifice, during a gift-giving, while performing the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), at the two twilights (saṃdhyā), and in the company of virtuous men.
In the fire-sanctuary, at a wedding, during Vedic study, and likewise while eating—
one should raise the right hand for Brahmins on the path of compassion.
"One should lift the right hand" means that having placed the cloth over the left shoulder, one should bring the right arm out from under the upper garment (*uttarīya*). Baudhāyana [1.10.18] states:
"One engaged in ritual action should avoid touching anything below the navel."

Yogiyājñavalkya states: "Having recited the *vyāhṛtis* and touched oneself after reciting mantras dedicated to Rudra, the ancestors, or the Asuras, as well as those intended for malevolent sorcery, one should touch water and perform other rites."
Kātyāyana in the *Chandogapariśiṣṭa* [1.2.13–14]:
In the recitation of mantras dedicated to the ancestors (*pitrya*), in touching oneself, in looking [at something impure],
in the emission of downward wind (flatus), in loud laughter, and in speaking untruths;
Upon touching a cat or a mouse, when reviled, when anger arises,
and on all such occasions, one performing ritual acts should touch water.

In the recitation of ancestral mantras (*pitryamantra*), that is, in the utterance of mantras dedicated to the ancestors; in the touching of oneself (*ātmālambha*), which is the prescribed touching of the heart as the seat of the self at the beginning of a sacrifice and similar rites; in the gazing (*avekṣaṇa*) at that very same [heart], both of these being prescribed at the start of a sacrifice and so forth; and in being reviled (*ākruṣṭa*), that is, in the speaking of harsh words—[these occasions require expiation]. Yogi-Yājñavalkya says: "If, in any way whatsoever, there should be a lapse of vocal restraint during recitations (*japa*) and other such acts..."
One should either recite a Vaiṣṇava mantra or remember the imperishable Viṣṇu.
Likewise: "If, through ignorance or delusion, one should falter during the sacrificial rites, that [defect] becomes complete simply by the remembrance of Viṣṇu; such is the Vedic revelation. [64]
Out of delusion— that is, from erroneous cognition—
one should not cause pain to anyone by means of action, mind, or speech.
But while performing the consecration and practicing other rites, one should act accordingly.
Baudhāyana [1.3.40]:

Eating, offering oblations, giving, presenting offerings, and receiving gifts—these acts should not be performed with the knees outside; the same is prescribed for the ritual sipping of water (ācamana).
*Upahāra* is the offering of food and other items for the sake of deities and others. Aṅgiras states:
"At both twilights, during the recitation of prayers, while eating, and while cleansing the teeth..."
In rites for the ancestors and in rites for the gods, as well as when voiding urine or excrement.
By maintaining silence especially when giving gifts or practicing yoga in the presence of gurus, a human being attains heaven.
In the Vāyu Purāṇa:
"Giving, receiving, burnt offerings, eating, and even the offering of oblations—these must always be performed with the thumb; otherwise, they belong to the Asuras."

"With the thumb together with the fingers" means with the thumb joined to the fingers. These very same acts, such as giving gifts and so forth, should especially be performed with the hands between the knees; O King, the same applies specifically to the ritual sipping of water (ācamana).
[65] The meaning is that one should act so that the two arms are positioned between the knees, with the hands within the space of the knees.
Kātyāyana states in the *Chandogapariśiṣṭa* [1.2.2; 2.1.2–3]:
"Green *darbha* grasses are for sacrifices; yellow ones are for the five great sacrifices."
Those with roots are for the ancestors; those that are speckled are for the Viśvedevas.

Having placed *kuśa* grass in his left hand, he should perform the act of sipping water (*ācamana*). The *kuśas* used for ritual practice should be short, while those for the sacrificial strewing (*barhis*) should be long.

It is stated that *darbha* grass is the purifier (*pavitra*); therefore, in rites such as the twilight prayers (*saṃdhyā*), the left hand should be provided with water-vessels (*upagraha*), and the right hand should be equipped with the purifier (*sapavitraka*).

Those [vessels] which are to be employed—meaning those used for the performance (*anuṣṭhāna*) and having become the instruments thereof, existing in their respective states, and assigned to these specific tasks—in rites such as the twilight prayers, the mere *darbha* grass constitutes the purifier.
For it is said:

"A purifier (pavitra) made of kuśa grass, containing an infinite number of blades within, complete with its tip, consisting of two blades, and measuring one span (prādeśa), is to be known as required in any rite whatsoever. [1.2.10–12]
For this indeed is declared to be the characteristic of the *puñjūlī*;
that which is for the purpose of purifying the clarified butter (*ājya*) is likewise exactly of this same measure.
[66] Some declare that this very measure is a bundle (*puñjūlī*) consisting of a single *kauśī* stalk— either fresh with its flower-cluster, or dried and withered blossoms.
Kātyāyana states in the Gṛhyapariśiṣṭa:
"Darbha grass, the black antelope skin, the mantras, Brāhmaṇas, the sacrificial oblation, and the fires—
these are not exhausted by use and may be employed again and again."
"Unworn" means new; by this, its fitness for ritual action is indicated.
[Marīci]:
"And those balls of rice upon which Darbha grass was spread, and with which the libation to the ancestors was performed..."
For those who persist in impurity and uncleanness, their abandonment is prescribed.
Marīci says: On the new moon day of the month of Nabhasya, a heap of darbha grass is prescribed;
those darbha blades, being of undiminished potency, may be employed again and again.

[67] Laghuhārīta: One should avoid six types of *kuśa* grass: those used for the funeral pyre (*citidarbha*), those used for the husband’s rites (*patidarbha*), and those used on sacrificial grounds (*yajñabhūmi*) for spreading, as seats, or for the rice-balls (*piṇḍa*).
Those Darbha grasses that have been spread for the sake of the funeral rice-ball (piṇḍa), those by which the libation to the ancestors has been performed,
and those used for urine or food remnants— their disposal is prescribed.
[Some, however, say:

"Those darbha blades which are placed within the waist-knot (nīvī) and those which are made into the sacred thread (brahmasūtra)—one should know them to be purifiers; as are the bodies, so are the kuśa grasses."
The *nīvī* is the knot of the lower garment.
[Laghuhārīta]:
Having sipped water, the best of the twice-born, being constantly pure, [should perform his rites] with a purifier (*pavitra*).
One should not become impure by food remnants there; one must avoid what remains after eating.
During recitation, burnt offerings, giving, Vedic study, and the libations to the ancestors,
one should ensure that the hand is never empty, using gold, silver, or *kuśa* grass.
A twilight devotion performed without darbha grass, a gift given without water,
and that which is recited without counting— all that is entirely useless.
Kātyāyana in the *Chandogapariśiṣṭa* [1.8.17–18]:
"The sacrificial fuel stick (*samidh*) should never be thicker than the thumb;
it must not be stripped of its bark, nor infested with insects, nor split."
[68] A *viśākhikā* blade should not be longer than a span (*prādeśa*), nor shorter;
it should not have leaves, nor be devoid of potency, by one who is knowledgeable regarding the fire-oblations (*homa*).
The *viśākhikā* is that which possesses various branches;
this is stated in the *Brahmapurāṇa* following the word "fuel-stick" (*samidh*):
"Those produced from the *pālāśa*, *aśvattha*, *nyagrodha*, *plakṣa*, and *vaikaṅkata* [trees]."
The Aśvattha, Udumbara, Bilva, Candana, and likewise the Sarala;
The *śāla*, the *devadāru*, and the *khadira* are [trees] fit for sacrifice;
the *vaikaṅkata* is the tree for the *śruva* ladle; and the *marīci*.

The fuel-sticks should be offered with their tips pointing eastward, and in rites for specific desires they should be unsplit; in rites for specific desires they should also be fresh and leafy, whereas for one wishing to harm, they should be the opposite.
Those that are shattered, split, short, crooked, hollow,
thin, long, thick, or infested by woodworms cause the destruction of the success of one's undertakings.
Kātyāyana in the Chandogapariśiṣṭa [ii, p. 33] states:
"When the prescribed substance is unavailable, that which resembles it should be accepted;
just as wheat is a substitute for barley, and rice for paddy."
Of rice grains, specifically the *ṣaṣṭika* variety [as stated in 1.7.16].
Clarified butter (*ājya*) is prescribed as the substance for oblations (*juhoti*) when no other material is specified.
[69] It is established that Prajāpati is the deity of the mantra.

"In the absence of instruction" means in the absence of a specific mention; "of the mantra and the deity" is to be supplied as the ellipsis. Prajāpati is the deity, because all the *vyāhṛtis* together belong to Prajāpati. Paiṭhīnasi states:

"One should provide a substitute based on similarity in respect of stalks, roots, leaves, flowers, fruits, shoots, juices, scents, and so forth. In the event that none of these are available, barley becomes the substitute."
*Kāṇḍa* means stalk; *praroha* means sprout.
From the *Maitrāyaṇīyapariśiṣṭa*:
"In the event that a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) is to be obtained, one may give roots, fruits, or edible items as the fee; however, one should not perform the sacrifice in this manner."
Likewise:

in the absence of *darbha* grass, *kāśa* grass serves as a substitute; if that is unavailable, they perform the act of spreading with herbs that have joints and stalks—excluding *kaṭa*, *uśīra*, *śuṇṭhana*, *balvaja*, *palāla*, and *ulapa*. "With those having joints" means with those possessing knots. *Kaṭa* and the others are specific types of grasses.

[70] Now, for the purpose of sacrificial fuel (*idhma*), one should use wood from the *pālāśa*, *aśvattha*, *khadira*, *rohitaka*, or *udumbara* trees; in their absence, from any forest tree (*vanaspati*), with the exception of the *tilvaka*, *dhava*, *nīpa*, *nimba*, *rājavṛkṣa*, *śālmali*, *bandha*, *kapittha*, *kovidāra*, *vibhītaka*, *śleṣmātaka*, and all thorny trees.
The *tilvaka* is commonly known as *cillaka*; the *nīpa* is the *kadamba*; the *rājavṛkṣa* is commonly known as *kiravāla*; and the *śleṣmātaka* is the *bahuvāraka*.

Rice and barley are for the purpose of the *puroḍāśa* cakes. If these are unavailable, they prepare the *puroḍāśas* from herbs that possess husks and grains, with the exception of *aṇu*, *cīnaka*, *kalmāṣaka*, *kuravaka*, *māṣa*, *masūraka*, *kodrava*, and *koradūṣaka*. These are used for the *puroḍāśas*. *Aṇu* refers to the *markaṭaka* grain; *kuravaka* is the yellow *kulattha*; *koradūṣaka* is wild *kodrava*. Ghee is the substitute for clarified butter (*ājya*); if that is unavailable, curd or milk may be used. They prepare the substances for clarified butter by mixing rice flour or barley flour with water.
In the Vāyu Purāṇa: "The threshing, the grinding, and likewise the scraping should always be performed only once for the ancestors (pitṛs), while for the gods (devas) it is said to be three times."
[71] For *ullekhana* is the act of drawing lines by means of not turning away from them.
Yajñapārśva says:
"For the sake of the ancestors, one should offer on the ground or upon the sun [i.e., a mirror], provided with *darbha* grass."
Yajñapārśva says:
At all [sacrifices] beginning with the Garbhādhāna, one should feed ten Brāhmaṇas;
at the Āvasathya, twenty-three; and at the Agnyādheya, more than ten.
In the Āgrayaṇa sacrifice, as an expiation, one should feed fifteen Brahmins;
in the Soma sacrifice, one thousand; and in the Paśu sacrifice, one hundred Brahmins.
In the Cāturmāsya sacrifice there are four, and likewise five in the Surāgraha;
ten thousand in the Vājapeya, and four times that in the Aśvamedha.
The connection is with "four hundred.
Kātyāyana states in the *Chandopariśiṣṭa* (1.9.11–15):
"An offering made with the hand consists of filling [the vessel] twelve times."
The man who offers oblations into a fire that has no flames or whose embers are extinguished is born with weak digestion, prone to disease, and impoverished.
[72] Therefore, one should offer oblations only when the fire is well-kindled, and never when it is not kindled; that is, when it is without embers or when the embers have vanished—
by one desiring health, long life, and likewise ultimate prosperity.

Whether intending to offer an oblation or while the oblation is being offered, one should not blow upon the fire with the hand, a winnowing basket, a wooden sword, or a piece of wood; nor should one do so with a fan or similar objects.
"One should blow upon the fire with the mouth alone, for it was born from the mouth";
as for the statement "not with the mouth," that applies to the case of ordinary fire.
Desiring to offer, wishing to sacrifice.
Now, regarding the sacraments (saṃskāra),
Manu says here [2.26]: "For the twice-born, the rites beginning with conception (niṣeka) are performed through meritorious Vedic rituals."
The purifying refinement of the body should be performed, for it leads to sanctification both in this world and after death.

By means of meritorious acts prescribed in the Vedas, such as touching [the body] and so forth—which produce excellence—the refinement (*saṃskāra*) of the body occurs; here, the word "body" (*śarīra*) functions through *ajahatsvārthalakṣaṇā* (non-abandonment of its own primary meaning) to refer also to its cause. It is purifying (*pāvana*), meaning it destroys sin.
Yājñavalkya [1.10]:
"The Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras are the castes (*varṇa*); however, the first three are twice-born (*dvija*)."
For them, indeed, the rites beginning with conception and ending at the cremation ground are performed with mantras.

One who is born twice is a *dvija*. The second birth is the initiation (*upanayana*). [This includes] all rites ending with the cremation ground and their associated rituals. Regarding the continuation of the purificatory rites preceded by initiation, Yama states: "Even a Śūdra should be treated in this same manner, provided he is consecrated without the recitation of mantras."
Prajāpati did not combine him with any Vedic meter.
[74] Regarding the phrase "without a mantra," the reason is given as "by no one" and so forth. *Chandas* means the Veda. *Samasṛjat* means he brought about a connection or produced a union.
In the *Brahma Purāṇa*:
"Even a Śūdra should always receive the sacrament of marriage alone."

By the phrase "marriage alone," the ritual procedure for marriage is established. The word "alone" (mātra), however, serves to exclude other sacramental rites (*saṃskāra*) that have not been specifically prescribed. Because they lack knowledge of the Vedas, these rites are performed without mantras, and thus the worship of deities is excluded.
Yājñavalkya [1.13] states:
"These rites for women are silent; however, their marriage is accompanied by mantras."
Aṅgiras said:
Just as a painting is gradually brought to completion by means of many parts,
so too does the status of a Brahmin arise through consecrations performed according to the prescribed rules.
Manu [2.27]: By means of oblations for the fetus, the birth-rites, the tonsure, and the tying of the girdle of muñja grass,
the taint born of seed and the taint born of the womb are wiped away from the twice-born.
[75] That which arises from semen is *baijika*; that which arises from the womb, the uterus, or the hips is *gārbhika*. Impurity (*enaḥ*) is the state of being unclean. Thus says Hārīta.

Endowed with the rite of conception (*garbhādāna*), he establishes the *brahman*-womb; by the rite of male-conception (*puṃsavana*), he makes [the child] male; by the rite of bathing after pregnancy (*phalasnāna*), he dispels the evil derived from the mother and father. The injury to a womb arising from the semen of a Brahmin is fivefold in its gravity. By the birth-rite (*jātakarman*), he first dispels it; by the naming-rite (*nāmakaraṇa*), the second; by the first feeding (*prāśana*), the third; by the tonsure-rite (*cūḍākaraṇa*), the fourth; and by the initiation bath (*snāna*), the fifth. Through these eight purificatory rites for the womb (*garbhasaṃskāra*) and through the eight vows (*vrata*) beginning with the sacred thread ceremony (*upanayana*), one becomes purified from the injury to the womb. Those Brahmins who are measured by their mastery of the Vedic meters (*chandas*) become the supreme vessels for the gods and ancestors; they are indeed the abode of the meters.

“Like the *garbhādhāna*”: by means of the *garbhādhāna* rite, beginning with the mantra “May Viṣṇu prepare the womb” (*viṣṇur yoniṃ kalpayatu*). “Having approached a woman” (*upetaḥ*): having gone to a woman. “He conceives the embryo of Brahman” (*brahmagarbhaṃ saṃdadhāti*): Brahman is the Veda; he conceives—that is, he generates—an embryo fit for the reception of that [Veda]. “He makes it male” (*puṃsīkaroti*): he makes the embryo, whose gender was indistinct, into a male, based on the wording of the mantra: “May you find a son who is a male. “From the fruit-bath” (*phalasnapanāt*): from the *sīmantonnayana*, which has the fruit-bath as its ancillary part. “Born of mother and father” (*mātāpitṛjam*): produced through the medium of the mother and father. For one situated in the womb, the consecration of the offspring occurs through the consecration of the substratum (the parents). “Affliction” (*upaghātaḥ*) refers to a collection of sins. “Fivefold” (*pañcaguṇaḥ*): of five types. Jayasvāmin explains: “It is the transference of the fivefold sins consisting of minor offenses (*upapātaka*), those causing loss of caste (*jātibhraṃśakara*), those causing mixture of castes (*saṃkaraṇa*), those rendering one unworthy of receiving gifts (*apātrīkaraṇa*), and those making one impure (*malinīkaraṇa*). And here, “bath” (*snānam*) refers to the *samāvartana*. “The eight observances” (*vratacaryāḥ*) are the *mekhalā* and so forth, beginning with the initiation (*upanayana*), which will be described under the section on the “one whose semen flows upward” (*ūrdhvaretas*). “Internal observances” (*antarvratāni*) are the *Sāvitrī*, *Godāna*, *Kādityavrata*, *Aupaniṣada*, *Aṣṭakāmāsika*, *Mahānāmnī*, and *Mahāvrata*. “In accordance with their own will” (*svacchandasaṃmitāḥ*): conjoined with their own respective Vedas.

[76] Sumantu: For Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas, the rites of conception (garbhādhāna), parting the hair (sīmantonnayana), birth-rite (jātakarma), naming (nāmakaraṇa), first feeding of solid food (annaprāśana), tonsure (cūḍā), initiation (upanayana), observance of vows (vratacaryā), study (adhyayana), return home (samāvartana), marriage (vivāha), sacrifice (yajña), and so forth, are common to all.
Gautama [8.13–19].

The forty sacraments (*saṃskāra*) are as follows: conception (*garbhādhāna*), the rite for ensuring a male child (*puṃsavana*), the parting of the hair (*sīmantonnayana*), the birth ceremony (*jātakarman*), the naming ceremony (*nāmakaraṇa*), the first feeding of solid food (*annaprāśana*), the tonsure (*caula*), and the initiation (*upanayana*); the four vows of Vedic study (*vedavrata*); the ceremonial bath (*snāna*); union with a lawful wife (*sahadharmacāriṇī-saṃyoga*); the performance of the five sacrifices (*pañca-yajña*) to the gods, ancestors, humans, spirits, and Brahman; the eight offerings (*aṣṭakā*), the *pārvaṇa* sacrifice, the *śrāddha*, and the seasonal sacrifices of the full moon in the months of Śrāvaṇa, Agrahāyaṇī, Caitrī, and Āśvayujī—these constitute the forms of the cooked-sacrifice (*pākayajña*). The establishment of the sacred fires (*agnyādheya*), the fire-oblation (*agnihotra*), the new and full moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*), the first-fruits offering (*āgrayaṇa*), the four-monthly sacrifices (*cāturmāsya*), the independent animal sacrifice (*nirūḍhapaśubandha*), and the Sautrāmaṇī—these are the seven forms of the oblation-sacrifice (*haviryajña*). [The Agniṣṭoma, Atyagniṣṭoma, Ukthya, Ṣoḍaśī, Vājapeya, Atirātra, and Aptoryāma—these are the seven forms of the Soma-sacrifice. These are the forty sacraments.

The four Vedic vows (*vedavrata*) are prescribed for each Veda: the ritual bath (*snāna*), which is the return home (*samāvartana*); and the union with a partner who shares the same dharma, which is marriage (*vivāha*). The word "and these" connects these with the rites to be described hereafter, such as the *aṣṭakā*s and others.

Hārīta states: "Sanskara (purificatory rite) is indeed of two kinds: Brāhma and Daiva. That beginning with *garbhādhāna* and ending with the ritual bath (*snāna*) is Brāhma; the *pākayajñas*, *haviryajñas*, and *saumyas* constitute the Daiva."

One who is consecrated by the *brāhma* sacraments attains equality, residence in the same world (*salokatā*), and union (*sāyojyatā*) with the sages. One who is consecrated by the higher, divine sacraments attains equality, residence in the same world, and union with the gods.

The *saumya* rites are the Soma sacrifices, such as the *agniṣṭoma* and others. "Equality" means being equal; by this, similarity is expressed. "Union" (*sāyojyatā*): one whose body (*āyojya*) is the same is "united" (*sāyojya*). Manu [2.28]:
Through the private recitation of the Vedas, through vows, through burnt offerings, through the study of the three Vedas, through sacrifices, through sons,
and through the great sacrifices and other rites, this body is made fit for Brahman.

By *svādhyāya*, that is, by the acquisition of the Vedas; by *vratas*, such as the *sāvitrī* and others; by *traividyā*, that is, by knowledge of the meaning of the three Vedas; and by *ijyā*, that is, by the worship of the gods and other deities—[one attains] the *brāhmī* [power], which pertains to Brahman through the gateway of its knowledge. [78] Śaṅkha and Likhita state:
"The *pākayajñas*, the *haviryajñas*, and likewise the *somasaṃsthās*..."
For all conditioned phenomena end with the Agnihotra sacrifice, yet for one who is actually offering the Agnihotra—
Refined by prior purificatory rites and further refined by subsequent ones,
the Brāhmaṇa who belongs to the world of Brahman is eternally endowed with the eight qualities.
One who performs the triple sacrifice attains the state of Brahmā from which he does not fall again; he reaches the vault of heaven, glory, dharma, and the triple celestial realm.

For the *agnihotrin*, even without performing the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices, the performance of the *agnihotra* is prescribed; for him, there are the purificatory rites (*saṃskāras*) culminating in the *agnihotra*. These include the rites beginning with conception (*garbhādāna*) and preceded by the birth-rite (*jātakarma*), as well as the subsequent rites such as the establishment of the sacred fires (*agnyādheya*). He is endowed with the eight qualities beginning with compassion (*dayā*). He is "belonging to the world of Brahmā" (*brāhmalaukika*), meaning he is worthy of the world of Brahmā. "The back of the sky" (*nākapṛṣṭha*) refers to the summit of Mount Meru. "Triviṣṭapa" is the world of the gods. "Having sacrificed thrice" means by means of the *pākayajña*, the *havis-yajña*, and the *soma-saṃsthā* sacrifices. Mādhavasvāmī explains: "having performed the Soma sacrifice three times. He is wise (*budha*).

The rites of conception (*garbhādhāna*), the rite for a male child (*puṃsavana*), the parting of the hair (*sīmantonnayana*), the consecration of the lying-in chamber (*sūtikāgṛhasaṃskāra*), and the rite for a woman about to give birth (*soṣyantīkarma*).
The *soṣyantīkarma* is prescribed by Gobhila and others for the purpose of ensuring a swift delivery.
Yājñavalkya [1.11–12]:

The rite of conception (*garbhādhāna*) occurs during the fertile period; the rite for ensuring a male child (*pumsavana*) takes place before the fetus moves; the parting of the hair (*sīmantonnayana*) is performed in the sixth or eighth month; and these, along with the birth-rite (*jātakarman*), are performed at the time of delivery.

On the eleventh day the naming ceremony is performed; in the fourth month, the first outing; in the sixth month, the first feeding of solid food; and in the first year, the tonsure ceremony should be carried out according to family custom.
"Āite" means "having come," that is, when the son has been born;
[as stated] in the Gobhila Gṛhyasūtra [2.5.8–10]:

"When she has reached her season and the menstrual flow has ceased, that is the time for union. With his right hand he should touch her lap with the verse, 'May Viṣṇu prepare the womb,' and having concluded with the two verses beginning 'Conceive a fetus, O Śinīvālī,' they unite."
Having completed the two *ṛc* verses, they perform the union.
Baudhāyana says:
"One should procreate offspring by means of the application of medicinal mantras."

[80] Pāraskara [1.13.1]: If she does not conceive, one should fast on the day of the *puṣya* asterism and, having dug up the root of a white-flowered *siṃhī* (thorn-apple), pound it with water on the night of her fourth-day bath and pour it into her right nostril with the mantra beginning "This plant, the protecting one... (*iyam oṣadhī trāyamāṇā*).
*Siṃhī* is the thorn-apple (*kaṇṭakārikā*). The husband is the agent for both the fasting and the digging of the root.

Vaijavāpa says: If she has not yet established the sacred fires, she should fast for a lioness with white flowers; then, under the asterism Puṣya, having extracted the root, on the fourth day when she has bathed, she should cook a *sthālīpāka* sacrifice dedicated to Prajāpati at night. Having offered it to Prajāpati, she should have her lie down behind the fire on a hero’s bed, facing east and with her face upward. She should then grind the herb with water using the two *catu* verses and administer it as a nasal drop (*nastaḥ*) into her right nostril, saying: "This herb, the protecting one."
“A hero’s bed” refers to the ground that has not been covered over. Having laid him down means having caused him to lie. With two millstones. Into the nose means into the nostrils.
[81] Now follows the rite for securing the conception of a male child (*garbhāvalobhana*).
The *Āśvalāyanagṛhyapariśiṣṭa*:

Having ground unbroken *kapila* [seeds], one should pour them into the nostrils from the right side at the time of menstruation with the two verses beginning "Arise, O woman, you have a husband," ending with the utterance of *svāhā*.
*Akhaṇḍākapila* refers to the *kacchu* plant.
Now follows the *puṃsavana* (the rite for ensuring a male child) and the *anavalobhana* (the rite for preventing miscarriage).
Regarding this, the *Āśvalāyanagṛhya-sūtra* states [1.13.1–7]:

In the *Upaniṣad* [are described] the *garbhalambhana*, the *puṃsavana*, and the *anavalobhana*. If one does not study [this section], then in the third month of pregnancy, under the asterism Tiṣya, she who has fasted should eat two beans, a barley grain, and a drop of curds from a cow that has a calf of the same color, using her cupped hand. Having been asked, "What are you drinking? What are you drinking?", she should respond three times, "The male-making [rite], the male-making [rite]. She should do this with three such handfuls. Then, in the shadow of a round house, she causes an unblighted herb to be administered through her right nostril. Some do this with the two [verses] beginning "Possessing offspring" (*prajāvat*) and "Having living sons" (*jīvaputra*). [The verses are: "May your embryo enter the womb, a male like an arrow into a quiver; may a heroic son be born to you, ten months old. May Agni, the first of the gods, come; may he release her offspring from the noose of death. May King Varuṇa grant his consent to this, so that this woman shall not weep over the calamity of losing a grandson. Having offered an oblation of a *sthālīpāka* dedicated to Prajāpati, he should touch her heart region, saying: "What is placed within your heart, O fair-browed one, within Prajāpati—knowing that, I consider myself wise; may I not suffer the calamity of losing a grandson."

"In the *upaniṣad*," that is, in the portion of the Veda designated as the *upaniṣad*, it is traditionally taught—"the *garbhalambhana*, the *puṃsavana*, and the *anavalobhana*"; this is the ellipsis to be supplied. It is called *puṃsavana* because by this rite a male (*pumān*) is brought forth. *Anavalobhana* means non-seizing, that is to say, protection. "When he should not study"—that is, when one does not recite the *upaniṣads*—then the rites beginning with [the one performed] under the asterism Tiṣya must be performed; such is the meaning. Now, regarding the phrase "for her" (*asyai*), it refers to the *anavalobhana* rite for her. The dative case in *asyai* is used in the sense of the genitive due to Vedic usage. "The shadow of the circular house" refers to the shadow of a house shaped like a circle. *Ajītā* is white *dūrvā* grass. The mantra beginning with "May your embryo... (*ā te garbha*) is the "mantra for possessing progeny. The mantra beginning with "May Agni come first... (*agnir aitu prathama*) is the "mantra for having living sons."
It is stated in the Āśvalāyana-Gṛhyapariśiṣṭa:
"In the third month is the Puṃsavana rite; in the fourth, the Garbharakṣaṇa.
[Sāṃkhyāyana-Gṛhya 1.20.1–2]
In the third month, the *puṃsavana* rite is performed under the asterism Tiṣya or Śravaṇa;
likewise,
in the fourth month, the protection of the embryo is performed.
The Baijavāpa-gṛhya:

there he performs the Puṃsavana and Anavalobhana rites in the second month, before the fetus moves, during the waxing fortnight on an auspicious day, on a day when the moon is conjoined with a masculine lunar mansion.
Now, regarding the parting of the hair (*sīmantonnayana*):
on this point, Śaṅkha and Likhita state,
"The parting of the hair takes place upon the first movement of the fetus, or until delivery."

The Baijavāpa Gṛhya-sūtra: Now follows the parting of the hair (*sīmantonnayana*), to be performed in the fourth, fifth, or sixth month [of pregnancy], during the waxing fortnight, when the moon is conjoined with a male asterism. Pāraskara [1.15.1–3].
Now follows the parting of the hair (*sīmantonnayana*), which is performed like the rite for ensuring a male child (*puṃsavana*) during the first pregnancy, in the sixth or eighth month.
According to the *Śāṅkhāyanagṛhya* [1.22.1, 6]:

"In the seventh month, during the first pregnancy, the parting of the hair is performed. Likewise, the implements should be masculine, or the lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*) should be masculine; thus it is called *puṃsavana*."

The Āśvalāyana Gṛhyapariśiṣṭa: The parting of the hair (*sīmantonnayana*) takes place during the first pregnancy. Regarding this, there is a Vedic revelation (*śruti*): "The sacrament of the parting of the hair is a sacrament for both the fetus and the vessel.
[84] This refers to the fetus and the vessel; the term *gārbhapātra* means the fetus situated within the womb and the vessel—that is, the woman—who serves as its support.
Hārīta says: "The wives of the twice-born, having been consecrated once by the *sīmantonnayana* rite,
shall have every fetus they give birth to as consecrated."
Devala says: A woman who has been consecrated once is considered consecrated for all subsequent pregnancies.
Now follows the ritual for one about to give birth.

In that regard, Gobhila’s Gṛhyasūtra [1.7.13–14] states: "Now follows the *soṣyantī-homa* (the oblation for one about to give birth). When the fetus has become established, having strewn grass around the fire, he offers oblations of clarified butter with this verse, ‘She who lies across...’, and with ‘The wise one brought forth the tail. "When the fetus has become established" means when it has reached the region of the womb. Once the embryo is situated there, the *soṣyantī-homa* must be performed.
In that regard, Soma says:
"The rite for the birth (jātakarma), the secret naming (guhyānāmakaraṇa), and the consecration of the lying-in chamber (sūtikāgṛhasaṃskāra) ending with the delivery.

This is the meaning: having performed the consecration of the lying-in chamber, the rite for the birth—which constitutes the conclusion of the delivery—should be performed. Here, by the word "end" (anta), the rite connected to that conclusion is indicated.

[85] *Sāṃkhyāyanagṛhya* [1.23.1]: Having ground the roots of *kākādanī*, *mecakarātanī*, *kośātakī*, *bṛhatī*, and *kākātaka*, one should smear the place where [the child] is to be born, for the purpose of warding off the *rakṣases*. Here, *kākādanī* is the *kākajaṅghā*; *mecakarātanī* is the *kākamācikā*; *kośātakī* is the *ghoṣaka*; [and *bṛhatī* is the *kaṇṭakārikā*; *kākātaka* is the black *guñjā*].
In the *Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa*:
"And likewise in a lying-in chamber that is devoid of fire and water, lacking a sacrificial post,
without a lamp, a weapon, or a pestle, and bereft of *bhūti* ashes and mustard seeds."
O twice-born one, having entered [the womb] and carried away the child born from her own self, she who gives birth for only a moment abandons the infant right there.
She is named Jātahāriṇī, a most terrible flesh-eater;
therefore, one must take great care to protect [the child] in the lying-in chamber.
The sacrificial post (*yūpa*) here refers to a specific type of wood having the shape of a post. Now, regarding the birth-rite (*jātakarma*), Hārīta says:

When a son is born, because of the joy of the ancestors, that day is meritorious; therefore, having invited Brahmins, one should offer *svadhā* to the ancestors and to Prajāpati with vessels full of sesame seeds and containing gold. Before the cutting of the umbilical cord, they perform rites for the sake of purification and merit; once it is cut, impurity begins.

In the *vṛddhi-śrāddha* prescribed by such statements as “at the birth-rite (*jātakarman*) for children,” there is a rule regarding the substance of a golden vessel. Because the word *svadhā* brings to mind the *śrāddha*, one should offer a vessel of sesame seeds along with gold to Prajāpati. The *saṃskāra* is the birth-rite (*jātakarman*). [One should perform] acts such as giving, which have merit as their purpose—that is, those whose aim is merit.
In the *Brahmapurāṇa*: “When a son is born to twice-born men, both the gods and the ancestors [are honored].”
Therefore, that day is meritorious and always worthy of worship.
Therein one should give gold, land, a cow, and likewise a horse;
as well as an umbrella, a goat, a garland, a bed, a seat, and a house.

When a *śrāddha* has been performed, one should not offer cooked food even to Brahmins. Baijavāpa says: "When a son is born, having churned fire from the two kindling woods (*araṇi*), he offers oblations for long life (*āyuṣya-homa*) in that fire. In that same fire, the rites of tonsure (*cūḍākaraṇa*), initiation (*upanayana*), instruction in the vows (*vratādeśa*), and the parting of the hair (*godāna*) are performed; in that same fire, they should marry him off."
In that domestic fire (śālāgni),
Manu says: "The birth-rite (jātakarma) for a male child is prescribed to be performed before the cutting of the umbilical cord."
And there is the ritual consumption for him of gold, honey, and clarified butter, accompanied by mantras.
Vardhana is cutting.
Śaṅkha and Likhita state:

Upon birth, the *jātakarman* rite is performed; there is the consumption of barley flour, honey, and clarified butter accompanied by mantras. For a Brāhmaṇa, one performs this by means of the ring finger with a piece of gold placed between [the finger and the child's mouth], thereby increasing his intelligence. The same applies to the other two [castes].
This [rite] produces superior intelligence. For the other two—the Kṣatriya and the Vaiśya—it is as follows: the ring finger is the finger adjacent to the little finger.
According to the *Āśvalāyanagṛhya*:
"Before the newborn boy is touched by others, one should have him eat clarified butter and honey mixed with the scrapings of gold, using a piece of gold."
Before being touched by others—that is, before being touched by anyone other than those attending the birth—according to the *Baijavāpa-gṛhya*:

here, while the umbilical cord of the newborn boy is still uncut, one should cause him to sip water mixed with gold; then, with various mantras, one causes him to eat curd, honey, and ghee with gold, saying: "O Earth, I place thee within him."
Pāraskara [1.16.3–4]:

For the newborn boy, while the umbilical cord is still uncut, one performs the rites for the production of intelligence and long life. With the ring finger, covered with gold, he feeds him honey and clarified butter, or clarified butter alone, saying, "Bhūḥ, I place [long life] in you," and so forth.
There is also the muttering of mantras such as, "May Agni grant long life; may he be long-lived," and so on.
[88] The ritual manual of Baijavāpa.

Now he performs the rite for generating intelligence (*medhājanana*) for him. Placing [his mouth] against the right ear, he says "Vāk, vāk" three times. Then he gives him a secret name. "Placing against" means having brought it face-to-face. The "secret" name is to be known only by the mother, father, and brother.
Aṅgiras says:
The deities named Janmadās (Givers of Birth) reside in the lying-in chamber;
for the purpose of performing a sacrifice to them, purification at birth is prescribed.
On the sixth day, one should perform the night-sacrifice for the progenitors;
then follows the naming ceremony, regarding which Manu says [2.30]:
One should have his naming ceremony performed on the tenth or the twelfth day,
or on an auspicious lunar day, at a favorable moment, or under a constellation endowed with excellent qualities.

The phrase "on the tenth day" applies to those for whom purification occurs before the end of ten days. It should be on an auspicious lunar date, not on a *riktā* (void) day; at a moment endowed with favorable qualities, such as *abhijit* and others.
In the *Bhaviṣya Purāṇa*:
"O King, some desire that the naming ceremony (*nāmadheya*) take place on the tenth day."
On the twelfth day, or at night, or when another month has been completed.
Other wise men say that it should be on the eighteenth day,
or on an auspicious lunar date, at a favorable moment, or under a constellation endowed with excellent qualities.
[89] Yājñavalkya and Bṛhaspati [Yājñ 1.12; Bṛh Saṃs 58]:
On the eleventh day, the naming ceremony [is performed]. Viṣṇu [27.5].
The naming ceremony occurs at the end of the period of impurity. By this, the rule "on the tenth day" is understood to refer to cases where the impurity has already ceased.
Gobhila [2.8.8] states:
"When ten nights, a hundred nights, or a year have passed since birth, the naming ceremony is performed."
When the night has dawned and passed, Śaṅkha and Likhita state:

Having raised [the child] on the tenth day, one should perform the *piṇḍavardhana* for the ancestors, because of the scriptural teaching regarding their presence there. Having first offered an oblation to Brahmā and having obtained the permission of the ancestors, one should perform the naming ceremony (*nāmakaraṇa*) on that very day. The father, or another elder of the family, should perform it, connecting the name with the family deity or the lunar mansion. For males, the name should consist of four or two syllables, beginning and ending with a sonant consonant (*ghoṣavat*), and containing a semi-vowel (*antastha*). For females, the name should end in the vowel *ī*. When the name has been thus established, the family becomes pure.
"Having raised up the woman who has given birth"—this is the ellipsis. "He should perform the *piṇḍavardhana* Śrāddha"—this is the implied meaning. [90] Pāraskara [1.6.17.1–5]:

On the tenth day, having raised her up and having fed the Brahmins, the father performs the naming ceremony (*nāmakaraṇa*). He should give a name consisting of two or four syllables, containing a sonant letter at the beginning or end, with a semi-vowel (*antastha*) in the middle, ending in a long vowel or a nasal (*abhiniṣṭhāna*), and formed with a *kṛt* suffix, not a *taddhita* suffix. For a female child, he should give a name with a following vowel, ending in the vowel *ā*, and formed with a *taddhita* suffix.

The second, fourth, and fifth letters of each *varga*, as well as the letter *ha*, are possessed of *go* (the *u* vowel). "Internal" (*antaḥ*) means in the middle; the semi-vowels (*antasthāḥ*) are *ya*, *ra*, *la*, and *va*. "Abhiniṣṭhāna" means the final stop. "Kṛta" refers to that which ends in a *kṛt* suffix, not one ending in a *taddhita* suffix. Furthermore, for a female, the name should have an odd number of syllables, end in the vowel *ā*, or end in a *taddhita* suffix with an odd number of syllables.

It is the *gṛhya* tradition of the Baijavāpas: the father gives a name consisting of one syllable, two syllables, four syllables, or an unlimited number; likewise, for a female, it may consist of three syllables and end in the vowel *ī*.
"Immeasurable syllables" means a number exceeding the count of the syllables already mentioned. Manu [2.31] states:
"The name of a Brāhmaṇa should be auspicious; that of a Kṣatriya should be endowed with power."
That of a Vaiśya is associated with wealth, while that of a Śūdra is contemptible.

A *maṅgalya* name conveys auspiciousness, such as Lakṣmīdhara. A *balānvita* name conveys valor, such as Yudhiṣṭhira. A *dhanasaṃyukta* name is one joined with a word conveying wealth, such as Mahādhana. A *jugupsita* name is one joined with a word conveying censure, such as Naradāsa or Yama. Furthermore: "The names Śarman and Deva are for a Brahmin; Varman and Rāja are for a Kṣatriya."
A *gupta* and a *datta* slave may be employed by a Vaiśya, while a Śūdra may employ a *dāsa*.
Manu [2.32–33]: "The name of a Brāhmaṇa should end in a word denoting 'happiness' (śarman); that of a Kṣatriya should be endowed with the word 'king' (rājan);
that of a Vaiśya should be connected with 'prosperity' (puṣṭi); and that of a Śūdra should be connected with 'service' (preṣya)."
For women, [names] should be easy to pronounce, yet firm, with clear meaning, pleasing to the mind, auspicious, ending in long vowels, and containing words of benediction.

It should be endowed with prosperity, as in "Dhanapuṣṭa"; easy to utter and easy to pronounce, as in "Yaśodā" and so forth; not harsh and not terrifying; and containing a benediction, as in "Subhadrā. In the *Viṣṇupurāṇa* (3.10.9–11), it is stated:
"A name consisting of the words 'Gupta' or 'Dāsa' is indeed recommended for Vaiśyas and Śūdras."
It should not be devoid of meaning, nor should it be unpropitious, nor likewise should it be possessed of corrupt words.
One should give a name that is not inauspicious or contemptible, consisting of an even number of syllables,
neither too long nor too short, and not composed of excessively heavy syllables.
One should choose a name that is easy to pronounce and consists of flowing syllables;
it should not be inauspicious, such as those ending with the word *bhūta* (spirit) and so forth.
Now, the departure.
In that regard, the *Bhaviṣyapurāṇa* states:
"O Indra among kings, on the twelfth day, the infant's departure from the house (*niṣkramaṇa*) should be performed;
O Lord, others hold the view that it should be done in the fourth month."
"On the twelfth day" refers to an alternative according to different Vedic branches. Yama says: "Then, in the third month, the sight of the sun should be performed."
In the fourth month, the infant's first viewing of the moon should be performed.
Because their purposes are not identical, there is a conjunction of the observations of the sun and the moon. Laugākṣi says:
"In the third half-month, there is the observation of the sun."
The meaning is "in the third fortnight. Viṣṇu [27.10]:
"In the fourth month, there is the sight of the sun."

In this case as well, there is an option (*vikalpa*) due to the differences between the Vedic schools (*śākhā*). However, for these two—the observation of the moon and the sun—there is no *ābhyudayika* śrāddha. As it is stated in the *Chandogapariśiṣṭa*: "Regarding the rites for the sun and the moon, no śrāddha is prescribed for them."
The first feeding with solid food (annaprāśana) [then Yama says:
"Thereafter, the annaprāśana should be performed according to the rules in the sixth month"].
In the eighth month, whatever auspicious rite is desired by the family should be performed.

Manu states: "The first feeding with solid food (annaprāśana) should take place in the sixth month, or whatever auspicious rite is desired in the family. The phrase "or whatever" follows the sequence of time; thus, this option pertains specifically to the timing. Therefore, the meaning is this: it should be performed at that time which is desired—that is, approved—as the proper time for the first feeding of solid food within one's family.
Śaṅkha and Likhita state:
"The first feeding of solid food takes place in the first year.
Laugākṣi says:
[The first feeding of solid food (*annaprāśana*) takes place] in the sixth month, or when the teeth have emerged.
Regarding this very occasion, there are secondary results (*guṇaphala*);
on this point, Pāraskara [states] at 1.19.5–13.

At the conclusion of the consumption [of the food], having set aside all the flavors and all the food together, he should then feed him either silently or with the words "Hanta" (Come, eat), according to the Śruti: "The *hantakāra* belongs to human beings. According to the tradition of Bhāradvāja: with meat for one who desires eloquence; with the meat of a *kapiñjala* partridge for one who desires food; with fish for one who desires speed; with the meat of a *kṛkaṣā* for one who desires long life; with the meat of an *āṭī* for one who desires spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*); with all [the meats] for one who desires everything; or alternatively, by means of various kinds of food. Then follows the feeding of the Brahmins.

[Regarding *bhāradvājyā*: of a woman of the *bhāradvāja* bird species. *Vākprasāritam* means the extension of speech. A *kapiñjala* is a grey partridge. A *kṛkaṣā* is a monitor lizard. [Regarding *āṭyā*: of a female bird of the *śarāli* species. By way of food, that is, by way of a sequence of foods. The *Śāṅkhāyanagṛhya* (1.27.1–6) states:

"In the sixth month, the first feeding of solid food (*annaprāśana*) takes place. One desiring food and the like should give goat meat; one desiring Vedic luster (*brahmavarcasa*) should give partridge; one desiring speed should give fish; one desiring vigor (*tejas*) should give rice cooked with ghee. He should cause [the child] to eat food mixed with curd, honey, and ghee."
The impulsion is the seed.
Now, regarding the tonsure ceremony, Manu says [2.35]:
The tonsure ceremony for all twice-born classes must be performed according to dharma in either the first or the third year, as enjoined by the Vedas.
When the first year has passed, following the first feeding of solid food, Yama says:
"Then, when the year is complete, the tonsure ceremony (cūḍākarma) is prescribed."
It should be performed on either the second or the third day, according to the injunction of the Śruti.

The phrase "when the second is complete" is to be supplied as a continuation. Otherwise, since that would already be understood from the expression "when the year is complete," the word "in the second" would be unnecessary; for according to the statement of Laugākṣi, "When the third has mostly passed.
Śaṅkha and Likhita state:
"The tonsure ceremony (cūḍākaraṇa) takes place in the third year or in the fifth."
Āśvalāyana Gṛhyasūtra [1.17.1]: "In the third year, the tonsure ceremony (caula) is performed according to the family custom. Laugākṣi.

When the greater part of the third year has passed, the tonsure ceremony (*cūḍākaraṇa*) takes place. For the Vasiṣṭhas, the hair is left on the right side; for the Atris and Kaśyapas, on both sides; the Bhṛgus are clean-shaven; the Aṅgirases have five tufts of hair (*pañcacūḍā*); some keep a single lock of hair (*vājin*) for the sake of auspiciousness, while others keep a crest-lock (*śikhin*). Or it may be according to the family custom. It is performed when the boy is pure or on an auspicious day. "The greater part" means the largest portion. "Kamuñjā" refers to a tuft of hair. "Vājin" refers to a row of hair. "Pure" means bright white. (Āśvalāyana Gṛhya Sūtra 1.4.1–2)

The tonsure ceremony (*caula*), the initiation (*upanayana*), the godāna, and marriage should be performed during the northern course of the sun, in the waxing fortnight, under an auspicious lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*). Some authorities maintain that marriage may be performed at any time.

This alternative regarding the times for the tonsure ceremony is to be understood as established with respect to the differences between Vedic schools (*śākhā*). As for women, their sacraments (*saṃskāra*)...
"This entire sequence of rites for women must be performed without mantras, for the sake of purifying the body, at the proper time and in the proper order."
The marriage rite is declared to be the Vedic sacrament for women;
service to the husband is their residence with the teacher, and household duties are their tending of the sacred fires.
[This has been declared as the rite of initiation for the twice-born.]

The procedure (*itikartavyatā*) is as follows: the one who performs the initiation (*aupanāyanikaḥ*) [performs] the sacraments (*saṃskārāḥ*) ending with the tonsure (*cūḍākaraṇa*). Yājñavalkya [1.13]:
"These rites for women are performed silently; however, the marriage ceremony is accompanied by mantras."

Regarding the duties of one who has not yet been initiated (*anupanīta*), which must now be discussed in connection with initiation (*upanayana*), those things prohibited prior to that time are stated. In this regard, Manu [2.172] says:
"One should not utter the *brahman* (the Veda), except for the offering of the *svadhā*."
For he remains equal to a Śūdra as long as he is not born into the Veda.
From the pouring of the *svadhā* and from the *śrāddha* mantra.
Vasiṣṭha [2.3–7]: Now they also cite—
For no ritual act whatsoever exists for him prior to the binding of the girdle of munja grass;
indeed, until he is born into the Veda, he is equal to a Śūdra in his mode of life.
"Except for water-rites associated with *svadhā* and the ancestors.

This means, except for the water-libations (*tarpaṇa*) for deceased ancestors and so forth, and for *śrāddha* rites associated with the ancestors, as well as the giving of land, umbrellas, and other such items.
Thus says Dakṣa.
A child from birth until the age of eight years should be known as equal to a fetus, for it has manifested only its outward form.

The years are equal [in duration], but only by way of manifestation, not by way of entitlement to ritual action. There is fault for one who has been initiated when he performs censurable acts; yet this boy, until he reaches sixteen years of age, is not yet of legal age.

By this, it is indicated that he lacks independence in transactions such as the investment of wealth. Gautama [2.1–9]: Before initiation, he may act, speak, and eat according to his desire; he has not yet performed the *āhuti* offerings. He is a *brahmacārī*. He voids urine and excrement wherever he happens to be. No rule for ritual sipping (*ācamana*) applies to him, except for wiping, washing, and sprinkling. There is no impurity resulting from touching him. One should not employ him in the *agnihotra* sacrifice or the offering of oblations (*bali*). One should not cause him to recite the *brahma* (Vedic texts), except for the pouring of the *svadhā* libation.

By the phrase "acting, speaking, and eating according to his desire," it is established that [the student] is not prohibited from speaking vulgarities or eating stale food and the like by his own will. However, those acts which lead to absolute downfall (*patanīya*) are indeed prohibited, because expiations (*prāyaścitta*) for them are seen in other Smṛtis. "Not from what has not been offered" (*ahutāt*) means without having offered [into the fire]; it implies the non-eating of what has been offered. "A celibate student" (*brahmacārī*) means one who avoids sexual intercourse. "Discharging urine and excrement as they occur" means he need not observe rules such as facing the north and so forth. Regarding the "rule for sipping water" (*ācamanakalpa*), this refers to facing east, touching the ears, and so on; however, he does perform the actual sipping of water. Since a prohibition of all ritual prescriptions (*kalpa*) would otherwise follow, he states an exception with the words "except for... (*anyatra*). "Wiping off" (*apamārjana*) is the cleansing with water by hand of that which is smeared with food remnants and the like. "Washing away" (*pradhāvana*) is the rinsing of that which is smeared with feces and the like. "Sprinkling" (*prokṣaṇa*) is the sprinkling with water of that which has been touched by something impure. By this, there is no impurity upon touching someone who has already performed the wiping and other such acts. Regarding the injunction "he should employ him in the fire-oblation and the offering of bali," the remainder [of the sense] is that he may do so even as an assistant.

"Neither a maiden, nor a young woman, nor one of little learning, nor a fool [should perform it]," because this constitutes a direct prohibition against a child performing the *sākṣād-homa* (direct fire-oblation). Thus says Vṛddha-Śātātapa.
Before the performance of the tonsure ceremony he is a *bāla* (child); before the first feeding of solid food he is a *śiśu* (infant);
but he is to be known as a *kumāra* (youth) until the tying of the girdle of muñja grass.
[99] Sprinkling with water is prescribed for an infant, while sipping water (ācamana) is traditionally taught for a young child;
however, upon contact with a woman in her menses or similar persons, the boys must bathe.
In the context of the continuation [of the rule] "one should avoid," Gautama [states]:
"A Brāhmaṇa [should avoid] liquor always. [This is also stated] in the Brahmapurāṇa.

Furthermore, a child eating the remnants of its mother and father shall be happy. Āpastamba [2.15.19–25]: Until the first feeding of solid food (*annaprāśana*), fetuses do not become impure. Some say until one full year has passed; or as long as they cannot distinguish the directions; or until the initiation (*upanayana*), according to another view. For it is at this point that eligibility for the sacred scriptures arises; that is the finality, and so too is the traditional law (*smṛti*).
Now, regarding the initiation (*upanayana*), Devala says:

"First, having been consecrated by the father and mother through the *garbhādhāna* and other rites, one becomes eligible for initiation in the eighth year from conception. In that regard, the teacher (*upādhyāya*) is the father, and the mother is the *Gāyatrī*. Thus initiated, the twice-born (*dvijāti*) shall have two fathers."

"Dvipitṛka" means having two fathers, and "dvimātāpitṛka" means having two mothers and two fathers, according to the rule of retaining only one term (*ekaśeṣa*). Manu [2.169] states: "The first birth is from the mother; the second is from the binding of the *mauñjī* (sacred grass girdle)."
The third [is performed] by a twice-born during the initiation for sacrifice, according to the injunction of the Śruti.

Āpastamba [1.1.19]: One should initiate a Brāhmaṇa in the spring, a Rājanya in the summer, and a Vaiśya in the autumn; specifically, a Brāhmaṇa in the eighth year from conception, a Rājanya in the eleventh year from conception, and a Vaiśya in the twelfth year from conception.
[Budha]

In the eighth year from conception, during the spring, a Brāhmaṇa should have himself initiated; a Kṣatriya in the eleventh year, during the summer; and a Vaiśya in the twelfth year, during the rainy season.

Regarding the phrase "should have himself initiated": this refers to cases where there is an absence of eligible authorities such as the father. By the word "rainy season" (*varṣā*), the autumn (*śarat*) is intended, because it is included within that [period], according to the rule "the season is a year.
Thus say Viśvāmitra and Yājñavalkya (Yājñavalkya-smṛti 1.14).
The initiation ceremony for a Brāhmaṇa should take place in the eighth year from conception;
for Kṣatriyas, in the eleventh year plus one; and for Vaiśyas, in the twelfth, or according to their respective family traditions.

The term *upanāyanam* is simply another form of *upanayanam*. Based on the grammatical connection in the rule “in the eleventh year for the Vaiśyas,” the meaning is that it occurs in the twelfth year. Regarding the phrase “according to family custom,” this means that it may also take place at another time in accordance with the specific traditions of the family.
Pāraskara [2.2.4] states the sequence of times for the initiation ceremony:
“Or, for all [castes], according to auspiciousness.”
The meaning is that it should be performed even at whatever time it may be done, provided that it serves as an auspicious rite for the family. Laugākṣi says:
"The initiation (upanayana) of a Brāhmaṇa is in the seventh year, of a Kṣatriya in the ninth, and of a Vaiśya in the eleventh."

The statement beginning with "in the seventh year" and so forth is intended to be consistent with the declaration of Laugākṣi and Manu; thus, the counting does not begin from conception (*garbha*), but rather from birth (*janman*). Paiṭhīnasi states:

"One should initiate a Brāhmaṇa in the fifth year from conception, or in the eighth from conception, or in the eighth [from birth]; a Kṣatriya in the eighth from conception, or in the twelfth from conception; a Vaiśya in the twelfth from conception, or in the sixteenth from conception."
In the context of the phrase "he should initiate," Āpastamba [1.1.20–26] states:

"Now follow the optional initiations: in the seventh year for one desiring spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*); in the eighth for one desiring long life; in the ninth for one desiring splendor (*tejas*); in the tenth for one desiring food; in the eleventh for one desiring sensory power (*indriya*); in the twelfth for one desiring cattle. Gautama [1.1.7–9, 13] states:

The initiation (*upanayana*) for a Brāhmaṇa should take place in the eighth year; in the ninth or fifth year, it is optional (*kāmya*). The calculation of years begins from conception. For Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas, it occurs in the eleventh and twelfth years respectively.
Manu [2.37] states: "For a Brāhmaṇa who desires spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*), it should be performed in the fifth year."
For a king seeking power, [the time for initiation] is on the sixth lunar day; for a Vaiśya seeking prosperity in this world, it is on the eighth.
Paiṭhīnasi states: "Twelve, sixteen, and twenty years—these, having elapsed, are times that are not prohibited."

The established rule here is as follows: By the statement of Āpastamba, “One should initiate a Brāhmaṇa in the spring,” the occurrence of the initiation ceremony (*upanayana*) during the spring and other seasons is prescribed. Since the eighth month from conception, the fifth from birth, and the eighth from birth for a Brāhmaṇa; the eighth from conception, the ninth from birth, the eleventh from conception, and the twelfth from birth for a Kṣatriya; and the eleventh from conception, the twelfth from birth, and the sixteenth from conception for a Vaiśya are heard of in the texts of Manu, Viśvāmitra, Yājñavalkya, Pāraskara, Laugākṣi, and Paiṭhīnasi without specific restrictive conditions, these are obligatory (*nitya*). Furthermore, for all castes, other times according to family custom are also obligatory. Even in this regard, because of their predominance and because they are agreed upon by all the authors of the *Smṛtis*, the eighth from conception, the eleventh from conception, and the twelfth from birth are respectively the primary [times] for Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas.
And so Manu says (2.36):
"One should perform the initiation ceremony for a Brāhmaṇa in the eighth year from conception;
for a Kṣatriya in the eleventh from conception; and for a Vaiśya in the twelfth from conception."

Regarding the fifth year from conception, Paiṭhīnasi prescribes the initiation (*anupabandha*) itself; and since the immediate recitation of the *Sāvitrī* and its mastery—which are seen in the tradition—can only be performed by someone of exceptional intelligence and clear speech, they are indeed obligatory (*nitya*). Furthermore, the daily recitation of the *Sāvitrī* follows the Śruti: "For a Brāhmaṇa, the choosing of the *Gāyatrī* occurs immediately. For a Kṣatriya, the eighth and ninth years from conception are obligatory according to family custom; likewise, the eleventh for a Vaiśya. Other years, such as the eighth and so on up to the twelfth, are not contradictory when following the order of the castes. This is because of Paiṭhīnasi’s statement: "Twelve, sixteen, and twenty—these are times that have passed and yet remain non-contradictory"; for it is stated that there is no contradiction when these later times are used in the absence of each preceding one, and because they constitute an unequal option (*asamaviśiṣṭavikalpa*). From the twelfth year onwards, up to the sixteenth, the twenty-second, and the twenty-fourth respectively for the castes, the transgression is slight, according to the Smṛti which states they are non-contradictory until the end of the twelfth. Beyond that, however, they become outcasts (*vrātya*) and are eligible for initiation only through the *Vrātyastoma* sacrifice. When the initiation in the fifth year and others is tied to a specific desire, they are both obligatory and optional due to the principle of "separateness of connection" (*saṃyogapṛthaktva*). However, for those cases where the Smṛti mentions them solely as tied to a desire—such as "the sixth for a king seeking power"—they are purely optional. Nevertheless, since the very nature of the rite is established thereby, the sacrament (*saṃskāra*) consisting of initiation is proven to be obligatory. Just as the fetching of water is accomplished by means of the *godohana* vessel, and one does not fetch water again with a *camasa* cup merely for the sake of performing a sequence, nor is there initiation for a three-year-old child; for in that case, there is no alternative position due to the lack of a specific scriptural injunction, just as one does not fetch water with an arrow. Now, regarding the transgression of initiation, there is the status of an outcast (*vrātyatā*). In this regard, in the dependent statements, the sequence of years, initiation, and caste should be understood as continuing.
Manu [2.38]: The Sāvitrī does not lapse for a Brāhmaṇa until the sixteenth year;
for a Kṣatriya until the twenty-second; and for a Vaiśya until the twenty-fourth.
The prefix *āṅ* is used in the sense of inclusion;
the period for initiation (*upanayana*) is up to sixteen years for a Brāhmaṇa,
for a Kṣatriya it is up to twenty-two, and for a Vaiśya it is up to twenty-four.
Thus, from the words of Vyāsa; and Yājñavalkya [1.38] states:
"From this point forward, these fall, being excluded from all religious duties."
Those who have fallen from the Sāvitrī are outcasts (vrātyas), except through the Vrātyastoma sacrifice.

Manu [2.40]: "Under no circumstances, even in times of distress, should one perform with these unpurified persons— whether through Vedic study or marriage— any connection with Brahmins according to the prescribed rule."
"By the impure" means by those who have not performed penance. The mention of "Brahman" is for the sake of illustration.
[105] Now follows the description of the teacher and the student.
In that regard, Yama states the characteristics of a teacher:
he should be truthful in speech, steadfast, skillful, and devoted to compassion for all living beings.
One who is faithful, devoted to the Vedas, and pure is called an Ācārya.

One who is perfected in the study of the Vedas, possesses a proper livelihood, has conquered his senses, is skillful, and is diligent in his vows. "Possessing a livelihood" means one who has a means of subsistence as prescribed by rule. — Hārīta.
One should not officiate for one who lacks a livelihood, nor should one choose such a person as a teacher;
for hands smeared with marrow are not purified by blood.
"By the marrow"—this is the instrumental case of the word *majjan*. Śaṅkha and Likhita state: "One should not perform the sacramental rites for those who are insane or mute."
One should not officiate at a sacrifice for someone who has not been examined; one should not teach him; one should not initiate him. Āpastamba [1.1.6].
The initiation of those who are not Śūdras and whose actions are not corrupt; "whose actions are not corrupt" means those who are free from drinking intoxicants and similar vices.
[106] Kātyāyana says:

One should initiate a Brāhmaṇa with the Sāvitrī, a Rājanya with the Triṣṭubh, and a Vaiśya with the Jagatī; or the Sāvitrī may be used for all. According to Lāugākṣi: "That excellent splendor of Savitṛ" is the Sāvitrī for a Brāhmaṇa; "Of that Savitṛ" for a Rājanya; and "All forms" for a Vaiśya.
Yama says: "Or one may perform everything, even without the mantra, while circumambulating to the right.

This should be understood as applying until the sixteenth year, in the event of some misfortune, in the absence of a teacher of the mantra, or when there is the possibility of the time for initiation having passed.
Gobhila [2.10.7]:
On the day that the young student (māṇavaka) is about to enter [the Veda], they feed him on that very day before dawn (*prag eva*).
"Before dawn" means precisely at early morning.
Regarding the section on leading [the bride], Pāraskara [2.2.5] states:
"One should feed Brāhmaṇas.
Śaṅkha and Likhita state:
The food of the twice-born consists, respectively, of milk, rice-gruel, and curdled milk (*āmikṣā*).
