This refers to those twice-born who are to be initiated, based on their eligibility for the *upanayana* ceremony. *Āmikṣā* is the solid portion of milk that has been transformed by the addition of curds.
Now, regarding the sacred thread (*upavīta*) and other items:
Regarding this, Manu [2.44] states:
"The sacred thread (*upavīta*) of a Brāhmaṇa should be made of cotton, consisting of three strands and twisted upward;
that of a Kṣatriya should be made of hempen threads, and that of a Vaiśya of woolen threads."
"Made of woolen thread" means constructed from woolen yarn.
Baudhāyana [1.8.5]:

"The sacrificial cord (*yajñopavīta*) should be made of silk or cotton, triple-stranded and threefold, reaching down to the navel; having raised the right arm and placed the left under it, one should place it over the head."
*Kauśa* is that which originates from *kauśa* worms; that is to say, it consists of silk thread.
And so it is stated in the *Ādityapurāṇa*:
"Whether made of linen, or cotton, or even of silk thread."
"He who wears the sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*)—crows do not harm him.
It is made of *karpāsa* (cotton) according to the Sūtra. "Threefold" (*trivṛt*) means three times [nine], i.e., nine strands; for the Śruti states, "Nine indeed is the threefold.
Kātyāyana says in the *Chandogapariśiṣṭa*:
The upper part should be made triple and the three threads should hang downwards;
the sacred thread (upavīta) should thus be triple-stranded, and for it, a single knot is prescribed.

[108] Having made three coils turning to the left, there should be nine coils by turning to the right. And thus it should be made with three strands; this is what is meant by the statement, "The sacrificial thread is triple-stranded.
Likewise:
"That which, when worn on the back, at the navel, or around the waist, remains [in place]..."
That sacred thread should be worn neither too low nor too high.

The meaning is that it should be made such that, when placed over the left shoulder and held against the back and the navel, it reaches as far as the waist. This specific rule regarding the measurement is stated by Kātyāyana in the *Chandogapariśiṣṭa* as a supplement to the injunction for wearing the sacred thread (*upavīta*).

Now, Gautama [1.19–23]: "For all [twice-born], the garments may be made of hemp, linen, bark, or *kutapa* wool; or cotton, provided it is not dyed. Some say even saffron-dyed [cotton is permitted]. A garment of tree-bark is for the Brāhmaṇa; those dyed with madder or turmeric are for the other two [castes]."

*Śāṇa* is made of hemp (*śaṇa*). *Atasī* is flax (*kṣumā*). *Cīra* is produced from *kuśa* grass and similar materials. *Kutapa* is made from the wool of mountain goats. *Avikṛta* means not dyed with coloring substances. Regarding the option of ochre-colored garments (*kāṣāya*): for a Brāhmaṇa it is dyed with tree-ochre; for a Kṣatriya and a Vaiśya, it is dyed with madder or turmeric. Vasiṣṭha [11.64–67]: "The garment of a Brāhmaṇa should be white or unwashed (*ahata*); that of a Kṣatriya, cotton dyed with madder; that of a Vaiśya, silk dyed with turmeric. Or, for all of them, woven cloth (*tāntava*) that is undyed."
*Kauśeya* is that which arises from the cocoon of a silkworm. *Tāntava* here refers to cotton. [109] *Śaṅkha* says:
garments made of linen (*kṣauma*), silk (*dukūla*), and wool (*sautra*) are for the three social classes (*varṇas*).
Yama says:
Linen, cotton, kutapa wool, skins, bark, and woolen blankets—all these garments should be worn white; such is the cloth for his lower garment.
"Pāridhānika" means that which serves the purpose of wearing. As Manu [2.41] states:
"The skins of the black antelope, the ruru deer, and the goat are for the religious student."
They should wear, in due order, garments made of hemp, flax, and wool.
*Kṛṣṇa* is a black antelope; *ruru* is a deer with many branched horns; *basta* is a goat; *āvika* is made from the wool of a sheep. Āpastamba [1.3.3–10].

The skin of a black antelope or a black deer belongs to a Brāhmaṇa; if it is black, he should not sleep on a spread-out seat. The skin of a Ruru deer belongs to a Rājanya; the skin of a goat belongs to a Vaiśya; the woolen skin belongs to all classes, as does the blanket. One who desires the increase of Brahmanic power should wear only skins; one who desires the increase of Kṣatriya power should wear only clothes; one who desires both should wear both—so says the Brāhmaṇa. However, he should always wear a skin as the upper garment.

*Aiṇeya* means derived from the *eṇī*, the female deer; when it is the skin of a black antelope (*hāriṇa*), one should not sit or lie down upon it. *Āvika* is the skin of a sheep. *Sārvavarṇika* refers to the connection with caste. *Uttara* means an upper garment (*uttarīya*). [110] Pāraskara [2.5.17–20]:

"The upper garment of a Brāhmaṇa is the skin of the *aiṇa* (black antelope); that of a Rājanya is the skin of the *raurava* (red deer); that of a Vaiśya is the skin of a goat or a cow. Or, in the absence of others, the skin of a cow may be used by all, because of its preeminence."
Yama says: [The black antelope skin for a Brāhmaṇa, the Ruru deer skin for a Kṣatriya, and the goat skin for a Vaiśya; however, for all of them, the Ruru deer skin may be used.]
The remainder is that for all [of these], other skins than those of the Ruru deer are not available.
"The sacred threads and garments are made of kārkaśa, śāṇa, and wool; the skins are of deer, tiger, and goat."
Paiṭhīnasi:
[The skins] of the black antelope, the ruru deer, and the spotted deer;
now, the girdles.
In this regard, Manu [2.42] states:
"The girdle of a Brāhmaṇa should be made of muñja grass, threefold, even, and smooth;
that of a Kṣatriya should be a bowstring made of mūrvā fiber; and that of a Vaiśya should be made of hempen threads."

"Trivṛt" means tripled. "Equal" means not thick in any place and not thin in any place. "Ślakṣṇā" means not thick. [111] Yama says: But even if these are unavailable, [the cord may be made] from kuśa grass, aśmantaka, or balvaja.
The girdles should be made triple-stranded, with either one or three knots.
The state of being "threefold" (*trivṛt*) is by means of three windings. As for the number of knots, it is established according to custom or by the number of one's *pravara* ancestors.
Āpastamba [1.2.33–37]:

A girdle made of muñja grass, triple-stranded and twisted to the right as far as possible, is for the Brāhmaṇa; a bowstring is for the Rājanya, or else a muñja girdle mixed with iron; a cord of sheep’s wool is for the Vaiśya, or according to some, one made of *sairī* or *tāmbūlī* fibers.

When the availability of *muñja* grass and other materials is possible within the scope of one's capability; "turning to the right" means turned clockwise, which refers to the suitability of materials such as *muñja* grass and so forth. "Mixed with iron" means mixed with iron wires. "Sairī" refers to the yoke-halter (*yoktra*) of a plow (*sīra*, i.e., a plough); thus says Kapardin. Gobhila [2.10.10] states:
"The girdles are made of *muñja*, *kāśa*, or *tāmbūla*."
Paiṭhīnasi states:

"The girdle of a Brāhmaṇa should be made of muñja grass or from aśmantaka; that of a Rājanya should be made of balbaja grass or from the sinew of a cow; and that of a Vaiśya should be made of hemp or linen.
[Aśmantaka is a specific kind of grass resembling kuśa.]
[112] Baijavāpa says:

"They lead the triple-stranded girdle around three times, spreading it out from left to right. This means it is fashioned by being spread out so as to proceed from left to right; they lead it all around, winding it three times in such a way that it proceeds from left to right.
Now, regarding the staff (*daṇḍa*), it is stated in the *Bhaviṣyapurāṇa*:
"For a Brāhmaṇa, [the staff] should be made of *bilva* or *pālāśa* wood; the third is likewise made of *plakṣa*."
Nyagrodha and khadira for the kṣatriya, and likewise another made from vetasa for the others.
O mighty-armed one, according to dharma, these three types of staffs— the pīlu, the udumbara, and likewise that made from aśvattha— are fit to be carried by a vaiśya.
Śaṅkha states: "Staves made of parṇa, pippala, and bilva wood are prescribed in that order."
*Parṇa* is *palāśa*. According to Paiṭhīnasi,
for a Vaiśya, it is made of *audumbara*, *khadira*, or *vāraṇa* wood.
The *vāraṇa* is that which originates from the *varaṇa* tree.

[Pāraskara Gṛhyasūtra 2.5.25–27] The staff of a Brāhmaṇa is made of *pālāśa* wood, that of a Rājanya of *bailva* wood, and that of a Vaiśya of *audumbara* wood; or alternatively, all [types of staffs] may be used by all [classes].
Yama:
According to the law, the staff of a Brahmin is prescribed as being made of *pālāśa* or *bilva* wood;
that of a Kṣatriya, according to the law, is made of *aśvattha* or *khadira* wood.
Now, for a Vaiśya, a staff made of Udumbara wood or Plakṣa wood is prescribed.
Likewise, if none of these are available, any wood fit for sacrifice may be used by all.
Manu [2.46]: "The staff of a Brāhmaṇa should be made to reach the hairline in measurement;
that of a Kṣatriya should reach the forehead, and that of a Vaiśya should reach the tip of the nose."
Regarding the continuation of the term "staff" (*daṇḍa*), Vasiṣṭha [11.55–57] states:
"For a Brāhmaṇa, it reaches up to the nose; for a Kṣatriya, it reaches up to the forehead; for a Vaiśya, it reaches up to the hair."
The staffs made of *pālāśa*, *khadira*, and *udumbara* wood should be equal in length to the hairline, the forehead, and the bridge of the nose, respectively. Paiṭhīnasi:
The length of the hair-tufts for the Brāhmaṇa and other classes is measured by the forehead and the neck. Manu [2.47] states:
"They should all be straight, without blemishes, and pleasing to the sight."
[114] Those who do not cause distress to men, who possess inner strength, and who are not pained by fire—

Gautama [1.27]: Unpressed, curved like a sacrificial post (yūpa), and with their bark intact. "Unpressed" means not damaged by being entwined with creepers and the like. "Curved like a sacrificial post" means having tips that do not droop, resembling a *yūpa*. "With bark intact" means possessing their outer bark. Because they are not mentioned in a compound, all [the trees] must be of this nature.
Āpastamba [1.2.38]:
For a Kṣatriya, it is made from the branch of a Nyagrodha tree and points downward.
Now follows the instruction on the Gāyatrī.
Now Hārīta says:

Therefore, they recite the Veda (*brahman*) to one who has been initiated, who has approached [the teacher], who has been examined, and who is being examined, but not to others; they call such persons "Vedic students" (*brahmacārin*).
In this context, the word *brahman* refers to the *Sāvitrī*.
Pāraskara [2.3.3–7]:

Then he recites the Sāvitrī to him—[the teacher] sitting to the north of the fire, facing west, while the student] is seated, has approached [for instruction], is looking on, and has been looked at by [the teacher]. Some say [he should recite it] to one who is standing to the south or even seated. He should recite it verse by quarter, then by half-verse, and finally the whole verse together with the third repetition. This may be done after a year, six months, twenty-four days, twelve days, six days, or three days; however, he should recite the Gāyatrī immediately to a Brāhmaṇa, for according to scripture, "The Brāhmaṇa is indeed of Agni’s nature."
[115] One should recite each quarter-verse (pāda) individually, and then repeat the entire verse together with the third quarter-verse.
Yama says:
"He who learns the Gāyatrī preceded by the syllable *oṃ*..."
And he who practices the holy life—he indeed is called a *śrotriya*.
The remainder is "the three great utterances (*mahāvyāhṛti*s). Manu [2.80]:
"One who is separated from this *ṛc* verse, as well as from the timely performance of one's own ritual duty..."
One born of the Brahmin, Kṣatriya, or Vaiśya lineage incurs reproach among the virtuous.
Now, regarding the practice of begging for alms, Manu [2.48] says:
"Having accepted the desired staff and having worshipped the sun,"
Having circumambulated the fire from left to right, he should go about for alms according to the prescribed rule.
Having approached and stood facing him; having circumambulated and encircled him.
Thus:
"An initiated, most excellent twice-born man should go about for alms, placing the word 'bhavat' (sir) at the beginning."
A Kṣatriya should address you as "bhavan-madhyaṃ," while a Vaiśya should address you as "bhavad-uttaraṃ."
In the future,
he should first beg for alms from his mother, or his sister, or his own maternal aunt— whichever among these would not treat him with contempt.
She should place gold, silver, or a jewel into his bowl.

The phrase "and she who would not despise him" means that any other woman may do so as well. Because this is stated following the introduction with the words "first," and because of the prohibition against daily alms from one's own kin and so forth, this refers specifically to the alms-gathering that occurs within the ritual procedure of the initiation (*upanayana*).
Following the word "he should beg" (*bhikṣeta*), Pāraskara [states]: [2.5.5–7]...

There are three who do not refuse; or six, or twelve in number. Some say the mother is the first. The word "those who do not refuse" is used in the nominative case instead of the locative. Thus says Śaunaka.
One should practice begging for alms seven times, and one should avoid both *kṣāṃ* and *hiṃ*.

Regarding the phrase "one should avoid both *kṣāṃ* and *hiṃ*," the meaning is that by way of figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*), one should avoid the alms-food, just as one avoids a staff or similar objects.
Likewise:
Among all the castes (*varṇas*), those such as the Brāhmaṇas who remain within their own caste; the word "should beg" is to be supplied. Vyāsa says:
Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas should go for alms every day,
either only among the houses of their own caste or among the houses of all castes.
Gautama [2.42]:
The practice of wandering for alms is common to all castes, with the exception of those who are accused of crimes and those who have fallen from their status.
Likewise [2.44–45]:
In the absence of others, one may seek from teachers, gurus, and kinsmen; among these, one should avoid each preceding category in preference for the following. Manu [2.183]:
[One should accept gifts] from those who are not deficient in Vedic study and sacrifices, and who are praiseworthy in their own duties.
A student of sacred knowledge (brahmacārī), being self-restrained, should collect alms daily from the houses [of the faithful].
"Among those praised for their own duties" means among those who are steadfast in the correct performance of their respective tasks.
Likewise [2.184]:
"One should not beg from the family of the teacher, nor from the families of one's paternal or maternal relatives."
But if other houses are not available, one should avoid each preceding one in turn.

If it cannot be obtained elsewhere, one should beg from the teacher and others; even there, one should avoid each preceding person in favor of the next, provided the latter is unavailable. As stated in the *Bhaviṣya*:
"Or, if those previously mentioned are not available, one may wander through the entire village."
"Except for the last one, O mighty-armed one," said the Lord, the All-pervading One.

Restraining his speech and remaining self-controlled, he should also avoid meat; O joy of the Kurus, he should seek alms from members of all four castes, and if nothing is obtained, he should continue on.
Āpastamba [1.3.25]:

"Bringing all his gains to the teacher, he should go on his alms-round in the evening and morning with a vessel. 'All' means without remainder; 'gains' means what has been obtained. 'With a vessel' means with a vessel made of copper or other metals, excluding bronze. 'He should go on his alms-round' means he should perform it."
Yama says: Alms-food, condiments, and water that have been placed directly into the hand—
by eating these, one becomes impure, and the donor does not go to heaven.
Paiṭhīnasi:
He should wander for alms, being vigilant, pure, tranquil, and having his senses subdued.
"Vigilant" means attentive.

Regarding the practice of begging for alms, Āpastamba states [1.3.31–35]: Having collected that [alms-food] and set it aside, he should announce it to his teacher. He should eat what is prescribed by him. In the absence of the teacher, he should go to the teacher’s family; in their absence, to other learned Brahmins (śrotriya). He should not go out for his own sake.

[119] *Pradiṣṭam* means permitted. *Vipravāse* means in one's absence. *Ācāryakulāya* means to the family of the teacher, such as the teacher’s son and so forth. *Nātmaprayojanaḥ* means not for one’s own purpose, without having informed the teacher and others. Regarding *gurusamavāye*: when there is a gathering of many teachers, the meaning is that at that time, one should undertake [the study] with whichever one he is attached to. Likewise [Gṛhyasūtra 1.7.15–18]: "Upon returning home, he should give [the fee] to his mother. The mother should send him to the husband. The husband [should send him] to the teacher. He should employ him in religious duties."
The term *samāvṛttaḥ* refers here specifically to one who has returned home after completing his studies while remaining in his father’s house;
this is the view of Gautama (2.46–48):

“Having announced [his meal] to the teacher and being permitted by him, he should eat. In the teacher’s absence, he should announce it to his wife, his son, a fellow student (*sabrahmacārin*), or a virtuous person. Remaining silent, eating until satisfied, and not being greedy, he should have water placed nearby.”
A fellow religious student (*sabrahmacārī*) is one who studies together. From the virtuous (*sadbhyaḥ*), that is, from the good (*sādhubhyaḥ*).
Manu [2.51]: "But having collected that alms-food, as much food as there is, without guile..."
Having offered [the food] to the guru, one should eat, facing east, pure and having performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana).

Hārīta says: "The teachers maintain that when there is purity of food, there is purity of the inner being (*sattva*). That [purity] is of two kinds: that which corresponds to *ṛta* (truth/ritual order) and that which corresponds to *amṛta* (the immortal). That which is free from anger, hypocrisy, service for gain, and improper dealings is 'corresponding to *ṛta*. Alms-food that has been sprinkled with water, circumambulated by fire, shown to the sun, offered to the teacher, and permitted [by him] is 'corresponding to *amṛta*. Consuming that in the morning, the student (*brahmacārī*) attains the perfection of Brahman.
'Improper dealings' refers to [actions contrary to] friendliness and so forth. 'Circumambulated by fire' means that fire has been made to go around it on all sides."
Vyāsa: Having washed his hands and feet, and having eaten, he should sip water again. Vasiṣṭha [12.18–20]:
One should eat food facing the east. One should swallow the entire mouthful silently with the thumb, and one should not make a sound. Paiṭhīnasi says:

Having offered the oblation, having satiated the fire, and having placed a fuel-stick upon it, one should consecrate the food by reciting the mantra, "That which is the food, that food I eat. Having performed the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering three times and the fire-rite, one should eat, being silent and facing the east, once permitted [by the teacher]. Thus he says.
One should sit comfortably, neither too high, with the body balanced and not intent on food;
at the proper time, one should eat first what is light, quickly, and in small quantities, with liquids predominating.

"From a portion of the *havis*": this means from the food that has become the sacrificial offering (*havis*). "With a liquid as the final part": the meaning is that one should conclude the meal with a liquid, such as milk and so forth.

[121] Hārīta says: One who desires long life should eat facing the east; one seeking fame, facing the south; one desiring prosperity, facing the west. One should not overeat. One should not eat while seated on a seat, nor from a vessel of black iron, nor from an earthenware bowl, nor in a place that is strewn with refuse.
One should not overeat; one should not practice gluttony. In the case of being "avakīrṇa," meaning impure.
Yājñavalkya [1.31]: Having performed the fire-ritual, one should eat with speech restrained, by the permission of the guru.
Having first performed the *āpośana* rite, one should eat the food with respect and without disparaging it.

In accordance with the statement of Paiṭhīnasi, "having offered oblations with the *havis*," etc., that very same fire-rite (*agnikārya*) is intended here by the phrase "having performed the fire-rite. "Having honored" means having meditated upon [the food] as the cause for the origin and maintenance of living beings. "Without disparaging" means without proclaiming any defects in the food.
Likewise [at 1.32]:
"Remaining in celibacy (*brahmacarya*), one should not eat food from a single source except in times of distress."
A Brāhmaṇa may eat at a Śrāddha feast as much as he desires, provided he does not violate his vows.

One meal means one alms-begging; in times of non-distress, or even in distress when no other place for begging exists, it may be just one. However, at a *śrāddha* feast, it may be so even in times of non-distress. Without violating his vow—meaning avoiding honey, meat, and the like—a Brāhmaṇa may eat as he pleases, but not a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya.
For there is a statement by Manu (2.190): "And this practice is not prescribed for the Rājanya and the Vaiśya."
Baudhāyana [2.1.25–26]:
If he should fall ill, he may at will eat all the remnants of his teacher for the sake of medicine. He should treat himself with whatever he desires;
by "whatever" is meant even honey, meat, and so forth, which are otherwise forbidden to a religious student, provided they are the remnants of the teacher.
Vasiṣṭha says:
"In the Vājasaneyaka, honey consumed unintentionally is not considered a fault.
"Unintentionally" means having come into contact with it through negligence or the like, and thus being eaten.
Manu [2.54–55]: Upon seeing [the guest], one should rejoice, be gracious, and welcome him in every way;
for food that is always honored bestows strength and vigor.

*Prasāda* is the tranquility of the mind resulting from the removal of defects such as anger. *Pratinandana* is the expression of well-wishing for prosperity. *Bala* is power; *ūrja* is vigor. [123] In the *Brahma Purāṇa*:
"Having seen the food, one should first bow down and then speak with palms joined in reverence."
Then, with devotion, one should pay homage, thinking, "May this be ours forever."
Manu [2.56]: One should not give the remains of one's food to anyone, nor should one eat between meals;
one should not overeat, nor should one go anywhere while still impure from eating.
Medhātithi says "in between" means during the interval between the evening and morning times.

Having eaten himself, he should wash the vessel; he should not leave any remnant. If he is unable to do so, he should bury it in the ground or cast it into water, or hand it over to a noble person (*ārya*), or to a *śūdra* who serves as an intermediary (*antardhin*). One who is away from home should eat after having offered the alms-food into the fire. Alms-food is commended as being equivalent to the sacrificial oblation (*havis*); in this regard, the teacher (*ācārya*) represents the deity and the *Āhavanīya* fire. After feeding him [the guest], whatever remains he eats; that is indeed the remnant of the sacrificial oblation. Whatever other substances he offers as they are available, those are the sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*). This is the sacrifice of the religious student (*brahmacārin*), a constant vow. One should not give him any food remnant that is forbidden by the sacred revelation (*śruti*), such as alkaline salts, salt, honey, and meat. By this, other restrictive rules are explained.

He should gather it together, place it in a single vessel, and keep it nearby for the sake of the teacher’s servant who is away from home—that is, one who has gone elsewhere on the teacher’s business. Regarding "with the sacrificial offering" (*haviṣā*): this refers to whatever remains after the teacher has eaten and set it aside. And as for the phrase "not so": just as alkaline salts, salt, and the like are not given because they are prohibited by the *Śruti*, so too is the actual leavings [of food].
Likewise, one may eat the leavings of one's father and of an elder brother; however, if there is a lapse in their religious observance, it is not to be eaten.
Regarding misconduct concerning the Dharma and unrighteousness:
having introduced the enumeration of morsels, Vasiṣṭha, Āpastamba, Hārīta,
and Yama state that for a religious student (brahmacārin), the number is unlimited.
The ox, the religious student, and the one who has established the sacred fires—these three achieve perfection only while eating;
for them, there is no perfection for those who do not eat.
The mention of the ox is for the sake of illustration.
Gautama [8.5, 9] states:
"In the evening and in the morning, however, one should eat food that has been honored, without finding fault with it."
Now, regarding the ritual rinsing of the mouth (ācamana),
Devala says:
"Having eaten, one should rinse the mouth with a concentrated mind according to the prescribed rule."
One should cleanse both the mouth and the hands with cleansing agents and even by means of rubbing.
Regarding this, Manu [1.53] says:
"A twice-born man, having sipped water, should always eat his food with a concentrated mind;
and having eaten, he should sip water properly and touch the cavities of the head with water."
Gautama [1.37–41]:

One should perform purification facing either the east or the north. Seated in a clean place, having placed the right arm between the knees, wearing the sacred thread over the left shoulder, and having washed the hands up to the wrists, one should remain silent and, touching the heart, sip water three or four times. [One should wipe the mouth twice and sprinkle the feet; one should also touch the apertures of the head.]

The word “or” (*vā*) indicates an option depending on the purity of one’s internal state (*bhāva*). From the wrist—that is, from the region of the junction of the neck and the upper arm—[the water should reach] those touching the heart, meaning those that have entered within the heart. The *khāni* are the sense organs. The *śirṣaṇyāni* are those produced in the head. Hārīta says: Having washed the hands as far as the wrists, and the feet as far as the shanks; one who desires preeminence among kinsmen or who desires food should place his hand upon the big toe of the right foot, touch the vital breaths (*prāṇas*), and then touch the sense organs (*khāni*).
Devala says: First, standing facing the east, one should slowly wash one's feet;
or facing north for rites dedicated to the gods, and facing south for those dedicated to the ancestors.
Having tied his topknot and put on two clean, bright garments, he should remain silent and composed; he should neither rise up nor look around.
"Having composed the mind"—this is the ellipsis. "Rising" means standing up. "Looking at the directions"—this is the ellipsis, based on the statement of Śaṅkha: "and not looking at the directions.
Likewise: "neither walking, nor lying down, nor moving, nor touching another."
Neither stumbling, nor conversing, nor even looking at himself.

Trembling and shaking, he looked at himself—that is, his own heart; for according to the frequent observation of the *curādi* class of verbs, the suffix *ṇic* is used here in its own sense (*svārthe*). Without touching his hair, his waist-knot, or even the earth—if he should touch these again, he would wash his hand.
"Below the navel" refers to the region below the navel. "Without touching with the hand"—this is the ellipsis. Likewise:
"In this manner, having washed the two feet separately with water up to the knees."
And with his hands withdrawn from the wrists, he should sit restrained behind.
Then, from the first sacred water-place on the right, he should drink three times in equal measure— water that is not turbid, not overflowing, not above the knees, and free of bubbles.

From the first [application] pertaining to Brahmā; one should wipe the mouth twice with the base of the thumb so that it does not leak— that is, so that nothing flows out— and never with the tips of the fingers nor with the backs of the fingers.
Then, having touched the eyes, nose, ears, and navel with the fingers,
and having sprinkled the head and feet with water, one becomes pure.
With the backs [of the hands], that is, with the backs of the fingers and the hands. Vyāsa says:
"One should first sip water three times, and then wipe the mouth twice."
Having sprinkled water on his feet, he should immediately thereafter sprinkle it on his head.
Next, one should touch the eyes, the nostrils, the ears, and the lips;
thereafter, one should touch the region of the navel, and then touch water once again.
Viṣṇu [62.5]:

Seated in a clean place, with his knees enclosed [by his hands], facing either east or north, with his mind fixed on that [act] and with a cheerful mind, he should sip water that is neither hot from fire nor frothy, not poured by the hand of a Śūdra alone, and free from alkaline salt.
"With his mind fixed on that" means having his mind intent upon the act of sipping water.
In the Narasiṃha Purāṇa: Having first formed the right hand into the shape of a cow’s ear,
one should drink the water three times after looking at it, and wipe the mouth twice.
In the *Bhaviṣya Purāṇa*:
"O King, having made his two feet even and likewise having tied his topknot,
and having abandoned even extreme comfort, O King, from a very great distance..."
Likewise,
O King, having made his fingers and hand firm, the twice-born man, one-pointed and well-disposed,
should touch his eyes with his thumb and forefinger.
O King, one should touch the nose with the thumb and the ring finger;
O joy of the Kurus, one should always touch the mouth with the middle fingers.
He touches his ears with the little finger and the thumb;
likewise, he touches his arms with the fingers and the mandala with the thumb.
O best of the Kuru lineage, [the head] is from the navel, while the head itself is indeed formed by all [the veins].
By this very procedure, one who has sipped water attains purity;
having washed both feet and hands, one should drink water that has been inspected three times.
With this [water] to be described, he should wipe his face twice with the base of the thumb according to conventional practice; then,
having first gathered [the water] with three [fingers], he should thus touch his mouth.

The grammatical connection is: “Then, having closed the mouth, one should wipe it. “Thus” means “having closed it. *Tahā* [2.24–26]: “Afterwards, immediately following that, [one should touch] the nose with the thumb and the index finger.”
And with the thumb and ring finger, [he should touch] the eyes and ears again and again.
One should touch the navel with the little finger and the thumb, the heart with the palm, the head with all the fingers, and afterwards the two arms with the fingertips.

The *pradeśinī* is the index finger. Having first touched the mouth, one should afterwards touch the nose; immediately after that, the eyes, then again the ears, and then the navel—this is the sequence.
Śaṅkha (10.7–9) states:
"By joining the index finger with the thumb, one should touch the two nostrils."
Then, by joining the thumbs and middle fingers, one should touch the two eyes.
One should touch the two ears with the thumb and the ring finger;
then, one should touch the two shoulders using the little finger and the thumb.
By means of all [the fingers] joined together, one should likewise touch the navel, the heart, and the head; this is the rule for sipping water (ācamana).

Paiṭhīnasi says: One should touch the two nostrils with the thumb and the index finger; the two eyes with the thumb and the ring finger; the two ears with the little finger and the thumb; the mouth with the middle finger; and the navel with the thumb. One should touch the head with all the fingers. The index finger is Vāyu, the ring finger is Sūrya, the little finger is Maghavā (Indra), the middle finger is Prajāpati, and the thumb is Agni. Therefore, one touches all the locations together with that [thumb]. [One does this] so that these deities—Vāyu, Sūrya, Indra, Prajāpati, and Agni—may purify him. Thus it is said.

Having touched the nose, the two eyes, the two ears, the mouth, the navel, and then the head, one should touch the vital organs in that same order; then, having sprinkled water on the feet, one becomes pure.
And he should pour out the remaining water into his left hand.
"Vital breaths" refers to the sense organs (*indriya*). "According to their number" means without exceeding the specific number belonging to each respective sense organ. Śaṅkha and Likhita state:
"Having sipped water three times and wiped the mouth twice, one should touch the head, the eyes, the ears, the nose, and the heart."

Āpastamba [1.16.1–8]: One should not sip water while standing or while stooping. Sitting down, one should sip water three times with water that reaches the heart. One should wipe the lips three times; some say twice. One should touch them once; some say twice. Having sprinkled the left hand with the right hand, one should touch the feet, the head, and the sense organs—the eyes, the nostrils, and the ears. Then one should touch water again. The meaning is that one should not sip water while standing or stooping. Regarding the phrase "one should touch them once; some say twice," the connection is with "the lips. The words "the left hand" are to be supplied as the remainder of the sentence.

Hārīta says: Sitting facing east or facing northeast, having placed his two elbows between his thighs, he should drink water three times for the heart. Having wiped his lips twice, and having sprinkled water once on his head, his eyes, ears, navel, heart, and feet, and having touched them with water, he becomes pure.
Śaṅkha [9.10–13] says:
One should sip water three times; by that, the deities—Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra—are pleased for him. Thus we have heard.
The Gaṅgā and the Yamunā are pleased by the wiping [of the face];
the Nāsatyas and Dasras are pleased when both nostrils are touched.
When the pair of eyes is touched, the Moon and the Sun are pleased;
likewise, when the pair of ears is touched, Wind and Fire are pleased.
By the mere touch of his two shoulders, all the mountains are delighted;
by the constant touch of his navel, the nāgas are likewise ever pleased.
And when his heart is touched by this, all the deities are pleased.
By touching his head, that person shall become pleased;
[namely] the two Aśvins, the Nāsatyas.
This occurs immediately after the contact of the senses, according to the *Bhaviṣyapurāṇa*.
O Bhārata, whatever water or liquid a man pours upon the ground, by that he gratifies the Nāgas, headed by Vāsuki.
Without his sacred thread, likewise with his hair-tuft untied,
and with unwashed feet, a twice-born man remains impure even if he has sipped water for purification.
One who touches water with the knees outside [the knees], with water held in only one hand,
or while standing with shoes on, shall not attain purity at all.
[Devala]:
A man should not perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) while wearing shoes, or while standing in water, or with his hair disheveled,
or wearing a turban, or having his head wrapped in a cloth.
One who knows the true essence of the Vedas should not perform purification with streams of rainwater.
Marīci says: One should not do so with knees uncovered, nor in haste, nor while seated, nor while standing.
One should not [recite] while standing on sandals, nor without a focused mind, but rather being pure and with a disciplined intellect.
Having sipped water, a twice-born man always becomes pure and cleansed;
even while seated after eating, he should perform the ritual sipping (ācamana), but never at any other time.
Vyāsa says: Having covered one's head or neck, or even having one's lower garment or topknot hanging loose,
one becomes impure even after sipping water (ācamana) if one has not performed the cleansing of the feet.
If a Brāhmaṇa sips water from the tip of his fingernail, that is equal to the drinking of liquor; thus spoke the Seer.
In the *Brahma Purāṇa*: "Whether covering one's neck or head, or even while walking on a street or through a marketplace,
if one has not performed the purification of the feet, one remains impure even after sipping water (*ācamana*)."
A marketplace (*āpaṇa*) is a place for buying and selling. Baudhāyana [1.8.10]:
One should not sip water using the residue from washing the feet; if one should sip water, one should do so after letting it flow onto the ground.
"By the remnant" means by what remains.
Āpastamba [1.15.4–5]: "One should not sip water from raindrops, nor from water in a fissure, nor from heated water without a specific reason."
*Pradara* is ground that has split open of its own accord. "By reason of not being man-made" means apart from [water affected by] disease and so forth.

Regarding the rule "one should sip water," Vasiṣṭha [3.35–36] continues: "Water from a fissure is fit for the satiation of cows provided it is not corrupted in color or taste, nor is it of impure origin."

Inauspicious arrivals and inauspicious destinies; and the inauspiciousness of a destiny arises from entering into censured places, times, and so forth. "Corrupted in color and taste" means having their taste and color spoiled by contact with other substances.
Regarding the rule "he should sip water," Śaṅkha and Likhita state:

[one should sip] water that has been drawn up, strained, inspected, non-saline, not heated over a fire, and free of foam and bubbles; nor [should one sip water] offered by a Śūdra, an impure person, or with only one hand.

[Water] that has been thoroughly strained and from which impure substances have been removed; [it must not be] "offered by a Śūdra, nor by an impure person, nor with one hand"—for thus there is a general prohibition against rinsing the mouth with water offered by one hand. Furthermore, because of the statement of Āpastamba: "One becomes pure by rinsing the mouth using water that has reached the ground, or by having someone who is himself pure offer it to him," since the rule regarding the purity of the person offering it is required, it is thereby stated that rinsing the mouth with water offered by oneself is not a cause of purification. Vasiṣṭha says: "Having performed the necessary duties, the most excellent among those who know purification should rinse his mouth.
Because "thereafter" (tataḥ) is the subject under discussion, the connection is "of the water-pot" (kamaṇḍaloḥ).

Āpastamba [1.4.20–21]: One should not perform useless acts with the remnants of water used for fire, nor should one sip water (ācamana) with such remnants. Nor should one sip water with water stirred by the hand or with water drawn up by only one hand.

[134] "With the remnants of water used for fire" means with the remnants of water taken for purposes such as sprinkling around the fire (*paryukṣaṇa*); the meaning is that one should not perform "useless acts" (*vṛthākarma*) with it. "Stirred" (*saṃkṣubdha*) means agitated or churned.
Yājñavalkya [1.22]; Viṣṇu [62.9]:
"The twice-born castes are purified by water reaching the heart, the throat, and the palate respectively; a woman and a Śūdra are purified when it has merely touched their lips once."
"Ultimately, [it refers to] a part within the mouth. By this, non-eating is intended;
one seeking bodily purity should first sip water three times and then wipe the mouth twice, but for women and Śūdras, once each."
Thus, from the statement of Manu recorded in the *Mahārṇava* (5.139):
"Pure," being understood as the subject, the *Brahmapurāṇa* states:
"A woman or a Śūdra becomes pure by constantly washing their hands and lips with water."
Regarding the eligibility of Śūdras, Gautama [10.52] states:
"Some say that washing the feet is for the purpose of *ācamana*.
That is, for the purpose consisting of *ācamana*.
Regarding the phrase "for the purpose of sipping water, for the purpose of sipping water," Manu, Aṅgiras, and Bṛhaspati are the authorities here.
Having slept, having sneezed, having eaten, having spat, having spoken untruths, having drunk water, and when about to recite the Veda— even if one is already pure— one should sip water.
Regarding the occasions for sipping water (ācamana), the Vāyu Purāṇa states: "Upon spitting,
as well as upon anointing the body, upon washing the feet,
upon conversing with one who is impure, and upon being defiled by something unclean."
In all cases of doubt, as well as when the topknot has been loosened,
one should always perform the ritual sipping of water (upaspṛśet) in this manner, even without the sacred thread (yajñopavīta).
[Even upon touching or seeing those of the lowest birth when they are impure:

Having sneezed, slept, eaten, or being desirous of eating or studying; having drunk, bathed, spat, put on a garment, walked upon a road, voided urine or excrement, touched the bone of a five-toed animal that is not greasy, or conversed with a *caṇḍāla* or a *mleccha*, one should sip water for purification (*ācamana*).
In the *Brahma Purāṇa*: "Upon sneezing, upon the discharge of phlegm, when food has been eaten, upon conversing with one of low caste, or when one has slept or brushed one's teeth."
Having sipped water and become composed, a man then becomes pure.

[136] *Dhīte* and *pīte*: this is the form of the root *dheṭ* (meaning "to drink") in its past passive participle (*niṣṭhā*). Here, "one of low caste" (*avarṇa*) refers to a *caṇḍāla* and others. *Śaṅkha*.
Having voided urine or excrement, having bathed and being desirous of eating,
as well as after eating, sneezing, sleeping, drinking water, and immersing oneself [in water].
Devala states another rule for the ritual sipping of water (ācamana):
"In the discharge of semen, urine, or feces; during eating; and after fatigue from traveling—such purification is prescribed, and it is seen to apply elsewhere as well."

Regarding those ancillary elements of sipping water (*ācamana*) without which it is said, "one who has sipped becomes pure," even by omitting some of those ancillaries, such a state is achieved in a sipping performed for reasons other than those specified in passages such as "upon [contact with] semen or urine," provided one omits only a certain part of the procedure.
Likewise,
having touched a human being who is impure from food remains, one perishes upon obtaining food.
In the same way, by washing both hands and feet and performing the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), one becomes pure.
Such is the leavings.
Likewise: that water which, being freed from purification, reaches the ground and perishes.
Having touched something smeared with impurity, one becomes pure by washing it and sipping water (ācamana).

Having touched something devoid of purity that has been cast from a vessel containing pure water, and having touched moist ground through contact with that [impurity], as well as "having washed what is smeared with impurity"—meaning, having washed a limb smeared with impurity—and having likewise sipped water (ācamana) after touching it, one becomes pure; this is the meaning.

Having voided urine or feces, having washed those smears of urine and feces, smears of food, smears of remnants, and whatever smears of semen there may be, and having washed his feet and sipped water, he becomes pure.
*Annalepān* refers to food-smeared substances, such as ointments made from food-based unguents (*udvartana*). *Uccheṣam* means leavings or remnants. Paiṭhīnasi states:
"Having touched leavings, semen, or urine, one becomes pure by wiping [the area], sipping water, and washing that defiled spot three times."
A place "smeared with remnants" (*ucchiṣṭa*) and so forth refers to the location. Regarding the act of sipping water (*ācamana*), which will be discussed below, Hārīta states:
"Having stepped onto a road, or being about to sleep, or having voided urine or excrement, or having eaten, one should wash one's hands and feet and then sip water."
Āpastamba [1.16.14–15]:

Upon dreaming, sneezing, blowing one's nose, touching phlegm, blood, hair, fire, cows, a Brāhmaṇa, or a woman; upon walking along a high road, touching something impure, or touching a person who is not pure; and upon putting on the waist-cloth (nīvī)—one should touch water, or fresh cow-dung, or plants, or the earth.

*Singhāṇikā* is nasal mucus; *aśru* is the watery secretion from the eyes. Regarding the touching of these two: when one performs *ācamana* (ritual sipping of water) upon touching fire, a cow, or a Brāhmaṇa, that is caused merely by the touch of those prescribed objects and not by any impurity (*aprāyatya*) produced by such contact. A *mahāpatha* is a royal road. "Having tied the *nīvī*" means having made a knot [in the lower garment].
Baudhāyana [1.10.17]: Having loosened the *nīvī* and readjusted it, one should touch water; or one should touch moist grass, cow dung, or the earth.
"Having loosened and released.
Āpastamba [1.15.7–11]:

"With empty hands, having raised his garment, he should touch water. Even when capable [of performing his duties], he should not remain impure for even a moment, nor while naked. There is no requirement to purify oneself while remaining in the water; however, having emerged, one should sip water (ācamana)."

"With empty hands" means with hands devoid of clods of earth and the like. "To a bird" (*vayasa*) means to a bird. "Having raised" means having lifted; by the context, "the hand" is the word to be supplied. "Prayamaṇa" means exertion, which is to say, purification. [This is] Yama's rule:
"Having emerged from the water and sipped water, having descended [again], one should touch [the limbs]."
In this way, one shall be endowed with prosperity, and Varuṇa himself will be honored.
"Having crossed" means having emerged; "having descended" means having entered. Following the word "water," Hārīta states:
"One should not cross without having touched [the water]."
One should cross over and emerge.
Paiṭhīnasi says:

"If one sips water while standing within the water, one becomes pure internally; if one sips water while standing outside the water, one would be pure only externally. Therefore, having placed one foot inside and one foot outside, one should sip water; thus one becomes pure in all respects."
Pārāśara [12.19–21]:
Upon sneezing, spitting, and likewise when one has food remnants from the teeth,
as well as upon speaking with outcasts, one should touch the right ear.
The holy places such as Prayāga and the rivers such as the Gaṅgā—
these deities always abide in the right ear of a Brahmin.
Manu declared that Āditya, Varuṇa, Soma, Agni, and likewise Vāyu reside within the right ear of the Brahmin.

Āpastamba [1.16.10–13]: Having touched the lips as far as their dark edge, one should sip water. One does not become impure by the presence of beard hairs inside the mouth as long as one does not touch them with the hand. Regarding those drops that are perceived falling from the mouth, sipping water is prescribed for them; some say that one need not sip water for those which fall upon the ground. The "dark edge" refers to the two corners of the mouth where the hair grows in the opposite direction.
In the *Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa* [34.69–72]:
Having sneezed, spat, or put on a garment, a wise man should sip water;
likewise after eating, licking something, vomiting, and so forth, including spitting.
One should perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), touch the back of a cow, look at the sun,
and indeed also take hold of the right ear.
For this [practice] is according to one's means; indeed, in the absence of the former, the latter follows.
It is not accepted that the subsequent [offering] may be undertaken while the previously mentioned [requirements] are still present.
Now, regarding the occasions for sipping water twice, Āpastamba [1.16.9] states:
"One who is about to eat, even if already pure, shall sip water twice, wipe his mouth twice, and touch [the lips] once."
And this touching of the lips once is mandatory only for one who is about to eat; it is once, not twice. Even regarding the wiping, the settled rule is that it is done exactly twice. Vyāsa states:
"Having washed both hands and feet, one who is eating should touch [water] twice."
Yājñavalkya [1.196]: Having bathed, drunk, sneezed, slept, eaten, or walked upon a road;
and after putting on a different garment, one who has already sipped water (ācamana) should sip water again.
Śaṅkha and Likhita state:
"In cases of urinating, defecating, spitting, and so forth, as well as when uttering harsh words, one should touch water for purification again and again.
'Harsh' (śukta) means rough."

Paiṭhīnasi states: "Upon the onset of a cough or labored breathing (*kalila-śvāsa*), or when one has passed through a road, a crossroads, or a cremation ground, even if one has already sipped water (*ācānta*), one should sip water again.

*Kalila* refers to thick phlegm; here, *śvāsa* refers to an abnormal respiration caused by physical exertion and the like. A *catvara* is a place where offerings are made to spirits and other such beings."
Now follows the exception regarding the sipping of water (ācamana).
On this point, Manu [5.141] states:
"The primary drops do not make one impure by leaving a remnant, nor do those which fall upon the limbs."
Nor [should one eat] what has gone onto the beard, nor what remains between the teeth.

"Principal" means those located in the mouth. "Go" means they move. "Beard" refers to the facial hairs. "Gone to the mouth" means entered into the mouth. "Between the teeth" means within the teeth. "Situated" means entered. Gautama [1.44]:
Regarding what is stuck to the teeth, it is treated like the teeth themselves, except when touched by the tongue.
The meaning is that they are not perceived as distinct from the tongue and the teeth.
Likewise, some say: "prior to death" (prāk cyuteḥ).
[142] Some maintain that even when there is contact with the tongue, as long as one does not emit [semen], one remains pure.
Likewise [1.46]:
"One should know that in the case of those who have emitted [semen], it is like a secretion; while swallowing it, one is indeed pure."
Devala says:
After removing food particles stuck between the teeth, one should perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana).
One should regard a particle stuck between the teeth as being like the tooth itself, provided it cannot be removed; however, if it is a coating that can be removed, one should consider it as such.
One should not exert great effort again in extracting [the arrow] from there;
for if a wound is caused by piercing with grass, impurity would become absolute.
Vasiṣṭha [3.39]: "Nor is there impurity from what has gone onto the beard"; the word "impure" is to be understood as the remainder of the sentence.
Likewise (3.40):
"Regarding food stuck between the teeth, as well as what may be inside the mouth, one becomes pure by simply swallowing it, even after having rinsed the mouth; that which remains is pure."
Whatever remains from one who has sipped water due to negligence, he becomes pure by swallowing it immediately. Paiṭhīnasi says:
Drops that have fallen to the ground are pure; if they are touched, they are purified; droplets are clean; and if two hairs become wet [with water], one should sip water again.

"Bindavas" here refers to drops from sipping water (*ācamana*). "Touched" means contacted. "Pure" means they do not cause a state of ritual impurity (*aprāyatya*). Even those that have fallen on the limbs are indeed capable of moistening two hairs; thus they become the occasion for a fresh sipping of water. Yājñavalkya [1.195]:
"Drops originating from the mouth are pure, as are the drops from sipping water."
Having discarded the beard that has entered his mouth and remains between his teeth, he is then pure.
"The drops that touch the feet of one who is making others sip water for purification are to be known as equal to those on the ground; one does not become impure because of them."
Regarding Atri and Aṅgiras:

"In the honey-mixture offering (madhuparka), in the Soma sacrifice, in water, and in the offerings to the vital breaths (prāṇāhutis), a Brahmin shall not become impure from remnants; such is the word of Atri."

The phrase "in water" (*apsu*) refers either to the *āpośāna* rite obtained by association with the *prāṇāhuti* offerings, or to the drinking of water during the *ācamana* (sipping) ritual; for regarding drinking water at other times, there is the injunction for *ācamana*: "Having drunk water, and one who is about to study... [Parāśara 7.33]: "In the case of betel, sugarcane, fruit, and likewise after eating, using oil, or applying ointment..."
Manu has declared that in the case of the honey-mixture (madhuparka) and the Soma sacrifice, there is no such thing as "leftover" (ucchiṣṭa).
[144] Śātātapa says: A twice-born man does not become impure by the remnants of food when fruit, roots, edible items, oils, betel leaf, or sugarcane are stuck to his teeth.
Regarding fruits that are pungent, bitter, or astringent, such as nutmeg (*jātīphala*) and others, this is based on the practice of the virtuous.
Regarding the means for cleansing the mouth, Vasiṣṭha [3.42] states:
"If, while moving about in activities other than those involving food, one should happen to touch something that is impure from eating..."
Having set that vessel on the ground and performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), one should proceed once more.

In this context, the word *ucchiṣṭa* (impure) refers to that which is unfit for sipping water (*ācamana*). For if it were used to denote impurity requiring bathing and the like, it would contradict the injunction for mere sipping.
Śaṅkha and Likhita state:
"One who is impure while holding an object should set it down, sip water, and then sprinkle the object with water."
And this refers to edible substances;
as for that which is stated:
"But if one whose hand holds a substance is somehow touched by something defiled by food remnants..."
Without even setting that object down, one who has sipped water (ācānta) shall attain purity.
Thus says the statement of Manu (5.143). Viśvarūpa and Bhartṛyajña maintain that this refers to objects held in the hand other than food and condiments intended for consumption.
Baudhāyana (1.8.22–26): [text follows].

If he becomes impure by taking up something made of metal, he should discard it, sip water, and, before taking it up again, sprinkle it with water. If he becomes impure by [taking] something else, he should discard it, sip water, and, before taking it up again, sprinkle it with water. Now, if he becomes impure by [taking] water, he should discard it, sip water, and, before taking it up again, sprinkle it with water. This very same procedure applies in reverse for a vessel. And in the case of an object made of wood, there is an option.

“By another he would become impure from leavings”: by another who is impure from leavings. “With water”: in cases such as rinsing the mouth or drinking water. “This very same [rule applies]”: here the procedure for taking [the vessel] is reversed. Having cast that away and discarded it, one should rinse the mouth; the meaning is that one should not take it up again. Bṛhaspati [Ācāra 6–8; p. 310]:
“While partaking of his own food and drink, if he should touch anything that is impure from leavings...”
Having placed that object on the ground and performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), he should proceed once again.
In a forest, in waterless places, at night, or on a path infested with thieves and tigers,
one who has voided urine or excrement while holding an object in hand does not incur fault.
One should first perform purification; then one should wash the feet. Having sipped water and sprinkled it [over oneself], that which has been taken becomes pure.
Now, regarding purity:
therein, Manu and Śaṅkha teach the training in purity and so forth. [Manu 2.69]
Having initiated the pupil, the teacher should first instruct him in purity,
as well as in proper conduct, the fire-ritual, and the twilight devotions.
Yājñavalkya [1.15]: Having initiated the pupil, the teacher should teach him the Veda preceded by the Great Vyāhṛtis, and he should instruct him in the rules of purification and proper conduct.
Conduct (*ācāra*) consists of saluting one's guru and other such duties;
the rules for the voiding of feces and urine are found in the *Viṣṇupurāṇa* [3.11.12–15].
"Not on ploughed land, nor in the midst of crops, nor in a cow-pen, nor in a gathering of people; not on a path, nor at river-crossings and the like, O bull among men."
One should not perform the voiding of feces or the discharge of urine in water, nor on the bank of water, nor in a cremation ground.
O King, a wise man should discharge urine facing north during the day, and facing the opposite direction at night; he should likewise void excrement, except in times of distress.
Having strewn the earth with grass and covered his head with a cloth,
he should stand there for no very long time and should not utter anything at all.
Yājñavalkya [1.154]:
One should cast away remnants of food, feces, urine, and water from the feet from a distance. Manu [4.151]: [One should likewise avoid spitting, etc., from a distance.]
One should perform urination far from one's dwelling, as well as the washing of the feet;
likewise, one should keep food remnants and the water used for rinsing at a distance.
*Niṣeka* is the casting away of leftover substances.
Āpastamba [1.31.2]:
One should perform urination and defecation at a distance from the dwelling, toward the south or the southwest.
The word "having gone" (*gatvā*) is to be supplied. The south-west is the direction of Nirṛti.
Again, Āpastamba [1.31.3] states:
"When the sun has set, one should avoid performing the acts of voiding urine and excrement outside the village and at a distance from one's dwellings."
"Ārāt" means at a distance.
[148] Manu [4.49]: "One should void [excrement] after having placed aside a piece of wood, a leaf, a clod of earth, or blades of grass."
Restraining his speech with self-control, his body wrapped and his head covered.

"Having set aside" means having hidden; "prayataḥ" means pure; "having restrained his speech"—this is the grammatical connection (*anvaya*). "Saṃvītam" means *nivītam* (worn as a sacred thread over the left shoulder), according to the Taittirīya Śruti: "The *saṃvīta* is human. He whose limbs are in that state is "one with limbs *saṃvīta*" (*saṃvītāṅgaḥ*).
Baudhāyana [1.10.10] says:
"Having set aside dry grass, wood unfit for sacrifice, or a clod of earth, one should void urine or excrement during the day and night, facing north or south respectively, having covered oneself."
"Non-sacrificial" means other than *palāśa* and other wood suitable for sacrificial purposes. "One should urinate" means one should void urine;
this follows from the Vāyu Purāṇa's statement, "one should perform the voiding of feces and urine," which continues [in the context]:
"with dry grass, or with wood, or with leaves, or with a split bamboo leaf."
Or even by covering the earth with vessels made of clay.

Regarding the use of the water-pot (*kamaṇḍalu*), Baudhāyana [states]: "While voiding urine in the open air, he holds it in his right hand and keeps the water for sipping (*ācamanīya*) in his left. Hārīta says:

Having wrapped his nose and mouth with a cloth, having hung a clay vessel around his neck, and having placed a water-pot (*kamaṇḍalu*) on the side of his right arm, he should go forth. [A "clay vessel" (*mṛddhātrī*) is a vessel for carrying earth; a "water-pot" (*kamaṇḍalu*) is a vessel filled with water for the purpose of purification. "He should go forth" means he should perform the act of going forth. The remainder [of the sense] is "urine and excrement. Yama says:
One should cover one's head while voiding excrement or urine,
having covered the ground with dry grass that is unfit for sacrifice.
The *Sāṃkhyāyana Gṛhyasūtra*:

If one is wearing only a single garment, one should place the sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*) on the ear. One should not face the sun, nor should one face one's own back. During the day one faces north; at night, one faces south.
The prohibition "nor [face] one's back" excludes the possibility of facing one's own back due to extreme humility. At midday, one faces south.
Devala says:
One should always void urine and feces facing north in the morning and facing south in the evening; however, one must avoid doing so during the twilight periods.

The established rule here is as follows: according to the statement of Devala, during the morning and evening periods—each consisting of three *muhūrtas*—one should face north and south respectively. Thus, the statement of Yama applies to the forenoon and afternoon beyond those times, prescribing that one should face west and east.
Āpastamba [1.31.1] states: "One should eat food facing east; one should evacuate facing south; one should urinate facing north; and one should pour water for washing the feet facing west."

"One should recite facing south" refers to the period of evening and night, according to the statement of Yama and Devala; thus, one faces westward. And this statement concerns times other than the two junctions of day and night (*saṃdhyā*). Hārīta says:
"At both junctions, one should face north."
Manu [4.51]: In shade or in darkness, by night or by day, a twice-born man may perform [the purification] facing any direction he finds comfortable, as well as when there is danger to his life.

It has been stated that in cases of shadow or darkness, when there is danger to life, or when there is fear of tigers and the like, the restriction regarding the direction one faces is not to be observed. Furthermore, Manu [4.45] says:
"One should not void urine on a path, nor on ashes, nor in a cow-pen."
Not on ploughed ground, nor in water, nor on a funeral pyre, nor on a mountain.
In the city, at the site for the piling of the fire-altar;
likewise [as stated in 4.46–48]:
"Neither in a ruined temple, nor ever on an anthill."
He does not go into pits containing living beings, nor does he walk, nor does he stand there.
One should not study having reached a riverbank, nor on a mountain peak,
nor while looking at wind, fire, a Brahmin, the sun, water, or cows.

One should never discharge feces or urine [on a mountain]. Although the prohibition of the mountain peak is already established by the phrase "nor on a mountain" (*na ca parvate*), which prohibits sitting upon a mountain, that specific prohibition is reiterated for the sake of emphasizing the greater gravity of the offense. "Seeing the wind" means perceiving it directly in front of oneself.
— Devala.
One should not void urine or feces in a pond, a well, a river, a cow-pen, a shrine, on water, on a path, on ashes, in fire, in a place for ritual desire, or in a cremation ground.
A *caitya* is a tree well-known to the village. A *kāmya* is a desirable place such as a garden and so forth.
Yama says: "Ponds, lakes, rivers, and springs."
One should avoid earth from a mountain, cow dung, ashes, and land ploughed by a plow.
A *palvala* is a small pond; a *taḍāga* is an artificial lake. Likewise:
husks, charcoal, potsherds, and temples of the deities.
Royal highways, cremation grounds, fields, and threshing floors;
One who is under restraint should not frequent a shaded area, a visible crossroads, or a visible pleasant place. [The latter] means a beautiful place.
Likewise.
One should avoid water and the edge of a body of water, and one should avoid the path;
one should also avoid the roots of trees, as well as shrines, pits, and holes.

By the very statement, “and one should avoid a path,” the prohibition of royal roads and crossroads is already established; their specific mention again is for the purpose of indicating an excess of fault [in using them]. Hārīta says:

One should not void urine or excrement on a square (catvara) or at a side-gate (upadvāra); nor at a watering place (tīrtha); nor where crops are growing; nor on a sacrificial ground; nor beneath trees fit for sacrifice.
[153] A *tīrtha* is a path for descending into water. Regarding Vasiṣṭha [6.12]: "Not sown" means not those that depend upon grassy meadows.
*Śādvala* is a green and moist area of ground;
Viṣṇu [60.6] says it is not on saline soil (*ūṣara*).
Likewise [60.13]:
not in another's impurity.
Likewise [60.20].
"Not in the air.
This means one who is situated in a watchtower or similar structure in the air.
Likewise [60.22–23]:
One should not [void urine or excrement] facing the wind, fire, the moon, the sun, a woman, a teacher, or a Brahmin. Nor indeed with one's head covered.
Āpastamba [1.30.16–17]:
One should avoid performing the act of voiding urine or excrement in the shade; however, one may urinate in one's own shadow.
“*Svāṃ tu chāyām*” means “having relied upon one’s own shadow.
Likewise: “[1.30.18] One should not void urine or excrement while wearing sandals.”
Likewise [1.30.23]:
One should avoid the act of voiding urine or excrement while facing fire, the sun, water, a Brāhmaṇa, or deities associated with cattle. Gautama [19.13]: [states the same].
One should not discharge urine, feces, or impure substances while facing the wind, fire, a Brahmin, the sun, water, deities, or cows.
Yama says: One should not urinate facing the sun, nor should one look at one's own excrement.
Having seen [these], one should look up at the sun, as well as at a cow, fire, and Brahmins.
One should always face the sun, the wind, a cow, a twice-born man,
the moon, water, and the two twilights.
It destroys the wisdom and the very path of one who urinates [in these places];
and those who urinate upon these become ones whose life-span has departed.
Hārīta says: One who urinates on a road, at a crossroads, at a watering place, in a cremation ground,
or in a temple incurs disgrace and is deprived of long life.
One should always take food in secret and likewise dispose of waste in secret;
for when one is concealed, one is joined with prosperity, whereas in public, one is obstructed by prosperity.
[155] Regarding the rules for purification,
Hārīta says as follows:
"He should wipe it with a clod of earth or with dry wood," says Pāraskara [2.7.16].
Or he should wipe it with wood that has fallen off by itself.

Gautama [9.15]: One should not remove urine or feces with leaves, clods of earth, or stones. However, according to Hārīta, the rule regarding clods of earth applies when other materials are unavailable.
Āpastamba [1.10.24]:
One should avoid using a stone, a clod of earth, or fresh plants and trees broken off while upright for the cleansing of urine and feces.
Devala:
"One should not release the penis before purification during urination or defecation;
[so say] Yājñavalkya and Baudhāyana.
Having stood up with the penis held, one should [perform purification] with earth and water drawn from [a clean source].
One should perform purification untiringly so as to remove both odor and stains.
"Atandrita" means one who has become free from laziness.
In the *Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa*:
"Having drawn up water and taken clay, being restrained in speech..."
One should perform [the rite] facing north during the day, and if at night, facing south.
Likewise:
"One should apply earth to what is well-washed, and water at the end of the earth.
"Well-washed" means having the hands and feet thoroughly cleansed.
Dakṣa says: "One application of clay on the penis, three on the left [hand], and two applications of clay on both [hands] are prescribed;
'on the left' and 'on both' refer to the hands. 'Three' means three times. This much is the purification required after voiding urine."
Three applications of clay for drinking water, ten for one [hand], and seven for both;
this is declared to be the purification for a householder, while for the other three [orders], it is respectively as follows.
Twofold, threefold, and for the fourth, fourfold.
Earth and water should be taken in appropriate quantities for the purpose of discharging feces and urine,
as well as for the purification of the twelve bodily impurities.
Manu and Viṣṇu state: "Fat, semen, blood, marrow, urine, feces, earwax, nasal mucus,
phlegm, tears, rheum of the eyes, and sweat— these twelve are the impurities of men."
One application of clay should be made to the penis, three to the anus, ten likewise to one hand,
and seven to both hands by one desiring purification.
[157] This is the standard of purity for householders; it is double for students, triple for forest-dwellers, and fourfold for ascetics.
Yama says: One application of clay should be made on the penis, three on the anus, and fourteen on the left hand;
thereafter, seven applications of clay must be given with both hands.
Śaṅkha says: Seven applications of clay are prescribed for the penis, two for the male organ;
twenty for one hand, and fourteen for both hands together.
The *mehana* is the anus.
Likewise: "Three applications of clay should be made after having cleaned the nails."
But three [handfuls] should always be given on the feet by one who desires purification.
This is the standard of purity for householders and likewise for those living with their teachers;
it should be twofold for forest-dwellers and threefold for ascetics.

Paiṭhīnasi: Having taken earth, one application is for the penis, five for the anus, ten for one hand, and seven for both hands. This is the purification for householders; it is double for students (brahmacārins).
And for forest-dwellers it is threefold, and for ascetics it is fourfold.

Or, having washed away the smear of odor and rinsed his mouth, he becomes pure. [158] Hārīta says: Having gone to a secluded place, one should apply one application of clay to the penis, three to the anus; not out of fear of the defect of wind, one should wash the hands and apply ten applications to the left hand, six to the back, and seven to both together. For students (*brahmacārin*), it is double; for forest-dwellers (*vānaprastha*), triple; and for mendicants (*bhikṣu*), quadruple.
In the *Brahma Purāṇa*: "Two applications of clay should be given to the penis, seven to the anus in due order,
and thirty-two applications of clay should likewise be given to the left hand."
Furthermore, there are always sixteen [verses] for the two [feet], and seven for each;
having taken up two [verses] for the feet with well-washed hands.

Having sipped water twice, one becomes pure; then, having remembered the eternal Viṣṇu, Baudhāyana [1.10.11–14] states: for urine, there is washing with earth and water three times on the hand; the same sequence applies to feces, [three times for both the anus and the hand].
[Yama says: One application of clay on the penis, three on the anus, fourteen on the left hand;
thereafter, seven applications of clay must be given with both hands.
This purity is twofold for a householder, threefold for a student,
fourfold for a forest-dweller, and fivefold for a mendicant.
Śaṅkha says:
Seven applications of clay are prescribed for the penis, two for the male organ;
twenty are to be applied to one hand, and fourteen to both hands.
Devala says:
As long as one considers oneself pure, for that long purification is prescribed;
neither a fixed measure nor a specific number of items is taught by the learned.

In accordance with this statement, a systematic rule (*vyavasthā*) is established regarding the number of earth-clods mentioned by Manu, which exceeds the previously stated numbers, due to the concern that the application of fragrance and ointment might persist. However, when performing the practice according to the number prescribed as four or more, even if that higher number is reached, purification must necessarily be carried out up to the limit of the prescribed number.
As Dakṣa has said:
"One desiring purity through purification should not perform fewer or more [clods] than required."
"One should apply oneself to penances when a transgression of prescribed rules has been committed. Thus [it is said].
Following purification, Śaṅkha and Likhita state:
"Having touched the water-pot, having washed his hands and feet, and having sipped water (ācamana), he should meditate upon Īśāna in his mind."
Īśāna is the Lord of all.
Regarding the sequence following purification, Hārīta states:
"Having washed his feet with three [handfuls of water], and having wiped the water-pot with cow-dung or earth, he should touch water as before and gaze at the sun, the moon, or fire."

[160] Having performed the ritual sipping of water (upaspṛśya), one should look at the sun during the day, and at Agni or Soma at night. Dakṣa says: "The purification prescribed for the day is ordained to be half [the amount] at night."
For one who is ill, it shall be half of that; and for one on the road, it is traditionally held to be half of that.
The first clay is prescribed to be the measure of half a prasṛti;
the second and the third are proclaimed to be half of that [respectively].
In this case, it is declared that even at the funeral mound (liṅga), the three-fold rite is completed;
water should be offered until the clay has been entirely exhausted.
Purification may be achieved with inexpensive materials; there is neither affliction nor expenditure of wealth.
"With inexpensive materials" means with easily obtained materials. Thus, his character has been tested even in matters of ritual purity.

In the Viṣṇupurāṇa [3.10.16–17]: One should not take earth dug up by anthills or mice, nor that from within water, nor what remains after cleansing, nor that from a house which has originated as a smear.
A king should avoid all these types of earth when performing purification: earth inhabited by living creatures, and earth turned up by a plow.
"Filled with living beings within" means pervaded by living beings inside, in the middle. Yama says:
"A Brahmin should likewise fetch earth from a riverbank that contains sand."
Nor from what has been dug up by a nail, nor from an anthill, nor from dusty ground, nor from mud.
A wise man should avoid these: a path, saline soil, or the remnants of another's purification;
for such purification is considered futile.
Ākhu means a mouse.
Now, the procedure for the twilight devotions (*saṃdhyāvidhi*).
Regarding this, Viṣṇu states [28.1–2]:
"Now follows the residence of the student (*brahmacārin*) in the teacher’s house; he shall perform the worship of the two twilights."
Yogiyājñavalkya says: Hereafter I shall proclaim the determination regarding the twilight worship (saṃdhyopāsana),
by performing which one is liberated from the sins committed during the day and night.
A Brahmin who is devoted to the twilight worship remains steadfast in his Brahminhood even if he has entered another birth, regardless of his current condition.
"In every state" means one who is intent on censurable activities such as serving [low-caste people], or who is incapable of proper purification and so forth.
Manu [1.101]: "Standing while reciting the morning twilight prayer, one removes the sin of the night."
But sitting facing the west, one burns away the impurity created during the day.
Śātātapa says:
Falsehood, the smell of liquor, and sexual intercourse during the day—
even these are purified by the Śūdra’s food when the twilight prayer (saṃdhyā) has been performed outside.
A *vṛṣala* here is one who is unrighteous. As it is said in the *Mahābhārata*:
"For Dharma is indeed the Blessed Lord Vṛṣa; those who act contrary to him, the gods know as a *vṛṣala*. Thus it is stated.
Yama says: Whatever evil one commits during the day by deed, thought, or speech,
one destroys that by sitting for the evening twilight prayer and through breath-control exercises (prāṇāyāma).
Whatever evil one commits at night by deed, mind, or speech,
one dispels it by performing the morning twilight devotion through breath-control exercises (prāṇāyāma).
But those who constantly perform the twilight devotions with firm vows,
having shaken off their sins, go to the eternal world of Brahmā.
And this refers to the subject of sins committed through ignorance and so forth:
"Whether by day or by night, whatever has been done through ignorance—
all that perishes by performing the twilight devotions (saṃdhyā) at the three times."
Thus, from the statement of Yājñavalkya; and Baudhāyana [2.7.18] says:
"Whatever sin has been committed by the organ of generation, or whatever may have been committed by the feet..."
Whether it has been committed by the two arms, by the mind, or indeed by speech.
Having performed the evening twilight devotion (*saṃdhyā*), he is thereby released from that [debt].
Śaṅkha and Likhita state:
"One who observes his vows should perform the external twilight devotion."
"Accompanied by his vow" (*savratī*): that which is performed together with the vow, such as Vedic study and so forth, is "with the vow"; one who possesses this is a *brahmacārī*.
Manu [2.219]: "The sun should never set upon him [while he is still in the village], nor should it rise upon him anywhere."

"He" refers to the religious student (*brahmacārin*). "The sun should set" means it should go down; the intended meaning is that the rising and setting of the sun must be observed by the religious student outside the village. Śātātapa says:
"In the house, the twilight rite is considered natural; in a cow-pen, it is said to be a hundredfold more meritorious."
In the rivers near the presence of Śiva, there are hundreds of thousands, even infinite [beings].
The natural [sandhyā] yields a single-fold fruit;
thus says Saṃvarta:
"One should perform the morning sandhyā while the stars are still visible, according to the prescribed rule."
[165] He performed the evening twilight rite with the sun still present, when the orb of the sun was half-set.
Yogiyājñavalkya states: "The decrease and increase of the days occur constantly in due order;
however, the twilight (saṃdhyā) is traditionally held to be exactly one muhūrta, remaining equal during both decrease and increase."
For a mere moment, that is, for the duration of two *nāḍīs*. Likewise:
"One should perform the twilight worship (*saṃdhyopāsana*) at the junction [of day and night], neither when the sun has set nor when it has risen."

Baudhāyana [2.7.12–14]: One should begin the first [twilight rite] before the stars have appeared and complete it after the sun has risen; one should begin the latter [twilight rite] before the sun has set and complete it even long after the stars have appeared. When both twilights are accomplished, there is continuity between day and night.

"Before the stars have appeared" means at a time well before [the appearance of] many stars; by the word "even," it is meant that it may be done when only a few stars are present. "Even long after" means until the appearance of many stars; by the word "even," the meaning is that one should complete it even when only a few stars are visible.

Gautama [2.14–17]: Bathing in water; according to some, the Godāna ceremony and so forth; and performing the twilight devotions outside [the village].
