He should stand during the morning [devotion] and sit during the evening one, as long as the celestial light lasts, or until the stars appear, remaining silent. [166] The meaning is that certain teachers maintain that the bath and the performance of the twilight devotions outside [the village] begin from the time of the Godāna vow.

Viṣṇu [28.2–4]: One should recite the morning twilight prayer while standing and the evening one while seated. During the two periods of time, the rites for the single sacred fire (ekāgni) are to be performed. Immersion in water should be like a staff. Hārīta.
Whether one does not bathe or does bathe, it is like the rule regarding the staff.

In this regard, there is a settled option: one who is pure may not bathe, while one who is impure must bathe, according to the statement of Baudhāyana: "One who is impure may be consecrated, or one who is pure may remain unconsecrated" [2.7.2].
Āpastamba [1.2.30] states:
One should not bathe in water while boasting;
by boasting during the bath, one reveals one's own superior impurity.
Baudhāyana [2.7.1–4].

Now, therefore, we shall explain the rule for the twilight worship (*saṃdhyopāsana*). Having gone to a sacred bathing place (*tīrtha*), whether one has already bathed and is pure or is not yet bathed but is pure, having washed his hands and feet and sipped water (*ācamana*), he drinks water in the evening with the mantra, "May Agni and Wrath [protect me]," and in the morning with, "May Sūrya and Wrath [protect me]. With his hand holding a purifier (*pavitra*), he sprinkles himself with water that is fragrant, with verses containing the word *ap* (water), with those addressed to Varuṇa, with those of golden color, with the *pāvamānī* verses, with the *vyāhṛtis*, and with other purifying formulas; thus he becomes pure.

The verses beginning with *surabhimatī* and *dadhikrāvṇaḥ*; those containing the word "water" (*abliṅga*), such as *āpo hi ṣṭhā*; the three verses addressed to Varuṇa (*vāruṇyaḥ*) beginning with *yac cid dhi te viśaḥ*; the four verses beginning with *hiraṇyavarṇāḥ* and *śucayaḥ pāvakāḥ*; and the *pāvamānya* verses beginning with *pavamānaḥ suvarjanaḥ*. Furthermore, they cite this:
"Immersion in water for bathing is prescribed for all social classes (*sarvavarṇika*)."
"Sprinkling with mantras is also especially recommended for the twice-born.
Furthermore,
at the commencement of all ritual acts, prior to the time for the twilight worship (*saṃdhyopāsana*), one becomes purified by sprinkling oneself with this collection of purifiers.

And this ritual cleansing (*mārjana*)—beginning with “*agniś ca mā manyuś ca*” and ending with “*pavitraiḥ*”—is for one who has already bathed. However, the cleansing by means of mantras beginning with “*śaṃ na āpaḥ*” and ending with “*aghamarṣaṇasūktena*” from the *Yogiyājñavalkya-smṛti* should be understood as a subsidiary part of the rite intended specifically for one who is impure and unable to perform the primary ritual bath, due to physical incapacity or in consideration of time, strength, and other factors.
Some wise authorities maintain that there are seven types of baths, starting with the mantra-bath (*mantrasnāna*).

Thus, from the statement of Yājñavalkya the Yogin: "due to the defect of time" and "due to incapacity," [this applies] to all rites, including the *śrāddha* and others. The "collection of purifiers" refers to the group of mantras just mentioned, beginning with the *surabhimatī*.
Furthermore, they cite this:

Seated upon *darbha* grass, holding *darbha* blades, facing the east with his hand containing water, he should repeat the *Sāvitrī* one thousand times, or an unlimited number of times, or a hundred times by means of breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāma*). Or, with the *praṇava* at both the beginning and end, accompanied by the seven *vyāhṛtis*, he may repeat it ten times mentally. When exhausted by three breath-restraints, he worships the gift with the "Heart of Brahman" and the two verses addressed to Varuṇa: "This, O Varuṇa... and "To thee I go... Likewise, in the morning, standing and facing the east, he should worship the day with the two verses addressed to Mitra: "Mitra, the supporter of the people... and "Mitra, knowing [all things], impels the people... with these two verses.

[169] “Immeasurable” (*aparimita*) is intended to mean a number exceeding those previously mentioned. Regarding the phrase “or a hundred times by means of breath-restraints” (*prāṇāyāmaśo vā śatakṛtvaḥ*): “by means of breath-restraints” (*prāṇāyāmaśaḥ*) means through the act of *prāṇāyāma*. This is what is meant: one should perform as many *prāṇāyāmas* as are required for the *Sāvitrī* to reach a count of one hundred. Here, *prāṇāyāma* is defined merely as the restraint of the breath, since only the *Sāvitrī* was introduced previously. Regarding “or ten times mentally, with the *praṇava* at both ends and accompanied by the seven *vyāhṛtis*”: “at both ends” means one should place the syllable *Oṃ* at the beginning and the end. There is an option among these three alternatives depending on one’s capacity. Regarding “and being exhausted by three *prāṇāyāmas*, [one should recite] with the ‘Heart of Brahman’ (*brahmahṛdaya*)”: having performed one of the previously mentioned methods, one then performs three *prāṇāyāmas* with the *praṇava* (the Heart of Brahman); “exhausted” (*śrāntaḥ*) by them means weary. Being in such a state, one worships the night with the two verses addressed to Varuṇa, namely “*imaṃ me varuṇa*” and “*tat tvā yāmi*. Since the night has Varuṇa as its deity, by worshipping Varuṇa, the worship of the night is accomplished. By this, the rule “one worships the day with the two verses addressed to Mitra” is to be explained. Thus says the Taittirīya Śruti: “The day belongs to Mitra, the night belongs to Varuṇa.”
Yājñavalkya [1.22]: Bathing, sprinkling with water while reciting the mantras dedicated to the waters, restraint of the breath (prāṇāyāma),
worship of the sun, and the daily recitation of the Gāyatrī mantra.
Likewise [1.24–25]:
Having restrained his breath and sprinkled himself with water using the three verses addressed to the waters,
he should sit reciting the Sāvitrī until the appearance of the stars.

One should thus remain standing during the morning twilight until the sun appears, reciting the hymns addressed to the deities of the year, beginning with "āpo hi ṣṭhā. "Mārjana" is the sprinkling of water upon the head using *kuśa* grass held at the *devatīrtha*;
one should perform the cleansing of the head with *kuśa* blades and drops of water.

Thus, from the statement of Kātyāyana in the *Candogya-pariśiṣṭa*: "The worship (*upasthāna*) of the Sun" is the illumination [of the deity] with a solar mantra, beginning with "ud u tyaṃ jātavedasam. "Facing west" (*pratyak*) means having one's face toward the west; "facing east" (*prāk*) means having one's face toward the east. Yogi-Yājñavalkya says:
"The syllable *oṃ*, the seven *vyāhṛtis*, and the *gāyatrī* together with its head..."
The three verses beginning with "āpo hi ṣṭhā" and the Aghamarṣaṇa hymn.
For the sake of protecting the sun, it was created by the Self-born Brahmā himself in the past; day after day, in the evening and the morning, that is remembered as his mouth.
Likewise:
"However many foolish twice-born men there may be on this earth who abide in improper occupations—
for the sake of purifying them, the twilight devotion was created by the Self-existent One."

By whomsoever the twilight devotions (*saṃdhyā*) have been worshipped, by him Viṣṇu has been worshipped. Those who abide in improper actions (*vikarmasthāḥ*) are those who transgress prescribed duties and perform prohibited acts. Likewise:
There are thirty crores of well-known Rākṣasas called Mandehas;
day after day, they rush toward the thousand-rayed sun as it rises.
Day after day, they all desired to devour the sun;
then a most dreadful battle took place between the sun and them.
Then all the hosts of gods and the sages whose wealth is austerity worshipped him with the thought, "It is twilight," as they scattered that great water.
Conjoined with the Brahman of the syllable *oṃ* and consecrated by the *gāyatrī*,
those Daityas were consumed by that water which had become like a thunderbolt.
That Sun, conjoined with the Brahman of the syllable Om— that is, conjoined with the Brahman in the form of the syllable Om—
having known this, the Brahmin who worships him while his vows are well-observed shall obtain long life and is liberated from all sins.
Likewise: "The morning twilight is known as Gāyatrī, the midday as Sāvitrī;
that which occurs at the evening twilight should be understood as Sarasvatī."
Sāvitrī is white, Gāyatrī is red in color, and Sarasvatī is to be known as black; thus is the triad of junctions (saṃdhyā) described.
Likewise: "Because it is the meeting of the three deities beginning with Brahmā,
and the conjunction of all the gods, it is therefore called Saṃdhyā."
"It is more venerable than [the body] of living beings, for it is indeed the paternal body.
"The paternal body" refers to that of the Grandfather (Brahmā), who created the ancestors.
It unites [the self] with the supreme, subtle, qualityless [state], which awakens one to the qualities.
That which connects what transcends both primordial matter (pradhāna) and the person (puruṣa) is called the "junction" (saṃdhi).
"Saṃdhatte pare" means that by whom the *saṃdhyā*— which joins one with the Supreme, that is, the Supreme Self— is worshipped, by him Viṣṇu is worshipped.

Because this was stated previously: [He is] subtle (*sūkṣma*), not gross (*asthūla*); devoid of qualities (*nirguṇa*), meaning free from the qualities of transformation (*vikāra-guṇa*); the awakener of qualities (*guṇabodhin*), the knower of all qualities such as honor (*māna*) and the rest; transcending both *pradhāna* and *puruṣa*—*pradhāna* being the unmanifest (*avyakta*) and *puruṣa* being the individual soul (*jīva*)—transcending these two and distinct from them. [The term] *saṃdhita* means performing a conjunction (*saṃdhāna*). Because the sun is present, one should understand that he joins again with the sun as the locus—that is, there is a connection with the deity of the twilight (*saṃdhyā*) in that very sun—since it has been said, "she who is seated together as the twilight" (*saṃdhyeti samupāsīnā*). By this, the intention is that the designation "twilight" (*saṃdhi*) for that time is due to these two reasons for conjunction.
Likewise: "The knower of the Self, being a twice-born, should always perform the three twilight devotions (saṃdhyā).

A 'knower of the Self' is one who knows the Self as distinct from the body and the senses, and who understands that by failing to perform them regularly, he will become a partaker of suffering in the next world."
In this context, he mentions bathing as an incidental matter:
"Brahmins living as householders should bathe at both twilights;
however, an ascetic should bathe at all three twilights."
An ascetic, such as one in the forest-dwelling stage (vānaprastha) and so forth,
being unable due to the defects of time or lack of capacity,
should then recognize that purification (mārjana) seen by the sages through mantras is possible even for him.

[173] Due to incapacity, due to affliction by disease and the like, and due to seasonal defects such as extreme cold and so forth—one should perform purification with mantras, having learned this from the sages; this is the meaning. *Śaṃ no āpaḥ*, *Drupadā*, *Āpo hi ṣṭhā*, and *Aghamarṣaṇa*—the mantra-bath is declared to consist of these four Ṛgvedic mantras.
“May the waters be auspicious for us on the desert tracts,” so it is said in the Kaṭha Brāhmaṇa. The word "with four" refers to the hymn (*sūkta*) because of the plurality of its verses.

Bathing with mantras addressed to the waters, ritual sprinkling (*mārjana*), and breath control (*prāṇasaṃyama*) performed with the Aghamarṣaṇa hymn are equal to the purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*) at a horse sacrifice.
When a state of impurity has arisen, one should indeed perform a bath;
however, with the previously mentioned mantras, otherwise it is prescribed as mere sprinkling (mārjana).
Likewise: for the Aghamarṣaṇa Sūkta, the seer (ṛṣi) is indeed Aghamarṣaṇa;
the meter (chandas) is Ānuṣṭubh, and Bhāvavṛtta is the deity (daivata).
The application [of this rite] at the final purificatory bath (*avabhṛthaka*) of the horse sacrifice has been prescribed;
it has been proclaimed by the authors of the *Smṛtis* for the purpose of removing all sins.
[The Creator is "active in existence" (bhāvavṛttaḥ), meaning he is engaged in activity within the world which consists of existence.
Likewise:
he likewise [ordains] the maintenance, origination, and dissolution of the cosmic egg (aṇḍapiṇḍa) which has become reality.
Everything has been declared within this subtle [reality]; this is what is called the meaning of the mantra.
[174] “Of the cosmic egg,” that is to say, of the Brahmāṇḍa, which is the world itself—“in the subtle Brahman,” the “creation, maintenance, and dissolution” are “expounded” in this hymn.
“Even having slain these three worlds, one should mutter the Aghamarṣaṇa three times;
Manu has declared that it is just like the final purificatory bath of a horse-sacrifice.”
Just as the horse-sacrifice, the king of rituals, is the remover of all sins,
so too is the Aghamarṣaṇa hymn the remover of all sins.
Likewise:
Sindhudvīpa is the seer; Gāyatrī is the metre;
Water is declared to be the deity; and its application is for the purpose of sprinkling (mārjana).
In all cases, the purificatory rite for those lacking gender markers has been declared;
however, the case of the prince Kokila is said to follow the Ṛṣi tradition from Drupada.
The meter is Anuṣṭubh and the deity is indeed the Waters;
its application is at the purificatory bath (avabhṛtha) of the Sautrāmaṇī sacrifice.
That goddess named Drupadā is established in the Yajurveda;
by reciting it three times while submerged in water, one is released from the sin of killing a Brahmin.
Having taken water in both hands, one should recite the Drupadā verse three times;
by placing that water upon one's head, one is liberated from all sins.
Having thus understood the application of the mantras, O best of the twice-born,
learn now how they perform the twilight devotions (saṃdhyā) in the proper manner.
Facing the northeast, pure and with a restrained mind,
having sipped water for ritual purification (ācamana), he should sip water again after consecrating it with the mantra "Ṛtam".
In this way, food and drink defiled by internal impurities are indeed purified;
one should recite the Sāvitrī three times, as well as the Praṇava and the Vyāhṛtis.
Having likewise performed the sprinkling, one should sprinkle with the verse beginning "āpo hi ṣṭhā," inserting the half-verse and casting the [remaining] half-verse above and below.
When [the water] is discharged toward the lower part [of the body], the asuras go to their destruction;
however, bathing in all sacred fords results from sprinkling it upward.
Then one should perform the ritual sprinkling (mārjana) with the Aghamarṣaṇa Sūkta; thereafter, one should employ the "śaṃ na āpaḥ" verse and the "drupadā" verse on the left side.
One should recite the Gāyatrī preceded by the syllable "oṃ," as well as the Aghamarṣaṇa hymn beginning with the water-mantras (abliṅga).
This very Brahman is indeed constant; it was perceived of old by the Self-born One himself.
Having thus performed the sweeping as a means for external purification,
one should likewise practice breath control (prāṇāyāma) for the sake of internal purification.

*Sātatya* means "constantly," because it must be performed perpetually. "Brahma" refers to the god Brahmā. However, passages such as "May the waters be auspicious for us" (*śaṃ na āpa*) pertain to optional rites (*kāmya*). Śaṅkha [9.8–10] states that after speaking thus, one should then perform the cleansing in the water.
With the three verses beginning "āpo hi ṣṭhā," he should proceed duly and in the proper sequence.
Likewise, with the four *ṛc* verses beginning "hiraṇyavarṇā," as well as "śaṃ no devīḥ" and similarly "śaṃ na āpaḥ."
One should utter this mantra over the water:
"Having spoken thus," [beginning with] "I take refuge in the god Varuṇa" and ending with the collection of mantras "and may they protect me in every way.
Having sipped water (ācamana) in this manner, one should perform those rites for the cleansing of the sacred site (tīrtha) that were previously described.
One should sprinkle water consecrated by those mantras upon the head and likewise upon the ground.
By water sprinkled upon the head, his sin is destroyed;
by water cast upon the ground, the asuras, the enemies of the gods, are slain.
One should recite the *vyāhṛtis* as well as the imperishable syllable (*akṣara*).

Having sipped water (*ācamya*) according to the procedure for sipping just described, one should perform the cleansing within the water (*tīrthasaṃmārjana*) with the verses beginning with "āpo hi ṣṭhā" which were previously mentioned, and with the imperishable syllable in the form of the *oṃkāra*. Thereafter, one should ritually touch [the limbs] with this mantra in accordance with the law.
You move within all beings, dwelling in their secret cave, facing every direction.
"You are the sacrifice, you are the *vaṣaṭ*-call; you are the waters, light, essence, and the immortal.
Having "touched" [the water], that is, having sipped it, and thereafter facing the sun, [he should touch] the water.
One should cast [the oblation] with this mantra: "ud u tyaṃ jātavedas."
This very same procedure is prescribed for the two twilights by the twice-born.
"This very same" refers to that which was prescribed for midday.
One should recite the prayer while standing during the morning twilight, and likewise while seated during the evening twilight.
Then one should recite purifying mantras or a single purifier according to one's capacity;
by means of the long twilight devotions, the seers attained long life.

"Purifying rites" (*pavitrāṇi*) refer to the *aghamarṣaṇa* and others as declared by Śaṅkha. "The state of long twilight" (*dīrghasaṃdhyatvam*) means being occupied for a long duration through recitation (*japa*). And this performance of the long twilight rite is for one desiring long life. We shall explain the procedure for recitation (*japa*) regarding the obligatory daily time later on. Kātyāyana states in the *Chandogapariśiṣṭa*:
"Henceforth, I shall proclaim the rule for the worship of the twilights (*saṃdhyopāsana*). [Gobhilasmṛti 2.1–17]
[177] Since a Brahmin who omits the twilight prayers is traditionally held to be unworthy of performing sacred rites.
Having placed *kuśa* grass in his left hand, he should perform the act of sipping water (*ācamana*).
The left hand should hold the supporting grass (*upagraha*), while the right hand should hold the *pavitra* strainers.
“Upagrahas” are many blades of *kuśa* grass.
Having surrounded oneself with water for protection on all sides,
one should perform the sprinkling (*mārjana*) of the head with *kuśa* grass and drops of water.
"At the end" means at the conclusion of the previously mentioned ritual acts; the meaning is that protection should be performed by surrounding oneself on all sides with water.
"The *praṇava*, *bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ*, and the *Sāvitrī* as the third, and the three-verse hymn addressed to the Waters (*abdaivata*) as the fourth—this is the *mārjana* (sprinkling purification)."
These three, Bhūḥ and the others, are indeed the imperishable Great Utterances (mahāvyāhṛtis);
likewise, Mahas, Janas, Tapas, Satyam, and the Gāyatrī as the Head (śiras).
“*Āpo jyotī raso ’mṛtaṃ brahma bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ*” is the head;
one should utter the *praṇava* before each member and at the end of the head.
One should recite these [syllables] together with that [Om], likewise with these ten [vowels], while holding the breath;
this is called *prāṇāyāma*.
Having drawn up water with his hand and applied it to his nose,
he should mutter the Aghamarṣaṇa hymn either three times or once, without holding his breath.

Having risen, he should offer a handful of water toward the sun with the "triad"—that is, with the *vyāhṛtis*, this *gāyatrī*, and this *śiras*, together with these ten *praṇavas*; "he should offer" means he should cast it. Immediately thereafter, he should worship with the two verses beginning with "uc citram."

“Ut,” “ud u tyaṃ jātavedasam,” and so forth; “citraṃ,” “citraṃ devānām,” and “ud vayaṃ tamasas patiḥ. The wise say that this worship (upasthāna) should be performed at both twilights. However, in the middle of the day and at sunrise, the hymns beginning with “bibhrāṭ” may be used according to one’s preference.
The section beginning with "bibhrāḍ ādi" and "bibhāḍ bṛhat," the Śivasamkalpa, the Maṇḍalabrāhmaṇa, and the Puruṣasūkta—
these he should recite without his heels touching the ground, even if it be on a single foot or half a foot.
One should do so either with palms joined in reverence or with arms raised upward.

“That” refers to the [proper] posture. “With heels not touching” means that the parts of the soles near the ankles do not rest upon the earth. Where there is an abundance of hardship even for the wise who seek the highest good, there they say there is an abundance [of merit]; for it is through hardship that the highest good is attained.

One should remain standing during the first twilight until the sun rises, during the middle one according to one's ability, and during the last one sitting until the appearance of the stars; reciting the three [Vedic] collections during each.
This is declared to be the threefold twilight (saṃdhyā), which is the very foundation of Brahminhood;
he who has no reverence for it is not called a Brahmin.
The faults do not approach that man who does not neglect the twilight prayers and who is habituated to bathing, just as serpents do not approach Garuḍa.
“Until the rising of the stars” means until the appearance of the constellations. “That which is presided over” means that which is dependent upon it.
Śaṅkha and Likhita state:
“For the dharma of those who possess right conduct is indeed essential; thus, conduct is the established way of the sages, the behavior of the gods, and the duty of human beings. By this—
One should stand reciting prayers during the morning twilight for a long time at its proper hour, or likewise during the evening twilight;
by performing the twilight devotions for a long duration, the seers attained long life.

“Necessary duty” (*āvaśyakam*) refers to the acts of voiding urine, excrement, and so forth. “For a long time” (*ciram*) implies a connection with both twilights. “The state of having a long twilight” (*dīrghasaṃdhyatvam*) means being occupied for a long duration through the recitation of prayers.
[Manu 2.222]: Having sipped water and being purified, one should always remain composed during both twilights.
In a pure place, one should perform the recitation of the mantra according to the prescribed rule.
Likewise:
"One should stand reciting the Sāvitrī during the morning twilight until the sun appears;
but during the evening, one should remain seated until the stars are clearly visible."
Manu [2.76–79]: Prajāpati milked from the three Vedas the syllable *a*, the syllable *u*, and the syllable *m*, as well as the words *bhūr*, *bhuvaḥ*, and *svar*.
From the three Vedas alone, Parameṣṭhin Prajāpati milked out foot by foot that [first] quarter of this Sāvitrī verse beginning with "Tat."
A Brahmin who knows the Veda, by muttering this syllable and this [Gāyatrī] preceded by the Vyāhṛtis at the two twilights, becomes endowed with the merit of the Veda.

“This syllable” refers to the *praṇava*. “By the merit of the Vedas” means by the merit arising from the Vedas. Having practiced this triad externally a thousand times, a twice-born man is freed from even great sin within a month, just as a snake is freed from its skin.
In the Viṣṇu Purāṇa (3.11.102):
"Attendance at the two twilights is required of kings at all times,
except in cases of birth-impurity, ritual impurity, confusion, illness, or fear."
Delusion, fear, and agitation.
Yogi-Yājñavalkya: He by whom the twilight devotions (saṃdhyā) have not been understood and the twilight devotions have not been performed...
While still alive, he becomes a Śūdra and is censured in the world.
Manu [2.44]: He who does not attend to the morning [libation] and does not perform worship at the evening [libation] is to be excluded from all duties of the twice-born, like a Śūdra.
The skillful one [2.27]: "One who neglects the twilight prayers is perpetually impure and unfit for all ritual acts;
whatever other rite he performs, he shall not partake in its fruit."
Baudhāyana [2.7.15]:
Moreover, they cite here two verses sung by Prajāpati:
"Those who [miss] the previous [meal] before it has arrived, and those who [miss] the subsequent [meal] after it has passed..."
If Brahmins do not perform the twilight devotions, how can they be considered true Brahmins?
"Those Brahmins who do not constantly perform the twilight devotions (saṃdhyā) in the evening and the morning—
let the righteous king employ them at will in the labor of Śūdras. Thus says Śātātapa.
But that twice-born man who does not perform the morning twilight devotion before the sun has risen, nor the evening twilight devotion after the sun has set, is considered a shameless Brahmin.
Aṅgiras: That Brahmin who, remaining silent and composed at both twilights,
is honored in the world of Brahmā for a thousand divine years.
In this regard, Śaṅkha, Vasiṣṭha, Aṅgiras, Bṛhaspati, Paiṭhīnasi, and Baudhāyana state:
"One should recite the Gāyatrī together with the Vyāhṛtis, the Praṇava, and the Śiras three times while restraining the breath; that is called Prāṇāyāma."
Bṛhaspati [Ācāra 31]:
Having assumed the posture, restrained the breaths, and likewise remembered the ṛṣis and other [factors],
one should practice *prāṇāyāma* with eyes closed and observing silence.

Śaṅkha [12.7–12]: At the outset, one should recollect the deity, the seer (ṛṣi), and the meter (chandas). [Then, having first repeated the vyāhṛtis together with the praṇava, one should repeat the Gāyatrī. Now, Savitṛ is its deity, Viśvāmitra is its seer, and Gāyatrī is its meter. The syllable *oṃ* is called the praṇava. *Oṃ bhūḥ, oṃ bhuvaḥ, oṃ svaḥ, oṃ mahaḥ, oṃ janaḥ, oṃ tapaḥ, oṃ satyam*—these are the vyāhṛtis. *Āpo jyotī raso ‘mṛtaṃ brahma bhūr bhuvaḥ svar oṃ*—this is the head (śīrṣa). Dakṣa [2.51]: [The same as above.]
That [Gāyatrī] whose deity is Savitṛ, whose mouth is Agni, and which has three feet;
whose seer is Viśvāmitra and whose meter is Gāyatrī—that one is preeminent.
Yogiyājñavalkya says:
Having performed the restraint of the breath (prāṇāyāma), one should perform the sipping of water (ācamana) even while already pure;
because it causes internal purification, it is therefore remembered as "ācamana."
Now, regarding the fire-ritual (*agnikārya*) following the procedure for the twilight prayers (*saṃdhyā*), Yājñavalkya [states at 1.25]:
"Thereafter, one should perform the fire-ritual during both twilights."
Manu (2.186) and the *Bhaviṣya-purāṇa* state: "Having brought fuel from afar, he should place it above his house;
evening and morning, he should offer oblations into the fire with that fuel, remaining unwearied."
By this, the carrying [of the fire] by a disciple and others is refuted.
Āpastamba [1.4.14–21]:
Having fetched fuel from the forest, he should place it below.

There is an option regarding the lower and upper garments. One should not go out while the fire is still burning. Having kindled the fire and swept around it, one should add fuel in the evening and in the morning according to the instruction. Some say that the worship of the fire takes place only in the evening. While sweeping the kindled fire with the hand, one should do so using a broom; prior to that, however, one may act as one pleases. [184] “Samiddhāraḥ” means those who bring the fuel. “Yathopadeśam” means that one should perform the sweeping even according to the procedure stated in the *Gṛhyasūtra*.
One should not perform useless acts or sip water with the remainder of fire or water.
"Useless acts" are those whose purpose is solely for visible (worldly) ends.
Thus says Baijavāpa.

Before sunset, having gone toward the north-eastern direction, he should fetch firewood from the forest without causing injury. If he desires spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*), he should take dry wood; if he desires food, moist wood; if he desires both, both kinds. After sunset, he should place it on that fire as before.

“Before sunset”: once the sun has set, the fetching of fuel is prohibited. “Northeastern” means the direction of Īśāna. “Without harming”: not cutting more than what is required for the fuel. “When it has set”: when the sun has gone down. “In that fire”: in the *āhavanīya* fire. “As before”: as at the time of the initiation (*upanayana*). “He should place”: the word “fuel” is to be supplied. Paiṭhīnasi [says]: “Having sprinkled [water] around with the words ‘May he sprinkle together,’ one should attend upon the fire morning and evening, [worshipping] the Sun and Moon, Soma, Mitra, Vāyu, the Waters, and the Brāhmaṇas.”
“Paricaret” means he should pay homage; thus says Hārīta:
“In ancient times, Death indeed seized the religious student while he was practicing violence.”
Agni liberated him from that; therefore, one should indeed attend upon him.
When a religious student does not place fuel-sticks into the fire,
then Death seizes him and places fuel-sticks therein.
Now, regarding salutation and clasping the feet, Śaṅkha says [2.4]:
"Having risen at dawn, being self-restrained, having bathed, and having offered oblations into the fire..."
One should perform the salutation to one's teachers with devotion, bowing down in humility.
Viṣṇu [28.14]: Having performed the twilight worship (saṃdhyopāsana), he should perform salutation to his teachers.
Gautama [6.5].
In an assembly of those who know the rules, one should greet by pronouncing one's own name, saying, "I am so-and-so.
The phrase "in an assembly of those who know" refers to a gathering of people who are knowledgeable regarding the procedure for returning a greeting.
In greeting, one should utter the word "bhoḥ" at the end of one's own name;
for the sages have declared that the state of being "bhoḥ" is the very essence of the name itself.
When greeting a Brahmin, one should say, "May you be long-lived, O gentle one. Furthermore, the letter 'a' at the end of his name should be uttered with the preceding vowel protracted (pluta).
“By name” means by the name of the person to be saluted. “The state of becoming ‘bho’” means the word “bho. “Of this” refers to this salutation.
Following the phrase “one should salute,” the *Sāṃkhyāyana Gṛhya Sūtra* [4.12.5–6] states:
“Having announced one’s own name, saying ‘I am so-and-so, sir,’ with hands crossed, and having grasped the hand of the other person with the words ‘so-and-so,’ he invokes a blessing.”
“Of this” refers to the one who offers salutation.
Manu [2.126] states: “The Brahmin who does not know the proper response to a salutation...”
He is not to be saluted by a learned man; he is exactly like a Śūdra.

"Of salutation" (*abhivādasya*) means of the act of greeting. "The return-salutation" (*pratyabhivādana*) is a word of blessing, such as: "May you be long-lived, Devadatta! "He is not to be saluted" (*nābhivādyaḥ*) means he is by no means to be greeted. Āpastamba [1.5.12]:
"A student (*brahmacārī*), having always risen during the latter part of the night, standing before his teacher, should offer the morning salutation, saying: 'I am so-and-so, sir.'"
The meaning is that one should perform the salutation, called "abhivāda," as in the expression "he cooks the cooking of rice.
Again, Āpastamba [1.5.16–17] states:

A Brāhmaṇa should salute by extending his right arm level with his ear; a Rājanya, level with his chest; a Vaiśya, level with his waist; and a Śūdra, lowly, with palms joined. Furthermore, for the preceding castes, there is the elision of the name during both the salutation and the response to the salutation.

“*Nīcaiḥ śūdraḥ*”: lower than the middle [castes]. “*Plāvanam*”: the act of protracted pronunciation. “*Nāmnaḥ*”: meaning of the final vowel of the name. “*Pūrveṣām*”: of the Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas. The phrase “*abhivādya*” (having saluted) is the ellipsis to be supplied. Vasiṣṭha [13.44–46]:

He who knows how to salute should say, “I am so-and-so, sir (*ayam ahaṃ bho iti*”). And he who does not know [how to salute], when addressed, his final vowel in the response is protracted; likewise for a *saṃdhyakṣara* that is not *pragṛhya*, and for a change to *āy* or *au*, as in the case of the transformation into *bho*.

“‘He who would know how to respond to a salutation’—the meaning is that when a salutation has been performed, one should perform a return-salutation. One should salute such a person by mentioning one’s own name as a specific qualification. However, toward one who does not know how to respond to a salutation, the meaning is that one should simply say, ‘It is I here, sir. By the use of the word ‘and,’ this also applies to women. And thus Manu [2.123]:
‘To those who do not know how to respond to a salutation by name, a wise man should say, “It is I,” and likewise to all women.’”

How, then, is the return greeting performed? Regarding this, he says: "In the case of an *āmantrita* (vocative), at the end of the name which ends in the first case, the 'final'—that is, the final vowel—is to be made 'prolated' (*pluta*), consisting of three morae (*trimātra*). A 'diphthong' (*saṃdhyakṣara*) refers to *e*, *ai*, *o*, and *au*. 'Not a *pragṛhya*' means lacking the designation of *pragṛhya*. By the word 'and' (*ca*), it is understood that it also undergoes the state of *āy* and *āv* (i.e., *ai* and *au*). And it becomes prolated; this is the remainder of the sense. Āpastamba [1.14.20–21]:
"One should greet women using a general term [such as *bhavatī*]. One should greet a king and a Vaiśya by their name; some say one should also greet one's mother and the wife of a teacher [by name]."
“With a pronoun”: merely by saying, “I, sir, salute you. “Not with a name,” meaning not with one’s own name, but rather with a pronoun; such is the opinion of some. Manu [2.72]:
“The clasping of the feet of the teacher must be performed with the hands crossed.”
The left [hand] should be touched with the left, and the right with the right.
Baudhāyana [1.3.26–28]:

One desiring long life and heaven should perform the clasping of the feet with the right hand for the right foot and the left hand for the left foot. If permitted by the teacher, he may do so at his own will for another person of virtuous conduct, saying, "I am so-and-so, sir," while touching the ears for the sake of concentrating the mind, reaching from below the knees down to the feet.

The phrase "down to the feet" means that one should touch from the knees down to the feet. "For the sake of concentrating the mind" means for the sake of securing the attention of the person being saluted.

Āpastamba [1.5.18–23]: When the sun has risen, having met the teacher, there is the clasping of his feet; the salutation always follows. Some say that the teacher’s feet should be clasped after he has been saluted. One should clasp the foot with the right hand, touching the sole from below up to the ankle. Some say that both feet should be clasped while pressing them with both hands. “With both” means with both hands; “both” means both feet; “pressing” means pressing firmly.

Vasiṣṭha [13.41–43]: One should perform the clasping of the teacher’s feet. One should rise and salute the officiating priest (*ṛtvij*), the father-in-law, the paternal uncle, and the maternal uncle, even if they are younger than oneself. Furthermore, those whose feet are to be clasped include their wives, as well as the mother and father of the teacher. This is the essential meaning: for those such as the officiating priest who are younger, one should merely rise and address them. As for "those whose feet are to be clasped"—meaning those worthy of the clasping of the feet—those mentioned immediately after the six previously cited who are "younger" must also be addressed after rising.
Gautama [1.58]:
The clasping of the teacher’s feet takes place in the morning. Regarding the honoring of the teacher, Paiṭhīnasi says:
With palms turned upward, one should salute the right foot with the right hand and the left foot with the left hand.
Again, Gautama [6.1–4]:

The clasping of the feet occurs daily when meeting [elders]; it also occurs upon returning from a journey. This applies to mothers, fathers, their relatives, ancestors, teachers of knowledge, and the teachers of those teachers; as well as in the presence of another person.

“In a gathering” (*samavāye*) means in a meeting. “Having returned from travel” (*viproṣye*) means having come back after being away on a journey. “Of their relatives” (*tatsambandhūnām*) refers to maternal and paternal relatives of the same caste, such as maternal uncles, maternal grandfathers, paternal uncles, paternal grandfathers, and so forth. “Of those born before” (*pūrvajānām*) refers to elder brothers. “Teachers of knowledge” (*vidyāguravaḥ*) are those who have taught the auxiliary sciences (*aṅga*) and other branches of learning. “Of their teachers” (*tadgurūṇām*) refers to the teachers previously mentioned. “In the presence of another” (*saṃnidhāne parasya*): when all of these are present together, one must first perform the salutation (*upasaṃgrahaṇa*) to that person who is the most senior or principal among them. Āpastamba [1.5.12–15].

Standing before his teacher in the morning, he should perform the salutation with the words: "I am so-and-so, sir. He should also do so for other elders living in the same village before taking his morning meal, and upon returning from a journey. One who desires heaven and long life [should do this]. *Sāṃkhyāyanagṛhyasūtra* 4.12.1–4:
Day by day, one should salute the teacher and the other elders; likewise, upon meeting a learned *śrotriya*, and upon returning from a journey, one should salute even a non-*śrotriya*.

“Having come together” means upon meeting by the power of fate. Regarding the phrase “having returned after being away from one who is not a Śrotriya,” the meaning is that this applies even when there is no meeting by the power of fate. Pārṣṭhīnasi says: “Whatever is worldly, whatever is Vedic, and whatever else is consistent with Dharma...”
One should first salute that person from whom one receives knowledge.
“Connected with the Dharma” means related to the Dharma; “acquisition of knowledge” means the grasping of learning.
Manu and Yama state this in the first chapter, and Paiṭhīnasi states it in the fourth:
“Whether it be worldly, Vedic, or likewise pertaining to the inner self (ādhyātmika)...”
One should first pay homage to the one from whom one receives knowledge.
A Brahmin who is well-restrained is better, even if his essence consists only of the Sāvitrī mantra,
than one who is unrestrained, even if he knows the three Vedas, eats all things, and sells all things.
One should not sit upon a bed or seat already occupied by a superior;
likewise, while staying on a bed or seat, one should rise and salute him.
For the vital breaths of a young man indeed depart when an elder approaches;
he recovers them again by rising to meet him and by saluting him.
For one who is habitually respectful and constantly serves the elders, four things increase properly: lifespan, wisdom, fame, and strength.

“Worldly” refers to treatises on statecraft (*arthaśāstra*) and the like. “Spiritual” refers to the knowledge that establishes Brahman. “In what is practiced by the superior”—that is, by one who is excellent, such as a teacher—one “should not enter,” meaning one should not sit down together with them. “Those” refers to the vital breaths (*prāṇa*).
In the *Bhaviṣya* [Purāṇa]: “*Abhi*” is Lord Viṣṇu; “I shall cause to sound” is Śaṅkara.
By him who performs a respectful salutation, these two are honored.
Manu [2.132]: "The wife of a brother of the same caste should be saluted day after day;
however, upon returning from a journey, the women who are one's paternal or maternal relatives should be saluted."
“Relatives” (*jñātayaḥ*) are those on the father’s side; “connections” (*saṃbandhinaḥ*) are those on the mother’s side, as well as fathers-in-law and so forth. Likewise [2.212]:
“A young wife of one’s teacher, however, should not be saluted here by touching her feet.”
By one who has reached twenty years of age and understands virtues and faults.
“Having completed twenty years” is an indication of youth. Furthermore, “virtues and faults” refer to the pleasure and pain born of desire.
Likewise [2.216–217]:
“Indeed, on this earth, a young man may at will enjoy the company of youthful wives of his guru.”
He should perform the salutation according to the rules, saying, "I am so-and-so."
Having returned from a journey, one should clasp the feet of the teacher’s wives and offer salutations every day,
keeping in mind the dharma of the virtuous.
Likewise [2.210]:
The wives of one's gurus who are of the same caste should be honored like the gurus themselves;
however, those of a different caste should be honored by rising from one's seat and by salutation.
Viṣṇu [32.5]:
For women of lower castes who are the wives of one's teachers, there should first be a salutation (*abhivādana*), but not the clasping of the feet (*pādopasaṃgrahaṇa*).
Regarding the continuation of the topic of salutation, Gautama [6.6–8] states:

Regarding the greeting upon meeting a woman or a man, some hold that there is no fixed rule; others say that for women—excluding one's mother, paternal uncle’s wife, and sister—there is no requirement to rise up, nor is there any requirement to perform the formal salutation (*upasaṃgrahaṇa*) toward the wives of one's brothers or toward one's mother-in-law.

The phrase "in the union of woman and man" (*strīpuṃyoge*) means that at the time of marriage, because women possess a status of respectability (*gurutva*), some consider there to be "no fixed rule" regarding rising up and greeting. "From greeting" (*abhivādanataḥ*) means in the act of greeting.
Thus [it is stated in 6.9].

One must rise to greet officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), fathers-in-law, paternal uncles, and maternal uncles who are younger than oneself, but one need not perform the formal salutation (*abhivādana*) to them.

[193] The term "younger" (*yavīyasaḥ*) means those who are junior in age. Regarding the rule, "There is no clasping of the feet (*upasaṃgrahaṇa*) for the wives of brothers," this refers to women of a different caste (*asavarṇā*); however, the wife of a brother of the same caste (*savarṇā*) is to be saluted by clasping her feet even on every single day.
Thus, from the statement of Manu:
"They are to be stood up for, but not saluted," following this [rule], Gautama [says at 6.10]:
"Likewise, another who is senior—even a Śūdra—is to be treated as the equal of one's own offspring, provided he is at least eighty years old."

“Another” means one other than the officiating priests and others mentioned immediately above. “An elder” (*pūrva*) is so called in relation to age. “A fellow townsman” (*paura*) is one who dwells in the same locality. “At least eighty years old” (*aśītikāvara*): the term *aśītikā* refers to the number eighty; he whose lower limit is that [age] is thus described. If a *śūdra* is a friend of one’s father, or the father of one’s friend, then he should be saluted by rising up before him as if he were a son of an equal-born Brāhmaṇa.

Āpastamba [1.14.10–11]: One should rise and salute an officiating priest, a father-in-law, a paternal uncle, or a maternal uncle, even if they are younger in age; or one may simply clasp their feet in silence.

“One should salute” means one should address them respectfully. “One should clasp the feet” means one should grasp them closely, such as by holding them in one’s lap or arms. Clasping the feet is performed for those who are seniors in knowledge and the like; for others, mere respectful address is sufficient. Śātātapa says: “Kṣatriyas and others should never be saluted by a Brāhmaṇa.”
Even though these [beings] are endowed with the qualities of knowledge and action and are deeply learned.
The sacred tradition (śruti) states that Brāhmaṇas should pronounce blessings for all social classes;
however, among those of the same class, salutation (abhivādana) must indeed be performed by equals toward equals.
Aṅgiras says:
Those twice-born who offer blessings to a Śūdra who has not performed a prostration go to hell;
the Śūdra goes to hell as well, and the Brāhmaṇa immediately after him.
In the Devīpurāṇa:
"Even a Śūdra who is rich in qualification and adorned with the syllables of eloquent speech incurs a sin equal to a great transgression (mahāpātaka) if he lacks discipline."
Regarding obedience to the guru, Manu [2.202] states:
"One should not honor him while standing at a distance, nor when angry, nor in the presence of a woman;
likewise, if one is seated in a vehicle or on a seat, one should descend before saluting him."

Āpastamba [1.14.12–19]: A *śrotriya* who is three years senior deserves a formal salutation (*abhivādana*). When a difference in age is known, one should salute the more advanced in years. One should not salute a teacher while standing on uneven ground; rather, one should ascend to level ground and then salute. In all cases, however, one must rise before saluting. One should not be saluted by someone who is impure (*aprayata*); likewise, being impure oneself, one should not return the salutation to an impure person, nor to women who have reached their husband’s age. One should not salute while wearing shoes, with the head wrapped, or with the hands tucked away.

“Three years senior” means one who is the elder by three years. “To one who has gone to an uneven place” means to one situated on high or low ground. “Having ascended after” is an elliptical expression; one should salute even a teacher who has gone to an uneven place. “With hands joined” means with hands not occupied by any other object. Gautama [9.47] states:
“One wearing shoes should avoid eating, sitting, saluting, and prostrating.”

Śaṅkha and Likhita state: One should not offer salutation with a water-pot in hand, nor while wandering for alms, nor with flowers or other items in one's hands, nor while impure, nor while reciting prayers (*japa*), nor while performing rites for the gods or ancestors, nor speaking at will in the midst of an assembly. [Baudhāyana (1.3.32–33)]
One who has kindled the sacred fire, or one with a water-pot, flowers, or food in hand, should not offer salutation; nor should one do so when others are similarly engaged, nor in a crowded assembly.
“Carrying fuel” means bringing sacrificial wood (*samidh*). The meaning is that one should not salute him who is thus engaged. “In an assembly” means in a gathering.
Hārīta says: “One performing the sacrifice of recitation (*japayajña*), one standing in water, and those carrying sacrificial wood, flowers, *kuśa* grass, or fire [should not be saluted].”
One should not offer salutations to one who is carrying a water-pot and alms-food.
“And one who is engaged in the sacrifice of recitation (*japayajña*) while standing in water shall not perform a salutation. Hārīta says:
One should not address another person to whom one has already paid obeisance by someone else. One should address one's gurus and Brahmins, but not Śūdras before having eaten.
"Another" refers to the one who returns the salutation.
Yama says: "But he who does not first bestow a blessing upon one who greets him..."
Whatever evil he may have committed, from that he receives a share.
Therefore, one who knows the Dharma should be the first to speak, even to a *caṇḍāla*;
he should say, "Drink liquor," for in this way the Dharma is not violated.
One should say "Svasti" (well-being) to a Brāhmaṇa, "Āyuṣyam" (long life) to a Kṣatriya,
"Vardhatām" (may it increase) to a Vaiśya, and likewise "Ārogyam" (health) to a Śūdra.
That happiness which exists in the three worlds, free from disease and calamity,
and in which all desires are contained— that is designated as "well-being" (svasti).
Since the blessing (*āśis*) has been introduced by the statement, "But he who does not offer a blessing after a salutation," the connection is that this blessing is "designated as 'Svasti'.
[This is according to] Manu and Yama: "One should ask a Brāhmaṇa about his welfare (*kuśala*), and a member of the Kṣatriya caste about his health (*anāmaya*)."
Having approached a Vaiśya, one should ask about his welfare; however, for a Śūdra, one should ask only about his health.
Regarding the rules for hospitality, Gautama [5.42] states:
"Inquiries concerning welfare, health, and freedom from disease [should be made]; for a Śūdra, only the last [of these].
Āpastamba [1.14.23–28] states:

One should ask about the welfare of a virtuous person of lower age or a companion; about the health of a Kṣatriya; about his lack of loss [of property] regarding a Vaiśya; and about his freedom from disease regarding a Śūdra. One should not pass by a *śrotriya* without speaking to him, nor a woman in the forest.
A *śrotriya* is one who has studied the Veda and likewise practices its injunctions. "A woman in the forest" refers to the purpose of removing fear and other such dangers. —Yama.
"A Kṣatriya kills for three yugas, a Vaiśya kills for four yugas;
a Śūdra kills for seventy-one yugas—so said the Brāhmaṇas."
“Yuga” means birth. “Abruvan” means not speaking out of contempt.

Thus ends [the section] in the *Kṛtyakalpataru* composed by Śrī Mallakṣmīdhara, son of Bhaṭṭa Śrī Hṛdayadhara, the Great Minister for Peace and War to the illustrious Mahārājādhirāja Govindacandradeva.
In the section on the student's life (brahmacārikāṇḍa), [the rules for] salutation and clasping the feet [are concluded].
Now, those worthy of honor there are as follows:

the mother, the father, the father’s wife, the elder brother, the elder sister, the elder brother-in-law, the father’s friend, the preceptor, the teacher, paternal uncles, maternal uncles, mothers-in-law, fathers-in-law, and elders.
Hārīta says:

Service to the teacher (*guruśuśrūṣā*) is performed for the sake of knowledge, virtue, and wealth. In this regard, one should perform service to the teacher as a means of purchasing knowledge. Indeed, teachers are both those who dwell in heaven and those who dwell on earth. The gods, such as Agni and others, are those who dwell in heaven; one should perform service to them through recitation (*japa*), fire-oblations (*homa*), worship (*arcana*), and so forth. Those who dwell on earth are indeed the teachers, such as a Brahmin, one's mother and father, an elder brother, the wife of an elder brother, a sub-teacher (*upādhyāya*), the wife of a sub-teacher, an initiated person (*dīkṣita*), a renunciant (*pravrajita*), a king, and those advanced in age, advanced in knowledge, and advanced in austerity. One should perform service to them by approaching them, saluting them, offering the guest-offering (*argha*), providing hospitality, and so forth.
For thus it is said:
"The gurus are the root of Dharma, as well as of knowledge and austerity;
therefore, gurus should be served by a person with diligent effort."
The gods are indeed pleased with those men of meritorious deeds who constantly satisfy their elders dwelling on earth.
Those for whom the gurus are dissatisfied are ruined; they are the lowest of men. But for those whose gurus are satisfied, all prosperity is theirs.
For those consumed by anger toward their guru, no auspicious destiny exists.

The term "initiated" (*dīkṣita*) refers to one after the purchase of the *soma*; prior to that, however, Gautama’s statement—"and one who is initiated until the purchase"—indicates a state of equality [with the king]. Here, the term "king" (*rājā*) refers to the sovereign lord of the earth, as this is consistent with the singular testimony of Devala's statement, and not merely a member of the Kṣatriya caste.
Thus says Devala:
The preceptor, the father, the elder brother, and the sovereign;
the maternal uncle, the father-in-law, the protector, and the maternal and paternal grandfathers.
The eldest by caste and the paternal uncle are remembered as teachers among males;
likewise, the mother, the maternal grandmother, the teacher's wife, and the uterine sisters of both the father and the mother.
The mother-in-law, the paternal grandmother, the elder sister, and the nurse are female gurus.
"Gurvī" refers to the wife of a guru; "jyeṣṭhā" refers to the elder sister—this is the implied meaning. Likewise:
Thus has this group of gurus been described, divided twofold according to mother and father;
one should follow them through the actions of mind, speech, and body.
Upon seeing the teacher, one should rise and salute him with palms joined;
one should not sit together with these [elders], nor should one argue with them for the sake of gain.
One should accomplish what is prescribed and avoid what is forbidden;
one should always honor those worthy of worship and not abandon them in times of misfortune.
"In times of distress," that is,
in adversity; one should avoid anger, harshness of speech and punishment, arrogance, distorted vocal tones, jesting, laughter, and amorous play in the presence of the guru.
“Utseka” means pride; “narma” means playfulness; “hasa” means joking; “vilāsa” refers to amorous gestures. Likewise:
one should never harbor hatred even toward one's teachers for the sake of one's livelihood.
Even if elevated by other virtues, one who hates his guru falls downward.
Of all gurus, five are especially worthy of worship;
among them, three are said to be foremost, and among those, the mother is most highly honored.
He who imparts instruction, she who gives birth, he by whom one's knowledge is taught,
the elder brother, and the husband— these five are remembered as gurus.
“The supporter” means the nourisher.
One who desires prosperity should especially honor these five with all effort, even at the cost of one’s own life.
As long as both father and mother remain free from change,
for that long the son should renounce everything and be devoted solely to them.
If both father and mother are well-pleased by the virtues of their son,
that son shall attain the entirety of Dharma through that very deed.
There is no deity equal to a mother; there is no teacher equal to a father. Indeed, no repayment whatsoever can ever be made for them.
Having properly propitiated the teacher and being dismissed by his permission,
the disciple enjoys the fruit of the knowledge and, after death, attains heaven.
"Dismissed" means sent away.
That fool who disregards his eldest brother, who is like a father—
by that fault, after departing this life, he falls into a terrible hell.
Therefore, an elder brother is always to be honored like a father;
for in this world, respect arises from the benefit one receives, even in the case of a mother.
Indeed, for those men who sacrifice their own lives for the sake of their master’s sustenance,
the Blessed Manu has declared that they shall attain imperishable worlds.
The suffering that parents endure for the birth of human beings cannot be repaid even in hundreds of millions of eons.
He who always acts with kindness toward these three, especially toward his teacher—
for when these three are satisfied, all ascetic merit is fully accomplished.
Service to these three is declared to be the supreme austerity;
one should not practice any other duty without being authorized by them.
Likewise:
"All dharmas are honored by him by whom these three are honored;
but for him by whom these are not honored, all ritual actions are fruitless."
As long as those three may live, one should not perform any other [duty];
rather, one should constantly practice service toward them, devoted to their pleasure and welfare.
Whatever one may do belonging to others, one should perform it without causing them any obstruction; one should report each such act to them through the actions of mind, speech, and body.
For a man’s duty is indeed completed within these three;
this is the supreme dharma manifestly, while any other is called a secondary dharma.
By devotion to one's mother one attains this world; by devotion to one's father, the middle world; but through service to the teacher alone, one reaches the world of Brahmā.

A king, an officiating priest (*ṛtvij*), a learned *śrotriya*, one who restrains from unrighteousness (*adharmapratiṣedhin*), as well as an *upādhyāya*, a paternal uncle, a maternal grandfather, a maternal uncle, a father-in-law, and an elder brother—these, along with their relatives, are to be honored like a teacher (*ācārya*). Their wives are likewise to be honored if they are of the same caste (*savarṇā*). So too are a mother’s sister and an elder sister.
"One who restrains from unrighteousness" refers to one who prevents others from engaging in unrighteous acts and the like.
Śātātapa says:

A teacher is to be saluted, to be honored with prostrations, and indeed to be worshipped at his feet; he is the fire for the twice-born, and among the social classes, the Brāhmaṇa is the highest authority.
"The husband alone is the teacher for women; every guest is a teacher.
(From the Bhaviṣya Purāṇa). "A five-year-old Brāhmaṇa and a ten-year-old king..."
One should know them as father and son; however, among the two, the Brāhmaṇa is the father.
Thus, the wise have declared that even for a Vaiśya, a Kṣatriya may be a father, a grandfather, and a great-grandfather; and for a Śūdra, a Brāhmaṇa is so designated.
Manu and Viṣṇu state:
"Wealth, kinship, age, ritual action, and learning as the fifth—these are the grounds for respect; each subsequent one is weightier than the preceding."
Vasiṣṭha [13.56–57]: Learning, wealth, age, kinship, and ritual action are grounds for respect. When these coincide, each preceding one is more weighty than the following.
Gautama [6.20–24]:

Wealth, kinship, occupation, birth, learning, and age are grounds for respect, each being more authoritative than the preceding one. However, sacred learning (*śruta*) is weightier than all of them, because dharma is rooted in it, and because of the Vedic revelation (*śruti*).
"Birth" (*jāti*) refers to noble lineage, or specifically the status of being a Brahmin and so forth, which brings about superiority.

On this point, the following is the determination: Manu has stated that wealth is the very lowest [of the criteria], whereas Vasiṣṭha has stated it to be superior to mere learning (*vidyā*). In that regard, Vasiṣṭha’s statement concerning the superiority of wealth refers to wealth acquired through righteous means (*nyāyārjita*) intended for the practice of dharma. Thus, among Manu, Gautama, and Vasiṣṭha, the superiority, mediocrity, and inferiority of action (*karman*) should be understood as being based on the threefold distinction of the excellence of causes such as faith (*śraddhā*), or on the basis of its abundance. As for Gautama’s description of learning as inferior to age (*vayas*), this is intended merely as a sequence of enumeration; for he himself has stated, "Scriptural knowledge (*śruta*) is weightier than all [the others]. Here, "age" refers to the tenth stage of life, whereas for Manu and Vasiṣṭha, it refers to age in general.
Among the three castes, he who possesses the five qualities in abundance and is meritorious is worthy of honor here, even if he be a Śūdra who has reached his tenth decade.

“Of the five” refers to the previously mentioned [categories], beginning with wealth. “In the three castes” refers to those such as the Brāhmaṇas and so forth. “Virtuous” means preeminent. “The tenth” refers to the stage of life exceeding ninety years. Vasiṣṭha [13.58–60]: On the meeting of paths, the way must be yielded one after another to the elderly, the young, the sick, those carrying heavy loads, women, and those riding in chariots. [On the meeting of a king and a Snātaka, the way must be yielded by the king to the Snātaka. When a bride is being carried away, the way must be yielded by all.
"At the time of being carried away" means at the time of marriage;
this follows from the rule "the way should be given," as stated in the *Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa* (34.40–41):
"And for those who are mute, blind, or deaf, and for one who is intoxicated or insane..."
Of an unchaste woman, of one who has committed enmity, of a child, and of an outcast.

A "puṃścalī" is an unchaste woman. Regarding the rule "the path must be yielded," Śaṅkha and Likhita state [as follows] in continuation: [one must yield the way] to children, the elderly, the intoxicated, the insane, those with impaired bodies, those burdened by heavy loads, women, pregnant women, Snātakas, renunciants (pravrajita), and those distinguished by learning, craft, or virtue.
“With a body afflicted by flowers” means by sinful diseases and the like. “Virtue” (*guṇa*) here refers to knowledge and so forth.
Devala and Bodhāyana [BauDh 2.6.30]:
“Way should be yielded to a Brāhmaṇa, to a cow, to a king, and to one who is sightless.”
To one who is aged, to one afflicted by heat, to a pregnant woman, and to one who is weak.

Āpastamba [2.11.5–9]: The path belongs to the king when he does not encounter a Brāhmaṇa; but upon encountering one, the path belongs to the Brāhmaṇa alone. Way must be yielded by all to a vehicle, to one burdened with a load, to the sick, and to a woman. It must also be yielded by the lower castes to those of higher caste. Way must be yielded by everyone for the sake of their own well-being to those who are ill-mannered, outcaste, intoxicated, or insane. Gautama [6.25–26]:
The way must be yielded to a wheel-turning monarch, one who stands at the tenth stage, a person worthy of favor, a bride, a student who has completed his studies, and a king;
however, by a king, it must be yielded specifically to one learned in the Vedas.
Yājñavalkya [1.117]:

"The way must be yielded to the elderly, the burdened, kings, those who have performed the ritual bath (*snātaka*), women, the sick, ascetics, and those who possess a wheel [of sovereignty]. O King, among these, the *snātaka* is to be honored even more than the king.
Thus are those to be honored.
Now, regarding the sequence for honoring one who is designated as an *ācārya*, Manu [2.140] states:
"That twice-born man who, having initiated a pupil, teaches him the Veda..."
They declare him to be a teacher who possesses the entire [teaching] along with its secret mysteries.

A *kalpa* is a text that prescribes ritual performance and is rooted in direct perception and the Vedas. The mention of *kalpa* is intended to include the auxiliary sciences (*aṅga*) by implication. A *rahasya* is an *upaniṣad*; it is mentioned separately because of its preeminence. Vasiṣṭha [3.21]:
"But he who, having initiated a pupil, teaches him the entire Veda, is an *ācārya*."

In this context, the word *kṛtsna* refers to being complete in its constituent parts (*sāṅgatva*), because the collection of both mantra and brāhmaṇa is indicated by the term *veda*. Manu [2.141–142] states:
"But [one who knows] even a single portion of the Veda, or likewise the limbs of the Veda..."
He who teaches for the sake of his livelihood is called an upādhyāya.
That Brahmin who performs the rites beginning with the impregnation ceremony according to the rules, and supports [the child] with food, is called a Guru.

“For the sake of subsistence” means for the sake of one’s own livelihood. “The rites beginning with conception” refers to the sacramental acts (*saṃskārakarmāṇi*) ending with the gift of the Veda. “He honors” means he causes [them] to flourish.
Thus [it is said]: “Whether it be little or much of sacred learning by which someone benefits another... [2.149]
One should know that person here as a teacher as well, by virtue of their assistance in providing sacred learning.
Yājñavalkya [1.34]: He is a *guru* who, having performed the rites, imparts the Veda to him;
he who initiates him and gives him the Veda is designated an *ācārya*.
Yama says: One who speaks the truth, is steadfast, skillful, devoted to compassion for all beings, a believer, dedicated to the Vedas, and pure— such a person is called an Ācārya.
One who is perfected in the study of the Vedas, possessed of good conduct, and has subdued his senses—
one endowed with these characteristics is a teacher at all times.

“He is called an *ācārya*”: he is to be honored like an *ācārya*. “He becomes a *guru*”: the meaning is that he is to be honored like a *guru*. As it says in the *Bhaviṣya*: “An *ācārya* is ten times more venerable than an *upādhyāya*; a father is a hundred times more venerable than *ācāryas*.”
But the mother exceeds the father a thousandfold in terms of venerability.
O mighty-armed one, those whom you have previously described as worthy of worship, beginning with the preceptor, are all considered inferior to the great guru.

“Superior to all” means most worthy of worship among all. And he is the “Great Guru,” as inferred from the verses to be spoken beginning with “The eighteen Purāṇas,” and so forth. This is the opinion of hundreds and thousands of teachers because of his omniscience:
“The eighteen Purāṇas, likewise the life-story of Rāma, the Viṣṇudharma and other scriptures, the Śivadharma, and the Mahābhārata.”
The fifth is to be known as the Kārṣṇa, which is remembered as the Mahābhārata;
and the Saura-dharmas, O King of kings, lord of the earth, as spoken by Manu.
The wise declare that "Jaya" is the name of these [ancestors];
thus, it is remembered as the most excellent designation for the entire assembly of Brahmins.
He who knows all these Purāṇas here is called the great preceptor of all four castes.
And the Bhārata, O mighty-armed one, is considered by men to be omniscient;
therefore, O Indra among kings, it should always be honored by the castes, beginning with the Brahmins.
Have you not heard the words spoken by the Lord, the All-pervading One:
"Whether it be little or much, he who benefits another through what he has heard [is a true teacher]"?
One should know that person also to be a guru here by virtue of that service of instruction; as Manu [2.143] says:
"The establishment of the sacred fires, the cooked sacrifices (pākayajña), and the great sacrifices such as the Agniṣṭoma..."
He who performs the rite for one who has chosen him is called that person's officiating priest (ṛtvij) in this world.
Hārīta says: [There are three kinds of officiants: the *kṣīrahotṛ*, the *āhāryavṛta*, and the *viśeṣavṛta*.

A learned scholar (*śrotriya*) who establishes his sacred fires for him is the *kṣīrahotṛ*. In his absence, if one chooses another for the sake of the obligatory rites, he is the *āhāryavṛta*. Furthermore, those others whom one chooses for successive sacrifices are the *viśeṣavṛta*.
Manu [2.145]: An Ācārya outweighs ten Upādhyāyas; a father outweighs a hundred Ācāryas;
but a mother outweighs a thousand fathers in terms of respect.
Gautama [2.57–58]:
"The teacher is the most excellent among gurus. Some say it is the mother.
Śaṅkha and Likhita [state the same].

A son should not take sides between his mother and father; he may, at his will, speak in favor of the mother alone, for she is both the one who bore him and the one who nourished him. A son is not released from his debt to his mother until he has performed the *sautrāmaṇī* sacrifice while still alive. Regarding the phrase "between mother and father," the meaning is that when a dispute arises, he should not "take sides," that is, he should maintain neutrality. "At his will" means that if he so desires, he may "speak in favor of," that is, speak agreeably toward, the mother alone. [This is stated] by Nārada in the section concerning the authority of parents.
Of those two as well, the father is superior, because the importance of the seed is observed;
in the absence of the progenitor, the mother [is superior], and in her absence, the elder brother.
Manu and Viṣṇu [Manu 2.146–48, 150; Viṣṇu 30.44–46]:
Of the progenitor and the giver of the Veda, the father who gives the Veda is more venerable;
for the birth from the Veda is eternal for a Brahmin, both after death and in this world.
One should know that the production [of a being] by the mother and father through their mutual desire is its "origination" (saṃbhūti), namely, that which is born from the womb.
[210] That birth which the teacher, having mastered the Vedas, produces for him according to rule with the Sāvitrī— that is true, and it is free from old age and death.
One who performs the rites of the Brahman birth and is the instructor of his own duty becomes,
according to dharma, the father of an elder even if he is a mere child.
Yama said: "One is not called an elder by birth, nor by gray hair, nor by the possession of twice-born status;
indeed, even if he be young, the gods recognize him as an elder who has studied the Vedas."
Neither by kinsmen, nor by wealth, nor by gray hair, nor even by years, did the seers establish dharma; he who is learned in the Vedas is great among us.
For an ignorant man is a child, while he who imparts the mantras is a father;
indeed, they call the father who bestows the mantras "the son" of the ignorant one.
[Manu 1.153] "The ignorant one is indeed a child; he who imparts the sacred mantras is a father. For they call the ignorant son 'child' and the father who gives the mantras 'father'."
Manu and Viṣṇu [Manu 2.155; Viṣṇu 32.18]:
"The seniority of Brahmins is by knowledge, that of Kṣatriyas by valor, that of Vaiśyas by grain and wealth, and that of Śūdras alone by birth."
Now follows the conduct toward the Guru and the Teacher.
Regarding this, Āpastamba states: [1.5.23–26; 1.6.1–37; 1.7.1–2].

He should apply himself diligently throughout the entire day and study without interruption. He should do the same regarding the duties for his teacher. Even during a time when study is forbidden, he should study mentally. When called, he should study. At night, he should always help his teacher to lie down after washing and massaging his feet; then, being permitted, he may lie down. He should not stretch out his legs toward him. According to some, there is no stretching out of the legs while the teacher is present. Nor, while lying down, should he speak to him. But if addressed, he should reply while sitting. If the teacher is standing, he should not rise to greet him; if he is walking, he should follow him; if he is running, he should run after him. He should not sit with shoes on, nor with his head wrapped, nor with his hands tucked away. He should attend upon his teacher like a god—without idle chatter, with an undistracted mind, listening to his words, unadorned, with the wind blowing from behind him, not leaning against anything with his hand, and not supported by anything except in an emergency. If he has two garments, he should wear the *yajñopavīta* (sacred thread); if he has only one garment, he should let the lower fold hang down. He should face the teacher while the teacher faces away from him. He should not sit too close, nor too far, but at a distance such that he can reach him with his arms while seated. He should not sit against the wind. If there are many students, they should sit facing the teacher’s right arm, according to available space. He should not sit where the teacher is standing, unless a seat is provided. And while the teacher is sitting, he should not lie down. [212] If the teacher wishes to perform a task within his capability, he should assist him. In the presence of the teacher, he should not greet someone of equal rank. Or, he may mention such a person by their lineage name (*gotra*). He should not rise to meet the teacher, nor rise after him, even if that person is also his teacher; however, he should move away from the spot and the seat. According to some, he may address his own teacher by name if he is a pupil of that teacher. But toward one who possesses the gravity of a teacher due to a non-teacher relationship, he should behave as toward the teacher’s equal. Having eaten in the teacher's presence, he should not offer the leftovers without rising, nor should he clear his plate without rising. Or he may rinse his mouth (*ācamana*) after addressing the teacher, saying, "What shall I do? He may then rise either silently or after saying this. He should not turn his back on the teacher; rather, having circumambulated him to the right, he should depart.

This is the meaning: "Immediate" (*anantara*) means not separated from the study of the Veda. "On the day of study" (*adhyāye*) means on a day suitable for study. The word "likewise" (*tathā*) extends the rule that he should be intent upon his duties for the teacher and remain immediate [in attendance]. Regarding "and mentally during non-study days," the phrase "other than non-study days" is supplied; by this, the meaning is that he should perform mental practice. "One who studies when called" (*āhūtādhyāyī*) means he should study only when summoned by the teacher for the purpose of study; the meaning is that he should be prompted to study with the thought, "I shall perform this task for him. "He should cause to lie down" means he should lay him [the teacher] to rest. "Having massaged" (*saṃvāhya*) means having rubbed [his feet]. "Him" refers to the teacher. "He should stretch out" (*abhiprasārayīta*); the word "feet" is supplied. By this, the previously mentioned stretching out of the feet while on a cot is prohibited. Therefore, the supply is "he should respond while on a cot. "With hands not occupied" means with hands not obstructed by a staff or similar object. Regarding "but one who has set out on a journey," the meaning here is that even one wearing sandals may sit [if necessary]. "If he does not sit" means if he is not engaged in receiving or communicating the teacher's command. "Not sitting with the thighs tucked under" means not seated with the other leg crossed over. "In a following wind" (*anuvāti*); the word "wind" (*vāte*) is understood. "Vītaḥ" means one whose signs of self-restraint have departed; the meaning is that he should not stand in that direction when the wind is blowing toward the teacher. "Unsupported" (*apratiṣṭhabdhaḥ*) means not making contact with the ground or other surfaces with his hand. "Not leaning elsewhere" means not leaning his back or side against a wall or similar object. "Wearing the sacred thread and having two garments" means he should place the upper garment over the sacred thread. "With the sacred thread hanging low" (*adhonivītaḥ*) means not covered by a portion of the lower garment. The construction is: "he should sit as far as he can reach with his arms while seated. "When he moves" (*ceṣṭati*) means when the teacher is performing an action; "within his capacity" (*tacchaktiviṣaye*) means within what is possible for him; "he should desire to do" (*cikīrṣet*). "One standing behind" (*anvaksthāninam*) means one who is not inferior to the teacher. "By lineage" (*gotreṇa*), not by name. "Him" refers to the one standing behind. "Even if he were his teacher" refers to the student. Regarding "he should not mention his pupil by name," the connection is "he should not mention. "By name" means by the name of the person worthy of honor. Regarding "but in whom respect and conduct arise from no relationship to the teacher," in the case of that best of the twice-born, "not because of a teacher-relationship" (*nācārye*), but due to the acquisition of knowledge, great learning, seniority in age, or the performance of his own duties, there is "respect" well-known in the world; the meaning is that "toward him, even though he is one standing behind, the 'conduct' (*vṛtti*)—that is, service—should be performed toward him just as toward the teacher. Regarding "and having eaten in his presence," having eaten in the presence of the teacher, "he should not rise and give the leftovers"; or "he should offer the remains to the teacher"—this offering of the remnants of the meal by the student to the teacher, which is prescribed, must not be done by one who has risen from his seat. "He should not turn away" means he should not walk showing his back while desiring to go on some business; rather, "having circumambulated [him]," he should "depart."

Gautama [2.29–39]: One should mention the name and lineage of one's teacher with respect. The same applies when honoring or when addressing a superior. One should respond after leaving one’s bed, seat, or standing place. One should go toward him upon being called, even if he is not seen. Upon seeing the teacher, one should rise from a lower position, a seat, or while sitting cross-legged, and should refrain from using the wind (passing wind). One should follow him as he departs. Having informed him of and reported one’s tasks, one should study when summoned. One should be intent on what is pleasant and beneficial.

“Properly bowed” (*samānataḥ*) means correctly inclined. “Superior” (*śreyān*) means preeminent in knowledge and other such qualities. If he is honored in the world, then whatever has been said regarding the teacher—such as salutation and so forth—all that is extended by implication and must be performed. “Position” (*sthāna*) means standing; “leaving that” means having moved slightly forward. “Responding” (*pratiśravaṇa*) here refers to accepting the teacher’s command. “Approaching” (*abhikramaṇa*) “from speech when not seen” means approaching toward him from the direction of the teacher’s voice; “not seen” means when the teacher is out of sight; “from speech” means from the giving of a command; “approaching” means going toward him. The word “should be done” is to be supplied. “Service against the wind” (*tiryagvātasevā*) means the voiding of urine and feces, according to Kapardin. “He should rise” means he should move from that spot to another place. “Having informed and declared the task”: the meaning is that the student should perform the teacher’s work after informing him, saying “I shall do this,” and having completed it, he should remain standing after declaring it done. “Diligent” (*yuktaḥ*) means devoted; the word “should be” is to be supplied. “Pleasant” (*priyam*) means doing what is agreeable at first sight. “Beneficial” (*hitam*) means doing what results in happiness in the long run.
Whether constantly urged by his teacher or even without being urged,
he should apply himself to his studies and to the welfare of his teacher.
Restraining both body and speech, as well as the faculties of perception and the mind, he should stand with palms joined in reverence, gazing at the face of his teacher.
One should always have one's hand ready for service, be pure in conduct, and well-restrained;
when told, "Be seated," one should sit facing the teacher.
One should not engage in responding or conversing while lying down,
nor while sitting, nor while eating, nor while standing, nor with one's face turned away.

Standing, one should attend to one who is seated; approaching, one should attend to one who is standing; going out to meet, one should attend to one who is coming toward oneself; and running after, one should attend to one who is running.
Facing one who has his back turned, approaching the presence of one who is far away,
bowing down to one who is lying down, and standing at the command of one who is seated.
