In the presence of his teacher, he should always use a low bed and seat;
within the range of the teacher's vision, he must not sit as he pleases.
One should not utter his name alone, even in his absence;
nor should one imitate his gait, speech, or gestures.
Wherever censure or revilement of the guru proceeds,
there one should cover one's ears or depart from that place to another.
[216] From slander one becomes a crow; indeed, the reviler becomes a dog.

"Slander" (*parīvāda*) is the proclamation of faults; the other is "reviling" (*nindā*). "From slander" means from causing the hearing of slander, because it is a subject of censure due to its being prohibited. Medhātithi maintains that this preceding prohibition is an explanatory statement (*arthavāda*).
One who consumes another's property becomes a worm; the envious person becomes an insect.

One should not pay homage to him while standing at a distance, nor when angry, nor in the presence of a woman; likewise, if one is seated in a vehicle or on a seat, one should descend before offering salutation.
One should not sit with one's teacher either downwind or upwind;
nor should one say anything at all in a place where the teacher cannot hear.
Likewise:
"Just as a man digging with a spade obtains water,
so does one who desires to listen obtain knowledge residing in the teacher."
"In a place where one cannot hear" (*asaṃśrave*) means a location where what is being spoken is not clearly heard.
In the *Bhaviṣya Purāṇa*:
"O King, one should not utter anything at all in the presence of the guru."

The term *āvṛṇvṛtti* means that he conceals the secret [of his teacher]. Śaṅkha and Likhita state: He should not perform those things he has learned from him except for matters of proper conduct (*ācāra*). Nor should he address others with the discourses of the Vasiṣṭhas.

“Trained” means that even those things not explicitly taught by the teacher—such as his movements, speech, and gestures—which one has understood for oneself from the presence of the teacher, one should not imitate this teacher. “Nor should one address him with stories of the Vasiṣṭhas” means that one should not speak in the presence of the teacher using stories not instructed by the teachers. Hārīta says:

"One whose vital energy is drawn upward" (*ūrdhvaretas*) should, while observing the vows prescribed by his teacher, perform service to the teacher. Furthermore, he should follow him with devotion—whether he is walking, standing, or lying down—by fetching water-pots, *kuśa* grass, flowers, sacrificial fuel, roots, and fruits, and by performing tasks such as sweeping, smearing the floor, and massaging the limbs. He must always do everything that is appropriate. Being observant of his vows, he must not step upon the teacher's discarded flower offerings (*nirmālya*), bed, seat, shadow, or sandals. "One whose vital energy is drawn upward" means one who has abandoned the emission of semen. "Massaging the limbs" refers to the act of rubbing the body. "One who does everything" means one who performs all that is fitting. Thus says Paiṭhīnasi.

One should please the teacher with tooth-sticks, bedding, seats, coverings, massage, kind words, and so forth. Āpastamba [1.2.19–20]: One should remain dependent on the teacher, except in cases that constitute a loss of caste; one should act for the teacher's welfare without contradicting him in speech.
"And not speaking in opposition," means not speaking words that are contrary to the teacher. Śaṅkha says:
"Neither by bathing, nor by burnt offerings, nor indeed by service to the sacred fire..."
The celibate student goes to heaven; he goes there by virtue of honoring his teacher.
One should perform what is beneficial and pleasing for the teacher with devotion, free from egoism. Yama says: One must never depart without having taken leave of the teacher.
Furthermore, whatever task is to be performed by a disciple or even by a servant, [that must be done].
While dwelling with his teacher, the student should be devoted to the tasks of the guru,
constantly intent upon sacrificial grass and fuel, dedicated to the fire-rituals, and pure.
With palms joined in reverence, he should say to his teacher: "O Blessed One, I shall study.
Regarding the phrase "or as a servant," even the work of a servant must be performed by the student.
Gautama states this in the context of the recurring rule "he should avoid" at [2.20–21].

Upon seeing the Guru, one must avoid covering the neck, sitting with the knees bound together (avasakthikā), leaning against a support, stretching out the feet, spitting, laughing, yawning, and cracking the fingers.

"Covering the neck" means veiling the throat. "Avasakthikā" is the binding of the hands over the knees. "Cracking [the fingers]" (avasphoṭana) is the snapping of the fingers or other limbs. Viṣṇu [32.10–12].
One should not engage in contentious debate with one's teacher, nor should one speak ill of him, nor anything that is disagreeable to him.
"Contentious debate" (*vigṛhyakathā*) refers to a debate for the sake of victory.
Nārada [verse 8, p. 142]:
Until he has mastered the knowledge, the student should remain diligent in service.
Āpastamba [1.4.22–28].

And he should avoid sleep. Furthermore, day after day, he should protect his teacher through actions consistent with dharma and artha. Having protected him, when going to bed, he should say: "Protect dharma; may I not be negligent. If the teacher should transgress a rule, whether through negligence or intentionally, the student should point it out to him in private. If the teacher does not desist, the student should himself undertake the necessary actions or cause them to be withdrawn. Now, regarding one who rises before others and goes to bed after them, they say that he does not sleep at all. For the religious student who has thus disciplined himself, all his duties here become fruitful, as do those belonging to the householder stage.

"One should avoid sleep. The ellipsis is "one should protect [the teacher] both before and after [sleep]," because of the injunction that follows: "Now, they say that he who rises first and goes to bed last does not sleep. "Engaged in dharma and artha" means engaged in activities conducive to dharma, such as gathering sacrificial fuel, flowers, and *kuśa* grass, and engaged in activities conducive to artha, such as fetching food. Regarding the phrase "mā jugupsam," the *luṅ* (aorist) is used with the particle *māṅ* [to express a prohibition]. Thus, the meaning is: "In this way I protect the teacher; now, may you protect me in accordance with dharma. "Transgression of the rules" refers to the failure to perform the honoring of guests and other such duties.
Paiṭhīnasi:
One who is steadfast and free from desire for praise should report [his progress] to the teacher:
"This has been done; this will be done. Thus he should report it.
Baudhāyana [1.3.21–22]:

He should be truthful, modest, and free from egoism; rising before [his teacher] and retiring after him; his word regarding the guru should be unimpeded in all matters, except in the case of a mortal sin. Manu [2.194]:
"In the presence of the teacher, he should always have inferior food, clothing, and appearance.

Even for one who has returned home from his studies (*samāvṛtta*), these same rules of customary conduct (*sāmayācārika*) apply regarding these matters, just as they did for the religious student (*brahmacārin*). He should not wear garlands, nor have his face smeared with unguents; he should not have his hair and beard oiled, nor be anointed or perfumed; he should not wear turbans, head-wraps, tunics, sandals, or shoes. He should neither perform nor cause others to perform these acts during the calls of nature, nor during private activities such as cleaning the teeth, rubbing the body, or shaving. Furthermore, the teacher should not mention the names of those items when they are used for his own purposes. However, some say that a *snātaka* (one who has completed his studies), when invited or approached at the proper time according to the rules, need not withdraw [from his seat] even if he is seated higher than the teacher. He should not sit on anything with more feet than the teacher’s seat—neither on a multi-legged stool, nor on anything supported by all four corners. He should not occupy a bed or seat already occupied by the teacher. If traveling on a journey, he may board a vehicle after the teacher. He may also use a public assembly hall, a gambling table, a mat, or a couch. He should not address the teacher with anything other than pleasant words unless he is first addressed himself. He should avoid poking, whispering, laughing at, calling out to, mentioning the name of, or giving commands to the teacher. Only in an emergency should he inform him of a matter. Living together, he should go to see the teacher every morning and evening unless summoned. Upon returning from a journey, he should see him on that very day. When the teacher and the teacher’s own teacher meet, he should first clasp the hand of the teacher’s teacher and then wish to clasp the hand of his own teacher; the latter should then forbid it. In the presence of the teacher’s teacher, the honor due to his own teacher is suspended. He should visit the teacher’s family frequently to see them, bringing whatever he can afford, even if it is only tooth-cleansers.

The meaning is this: “Just as for the student (*brahmacārin*), so for the one who has returned home (*samāvṛtta*)—the conduct (*vṛtta*), that is, the practice or observance, is exactly the same for the one who has returned home regarding the rules of customary conduct (*sāmayācārika*). “For the one who has returned home” means for one who lives together [with his wife] prior to marriage by virtue of necessity. “Wearing a garland (*mālī*)” means possessing a garland. “With an anointed face (*āliptamukhaḥ*)” means having the face completely anointed with sandalwood paste and the like. “With trimmed hair and beard (*upaliptakeśaśmaśruḥ*): here the prefix *upa-* is used in the sense of ‘properly’; he is one whose hair and beard have been properly prepared by cutting and so forth. “Smeared (*aktaḥ*)” means having applied collyrium to the eyes. “Anointed (*abhyaktaḥ*)” means having performed an oil massage. “Girded (*veṣṭitiḥ*)” means having wrapped a cloth around the waist. “A bodice-wearer (*kañcukī*)” means wearing a short-sleeved jacket (*kūrpāsaka*). “Shoes (*upānahī*)” and “sandals (*pādukī*)” are well known. “In formal greetings (*udācāreṣu*)”—that is, when formal acts such as the clasping of the feet (*upasaṃgrahaṇa*) are being performed toward a teacher or similar superior—these things, such as wearing a garland and so forth, he should not do himself, nor should he cause them to be done by another upon himself. The word *ca* (and), functioning in the sense of a restrictive particle (*tu-śabda*), states an exception to the wearing of garlands and the rest. “And in private matters (*svairikarmasu ca*)”—in matters concerning himself—he should not perform or cause these things, such as wearing a garland and so forth, to be done. He states what private matters are: “such as cleaning the teeth,” and so forth. “Scraping (*avalekhanaṃ*)” refers to grooming the hair with a comb (*kaṅkatika*) or similar tools. In this context, he incidentally states the duty of the teacher: “Of those articles (*tad-dravyāṇāṃ*)”—of the articles belonging to the resident pupil, such as clothes and so forth. “By way of personal connection (*ātmasaṃyogena*)”: here, personal connection is the relationship of ownership; for that reason, “he should not speak”—he should not engage in conversation. The meaning is that he should not speak of the qualities of the one who is anointed [with perfumes]. Again, he states the duties of the one who has returned home, beginning with “But the graduate (*snātaka*) at the proper time,” and so forth. At the time of returning home, “that which was brought according to rule (*yathāvidhy abhihṛtaṃ*)”—meaning that which was received with mantras, such as the umbrella, garland, ointment, and earrings—that is what is meant by “brought. “Then, when summoned (*athāhūto*)” by the teacher or by himself going toward the teacher, “having approached (*abhyetaḥ*)” or gone there, “he should not withdraw (*na pratisaṃharet*)” from his own body—so say “some” teachers. “On a multi-legged vehicle (*bahupāde*)” means on a carriage or similar conveyance. “When it is being used (*adhyācarite*)” means when it is being enjoyed. “If directed to mount a vehicle (*yānayukto adhvany anvārohet*)”—when told by the teacher, “Mount the vehicle,” he should mount behind on the road. “In an assembly or on a threshing floor (*sabhānikaṣe*)”—the construction is that he should mount [behind] when directed by the teacher. “Assembly (*sabhā*)” is a place where people gather. “Threshing floor (*kaṭaḥ*)” is a wooden tool made of wood and the like for leveling a field of loose soil. “Poking (*vyupetodaḥ*)” means poking variously with a finger or other means. “Whispering (*vyupajāpaḥ*)” means whispering variously nearby into the ear. “Mocking (*vyabhihāsaḥ*)” means joking in the presence of the teacher. “Calling out loudly (*udāmantraṇaṃ*)” means calling out loudly and from nearby to a teacher who is not deaf. “Mentioning by name (*nāmakaraṇaṃ*)” means that mentioning the name given by the father and others is forbidden, but not the name of another venerable person, as such is seen in the conduct of the learned. “He should make himself known for the sake of an emergency (*āpadyarthaṃ jñāpayet*)”: “in an emergency (*āpadi*)” means in distress; “for the sake of a purpose (*arthaṃ*)” means for a specific need. He should make himself known to the teacher by some other means while exerting effort. “On that very day (*tad ahar eva*)”—the mention of the day is illustrative; even at night, he should go at that very moment. “He should wish to clasp [the teacher’s feet] (*upasaṃjighṛkṣet*)” means he should manifest the desire to clasp [the feet] by extending his hand and so forth. “The other (*itaraḥ*)” refers to the teacher. “He should go for the sake of seeing him (*darśanārtho gacchet*)”—by implication, this refers specifically to the one who has returned home. “Regarding the elephant (*adhihastyaṃ*)” means he should go having himself taken roots, fruits, and so forth in his hand.
Regarding service to the guru, Śaṅkha and Likhita state:
"One should not remain alone on a seat or a bed, except during a sacrificial session, in a palanquin, while riding a vehicle, in a cart, or during festive occasions.
"Upayāna" refers to following after a corpse. "Abhyudaya" refers to one who assists at a sacrifice, such as a wedding and so forth, while standing [in attendance].
Manu [2.204]: One should sit together with one’s teacher on vehicles drawn by oxen, horses, or camels, on couches, on mats, on stone slabs, on wooden planks, and on boats.
Baudhāyana [1.3.35]:
There is no fault in sitting together on a boat, a stone slab, a wooden plank, an elephant, a palace, a mat, or on vehicles with wheels;
"on vehicles with wheels" refers to carts and the like.

Āpastamba [1.7.20–23]: But if the teacher has fallen into distress, he may take [wealth] from a Ugra or from a Śūdra. Some say that taking wealth for the sake of the teacher from a Śūdra or an Ugra at all times is lawful. Having given [it], he should not speak of it; and having performed [the service], he should not remember it.
"Fallen into distress" means one who has encountered calamity.
Hārīta says: The Guru indeed quickly washes away the disciple who is smeared with the mud of ignorance and struck by darkness, using the water of refined knowledge.
Whether one receives a verse, or a half-verse, or a quarter-verse,
or even a single syllable from another's presence, there must certainly be reverence shown therein.
Even a teacher, if he is arrogant, ignorant of what should and should not be done,
and has set out upon a wrong path, is ordained to be abandoned.
He who neither teaches nor studies, but conducts himself according to the ways of others—
a teacher endowed with such characteristics should be abandoned by one observing his vows.
But the disciple who shows contempt for a teacher who is acting rightly takes upon himself the teacher's misdeeds and goes to a birth among the animals.
Āpastamba [1.14.2–4]:

One should not refuse him whom one may urge for the purpose of study, nor should one perceive any fault in him; if a voluntary agreement is not reached, that is simply the way it is with him. Manu [2.144]:
He who covers both ears with truthful action should be known as one's mother and father; one should never bear him malice.
Viṣṇu [30.43]: One should never bear malice toward that person from whom one acquires knowledge, whether it be worldly, Vedic, or even spiritual.
Vasiṣṭha [2.10–11]: He who covers the ears with that which is not false, hearing the sorrowless and bestowing immortality—
One should regard him as both father and mother; one should not bear malice toward him for anything whatsoever.
Those Brahmins who, having been taught by their teacher, do not respect him in word, thought, or deed,
are just as unfit to be fed by the teacher as [those who have not studied].
In that very same way, that sacred learning does not benefit them.
[225] Likewise, there is an extended application (atideśa) in that regard concerning Viṣṇu [32.1–2].

A king, a sacrificial priest (*ṛtvij*), one learned in the Vedas (*śrotriya*), one who prohibits unrighteousness, a teacher (*upādhyāya*), a paternal uncle, a maternal grandfather, a maternal uncle, a father-in-law, a preceptor (*guru*), an elder brother, and paternal relatives are to be honored like a teacher; as are their wives of equal caste (*savarṇa*).
When the teacher’s own teacher is present, one should behave toward him as toward the teacher.
And one should not pay homage to one's own elders without having been permitted by one's teacher.

But this alone is the constant duty toward the teacher of knowledge: even toward those who forbid unrighteousness and who instruct one in what is beneficial, one must behave as toward one's own kinsmen.
One should always behave toward those who are superior as one does toward the guru—
toward the guru’s sons, toward those worthy of respect, and toward the guru’s own kinsmen.

“Of the guru” means of the one who initiates and imparts the Veda. “Like unto a guru” means in this very same manner. “Unreleased” means not commanded. “His own” refers to the guru’s sons and others. “The teacher of knowledge” (vidyā-guru) is the *upādhyāya*. “Constant” means pertaining to all times. “Among those of one’s own kin” (*svayoniṣu*) refers to paternal uncles and so forth. “Among superiors” (*śreyaḥsu*) refers to those perfected in learning and austerity. “Among those of good conduct” (*ācāreṣu*) refers to members of the three higher castes. Āpastamba [1.14.5–9].

Service toward one's mother and father is to be performed as toward a teacher (*ācārya*). Upon returning from his studies, all elders (*guru*) are to be saluted with clasping of the feet; likewise upon reunion after traveling abroad. Among brothers and sisters, the clasping of the feet is performed according to seniority. Constant worship is to be offered according to the instructions. "According to seniority" means according to age. "According to the instructions" means in the manner prescribed, such as "the left hand with the left," and so forth.
[226] Again, Āpastamba [1.13.12–18]:

There is no going outside the Veda. One should attend upon the teacher who instructs what has been assigned to him for as long as the study lasts; some say this applies constantly to one who is worthy. There is no going [outside]. But in the case of elders, when there is a mutual application regarding the sacred word (*brahman*), there is no going [outside]; they teach that "the sacred word increases."

“Not outside”: that which is outside the Veda, such as the Buddhist scriptures and others, from which there is no *apayānam*—that is, no access or path (*gati*) exists. “Access” (*gati*) is a term used by those following the *Smṛtis*. Regarding service (*śuśrūṣā*), when one is “instructed” (*samādiṣṭaḥ*) by the teacher with a view toward some other purpose, one should attend upon him while he is teaching what has been instructed, but only for as long as the study lasts, not otherwise. “One worthy of honor” (*arhantam*): one who deserves the salutation (*abhivādana*) performed by a student who has returned home (*samāvṛtta*); one should attend upon such a person worthy of honor constantly, even after returning home, starting from the time the instruction for study began, even if the formal study itself has ceased. “But there is no access for elders”: the meaning is that a teacher of knowledge should not require a pupil who is older in age to perform personal service for him. “In the case of the Veda” (*brahmaṇi*): when there is a mutual arrangement (*viniyoga*) for teaching one another at different locations, “there is no access,” meaning there is no [requirement of] service. “They teach that the Veda increases”: teachers prescribe service for the reason that “the Veda increases. Since that increase of the Veda is accomplished here simply through mutual study, separate service need not be performed.
Now follows the section on the conduct toward the teacher’s son and wife.
On this point, Manu states (2.208–209):
"Whether he be a child, of equal age, or a pupil, during the performance of a sacrificial rite..."
A teacher's son who instructs [others] deserves honor just like the teacher himself.

Regarding the phrase "in the sacrificial rite" (*yajñakarmaṇi*): a teacher’s son who is teaching a disciple of that Veda which is to be mastered through sacrificial rites deserves honor just like the teacher himself. However, he should not perform the massaging of limbs, the bathing, the feeding of leftovers, or the washing of the feet for the teacher’s son.
"Having taught him" means having taught another Veda or another portion thereof. "Utsādana" means rubbing with unguents; "avanejana" means washing.

Regarding the phrase "the conduct toward the teacher," Āpastamba [1.7.31], following the same context, states: For wives of teachers belonging to lower castes, there shall be salutation before them, but not the clasping of their feet. One should not perform for the wives of teachers such acts as rubbing their limbs, applying collyrium, dressing their hair, or washing their feet.
The wives of the teacher who belong to the same caste (savarṇā) should be honored like the teacher himself;
those of a different caste, however, should be honored by rising from one's seat and by salutation.
Anointing, bathing, massaging the limbs,
and the dressing of the hair— these must not be performed for the wife of one's guru.
This is the nature of women: they are the corruption of men in this world.
Therefore, the wise do not become heedless on account of women.
For in this world, women are capable of leading astray both the ignorant man and even the learned man who has fallen under the sway of desire and anger.
One should not sit in a secluded place with one's mother, sister, or daughter;
for the powerful collection of the senses drags away even a wise man.
“Secluded” means a secret place.
Now follows the restraint of the senses; regarding this, Manu [2.175–182] says:
"A student living with his teacher should observe these following rules."
Having fully restrained the collection of his senses for the sake of increasing his own ascetic merit.
Having bathed daily and become pure, he should perform the libations for the gods, sages, and ancestors,
as well as the worship of the deities and the placing of sacrificial fuel upon the fire.
One should avoid honey, meat, perfumes, garlands, flavors, women,
all fermented acids, and indeed the harming of living beings.
Anointing the body, applying collyrium to the eyes, wearing shoes and carrying an umbrella,
as well as desire, anger, greed, dancing, singing, and playing musical instruments.
Gambling, idle gossip, slander, as well as falsehood;
gazing at and touching women, and the harming of others.
One should always sleep alone and never let semen spill;
for by emitting semen out of desire, one destroys one's own vow.
He should fetch a water-pot, flowers, cow-dung, earth, and kuśa grass—
as much as required— and he should go out for alms every day.

“Flavors” (*rasān*) refers to substances such as molasses and the like, in which flavor predominates. “Sour things” (*śuktāni*) refers to naturally sweet fruits such as mangoes and the like. Here, “desire” (*kāma*) refers to an excessive longing for other sense objects, since desire for women has already been prohibited by the mention of “women” in relation to *manmatha* (the god of love). “Public gossip” (*janavāda*) means worldly rumor. Regarding the phrase “and the looking at and touching of women,” this refers to casting affectionate glances at and embracing women when there is a suspicion of sexual intent. Thus, following the recurring injunction “one should avoid,” Gautama [2.22] states: “One should avoid looking at and touching women when there is a suspicion of sexual intent.”
“Yāvadarthāni” means as many as are necessary for one’s purpose.
Yama says: One whose senses are not scattered, who is self-controlled, patient, pure, and free from anger.
Devoted to the private recitation of the Vedas, skillful, not eating more than once a day, and having his senses subdued.
One who has conquered sleep, is free from laziness, has subdued anger, and has mastered the self;
who is desirous of hearing [the teachings], free from egoism, and devoted to the worship of the guru and the gods.
He should avoid a high bedstead, a couch, and the cleaning of teeth;
he should sleep alone on *kuśa* grass and never let his semen be discharged.
"One whose senses are not scattered" means one whose senses are undisturbed. "Tamed" means one who endures the hardships of austerity.
Bṛhaspati [Saṃskāra 224, 223]:
One should avoid with effort those things that are prohibited by the scriptures.
He should meditate and perform what is beneficial for his guru, as well as the worship of the gods and sages.
A twice-born man who has been initiated should always perform service for his guru;
he should never be one who looks only for rewards, such as garlands, flowers, skins, beeswax, and the like.
“Garlands” refers to wearing garlands. “Wax” is beeswax, for the purpose of grooming the lips. By the word “and so forth,” the inclusion of ointments and other such items is intended.
Now, the rules for the religious student (*brahmacārin*):

Viṣṇu [28.11] states that one who performs a *śrāddha* [must avoid] salt, fermented acids, stale food, dancing, singing, women, honey, meat, collyrium, the remnants of others' food, injury to living beings, vulgar speech, and wiping [the body].

“Excluding *śrāddha*” should be understood as referring to one who has not been invited; for according to Yājñavalkya: “A Brāhmaṇa may eat at a *śrāddha* at his will, provided he does not violate his vow. “*Kṛḷlavaṇam*” means prepared salt (*kṛtalavaṇam*).

Gautama [2.18–19]: One should not look at the sun. One should avoid honey, meat, perfumes, garlands, sleeping during the day, collyrium, ointments, vehicles, shoes, umbrellas, lust, anger, greed, delusion, idle talk, playing musical instruments, bathing for pleasure, cleaning the teeth, exhilaration, dancing, singing, slander, and fear.
"Idle talk" (*vāda*) refers to excessive prattle. "Playing musical instruments" (*vādana*) refers to musical instruments. "Bathing" (*snāna*) refers to bathing for the sake of personal enjoyment.
Regarding the continuation of what is to be avoided, Gautama states (2.23–24):

gambling, service to the lowly, taking what is not given, violence, the names of one’s teacher, his son, and a consecrated person; and harsh words. [232] “Harsh” means cruel, according to the statement that they cause distress to others.

Āpastamba [1.2.22–29]: He should not eat without having designated [the food for a deity]. Likewise, he should avoid alkaline substances, salt, honey, and meat. He should not sleep during the day. He should not use perfumes. He should not engage in sexual intercourse. He should abandon self-praise. He should not wash his limbs. However, he may wash them if they are soiled with excrement or urine, provided it is out of the sight of his teacher.

"Without having designated" means that which has been intended for the sake of a deity or similar purpose. "Abandoning self-praise" means he should give up praising himself; the word "should be" (*syāt*) is to be supplied as the remainder of the sentence.

Hārīta says: "One who subsists on alms should avoid eating food from a single source, honey, meat, alkaline substances, salt, and prepared foods; he should not converse with barbarians, the impure, women, or Śūdras.
Baudhāyana [1.3.24] says:
One should converse with women only as much as is necessary for a purpose.
— Āpastamba [1.7.3–11].

One should not look at a naked woman. One should not smell plants or trees after cutting them off. One should avoid sandals, an umbrella, and a vehicle. One should not smile. For it is stated in the Brāhmaṇa: "If one should smile, one should smile while covering [the mouth]. One should not kiss a woman with the mouth. One should not desire her with the heart. One should not touch [her] without cause. For it is stated in the Brāhmaṇa: "One who is menstruating, one whose teeth are stained red, and one who speaks the truth [should be avoided]."

“If he should smile,” then he should “cover his mouth,” which is the implied meaning. “He should not touch a woman without cause”—this is the syntactic connection. Because the subject is under discussion, “one who is dusty” means one covered in dust. “One with stained teeth” means one whose teeth are red.
Manu [2.159]: “The instruction for the welfare of living beings should be carried out through non-violence alone.”
And speech that is sweet and gentle should be employed by one who desires dharma.

“By non-violence” means without excessive oppression. Here, the word *bhūta* refers to those who are to be instructed. “Instruction” (*anuśāsana*) means training (*śikṣā*). “Sweet” means pleasant. “Gentle” means speech that is not raised too loud.
And this duty toward the teacher has been mentioned by Manu [2.160–163] in this context:
“He whose speech and mind are pure and always properly guarded...”
He indeed attains the entire fruit that is reached through the Vedānta.
One should not be a wounder of others' vitals even when afflicted, nor should one’s mind be intent on deeds that harm others;
one should not utter that speech by which another is agitated, for such speech does not lead to the higher worlds.
A Brahmin should always tremble at honor as if it were poison;
he should always long for contempt as if it were nectar.
For he who is held in low esteem sleeps in comfort and wakes in comfort;
he moves through this world in comfort, while the scorner perishes.

"Pure" means faultless. "Properly guarded" means free from the fruits of faults. "All" refers to the fruit of liberation, which is attained through the Vedānta and propounded in the Upaniṣads, such as union (*sāyujya*). "One who pierces the vitals" (*aruṃtuda*) means one who causes pain to the vital organs. "Not to be looked upon" (*nālokyā*) means unchaste. Śātātapa says:
Just as a cow is nourished by grasses that produce nectar, so too...
In this way, through recitations and burnt offerings, the twice-born man is restored once more.

Hārīta says: One should avoid riding upon horses, elephants, chariots, sacred trees, or uneven terrain; gathering fruit; crawling through joints; descending into wells; crossing great rivers by swimming; and acts of great recklessness or those that are contrary to propriety. Furthermore, one should avoid fidgeting, negligence, committing faults, improper exertion, speaking like a conch-shell, sleeping during the day, and engaging in disputes.

“A shrine” (*caitya*) is a temple of a deity. “A junction” (*saṃdhi*) here refers to a place for the performance of ritual preparations. “Great rivers” are the Gaṅgā and others. “Great risk” (*mahāsāhasa*) here refers to traveling through difficult terrain and the like. “Opposition” (*viruddha*) is taking refuge with a teacher who is hostile toward the king and so forth. “Instability” (*calana*) is lack of steadiness in study and other such activities. “Negligence” (*pramādakaraṇa*) is performing practices without focused attention.

Āpastamba [1.3.11–15]: He should not watch dancing; he should not attend assemblies or social gatherings; he should not be habituated to gossiping about people; he should not be habituated to solitude; and he should not imitate the conduct of his teacher in his private actions.
Likewise [1.3.21–22]:
firm in resolve; untiring;
If one who is sleeping at will is awakened by the sun,
or if he should fall asleep out of ignorance while reciting prayers, he must fast for the day.

He may be shaven-headed, or he may have matted hair, or he may have a single lock of matted hair on the crown; the sun must never set while he is still within a village, nor should it ever rise upon him there.
“He should not set [the sun] on the western mountain,” meaning he should not let it go down.
Āpastamba [1.2.31–32]:
“He should wear matted hair; or, having a single lock of matted hair, he should have the rest shaved.”
Hārīta:
[He should be] one with matted hair and long nails and body hair.
If a woman or a younger person should perform any virtuous deed, one should practice all of that with diligence; and whatever brings him joy, that he should follow.
It is said that the good consists of dharma and artha, or kama and artha, or dharma alone;
or else, artha alone is the good in this world—such is the established position regarding the three aims of life.

The "inferior" (avaraja) is the Śūdra. Whatever is "better" (śreyaḥ), such as plastering and sweeping the teacher's house, he should perform it upon seeing that it is being undertaken even by women and Śūdras. Gautama [9.48–49]: One should not let the forenoon, midday, or afternoon pass fruitlessly; one should devote them to dharma, artha, and kāma according to one's ability. Among these, however, one should prioritize dharma.

The meaning is that one should make the [directions] beginning with the east fruitful for the sake of Dharma through their respective means, according to one's capacity, in their proper order. Among those—namely, among Dharma and the others—one should be "superior in Dharma," meaning one should make Dharma the primary concern. Hārīta says:
From the initiation ceremony onwards, one should wear the girdle, staff, deerskin, and sacred thread.
[236] Yama says:
While living with his teacher, he should maintain celibacy, subsist on alms-food, and carry a staff, a water-pot, and a girdle made of muñja grass.
Manu and Viṣṇu [Manu 2.64; Viṣṇu 27.28]:
Having thrown into the water a girdle, a skin, a staff, a sacred thread, or a water-pot that have become damaged, he should take others according to the prescribed mantras.

Now, Manu and Viṣṇu state regarding the second [stage]: "For one who has performed the initiation ceremony, the instruction in the vows and the acquisition of the Veda are prescribed in due order according to the rule. (Manu 2.173–174; Viṣṇu 27.28)
Whatever rite is prescribed for one, whatever sacred thread, whatever girdle, whatever staff, and whatever ablution— that each of these shall also be included in his vows.
Regarding "vratas," such as those prescribed in the Upaniṣads and other texts,
Śaṅkha and Likhita state:
"After the initiation ceremony (upanayana), there is the observance of the vow (brahmacarya)."
Manu and Bṛhaspati [Manu 2.108; Bṛh. Prāyaścitta 67]:

Having undergone the initiation ceremony, a twice-born man shall maintain the sacred fires, [live on] alms, practice begging for food, sleep on the ground, and perform what is beneficial for his teacher until his formal return home.

Regarding the observance of the duties of a religious student (*brahmacārin*), Gautama states [3.10]: "And this is not in conflict with those who follow later stages. "This" refers to what was prescribed for the student, such as the avoidance of gambling and so forth. That which is "not in conflict"—meaning that which is not contradicted by other scriptural injunctions or by worldly custom—should be followed by "those who follow later stages," namely the householder and others. However, that which is contradicted should be abandoned; for example, the practice of lifelong celibacy (*ūrdhvaretas*) is not applicable to the householder.
Regarding the conduct toward the teacher, Āpastamba [1.7.31] states: "Even for one who has returned home from his studies, this same conventional rule applies in these matters. Hārīta says:
From the initiation ceremony (*upanayana*) onwards, he wears a girdle, a staff, an antelope skin, and a sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*).
Regarding this, the *Kapardibhāṣya* states: "The 'conduct based on traditional rules' (*sāmayācārika*) refers to the connection between injunctions and prohibitions.
Furthermore, Āpastamba [1.13.5] says:
No formal instruction exists for one who has returned home.
"Instruction" (samādeśa) means performing duties solely by the command of the teacher. Now, Manu [2.163–164]:
By this sequential method, the twice-born whose self has been refined should,
while dwelling with his guru, gradually accumulate the austerity conducive to the realization of Brahman.
The entire Veda, together with its secret portions, must be mastered by the twice-born through various specific austerities and vows prescribed by rule.

Āpastamba [1.5.1–2]: The word *tapas* (austerity) refers to the observances (*niyamas*). Upon their transgression, the *vidyā-karma* and the *brahman* flow out from this person along with his offspring.

"Vidyā-karma" means the acquisition of knowledge. "Flows out" (*niḥsravati*) means it leaks away; that is to say, it becomes devoid of potency. "*Brahman*" means the Veda. "Along with offspring" (*sahāpatyāt*) refers to the student together with his progeny.
Likewise [1.5.9–11]:

"The rites to be performed for the gratification of the teacher, the rite for well-being (*svastyayana*), and the completion of one's studies—these are the duties. All other rites cease for the religious student (*brahmacārin*). One who maintains his private Vedic recitation, who delights in dharma, who practices austerity, and who is upright and gentle, succeeds as a religious student."

“Services to be performed for the gratification of the guru” (*guruprasādanīyāni*) are those acts, such as washing the feet, which bring pleasure to the teacher. “Auspiciousness” (*svastyayana*) is that which effects self-protection. For one approaching the foot of a tree at night, “the observance of study” (*adhyayanasaṃvṛttiḥ*) refers to the practice of Vedic recitation. “Other [acts]” refer to the construction of temples for deities and so forth. “Upholding the private recitation” (*svādhyāyadhṛk*) means steadfastness in the private recitation of the Vedas.
Hārīta says: Now, regarding this, they cite the following:
Through vows, the Vedic meters are perfected and become granters of desires;
for the sake of accomplishing the meters, the wise man should perform the vows prescribed by the scriptures.
Laghuvyāsa states: The study of the Veda should be performed by the wise who possess the purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*).
For one who is pure, it shall bear fruit; otherwise, it is declared to be fruitless.
One who knows the Dharma may study even the Ṛgveda by the prescribed method,
but never the four Vedas through improper means.
The Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas, even if acquired in great abundance by the twice-born through proper means,
do not confer the status of Brahmanhood if they are acquired in an improper manner.
Therefore, it is better to resort to silence than to cause the corruption of the Vedas;
for by corrupting the Vedas, a Brahmin goes headlong to hell.

[239] Atri, Vasiṣṭha, Aṅgiras, and Yama were in the second [generation]. Just as horses are useless without a chariot, or a chariot is useless without horses, so too is asceticism for one who lacks knowledge, or knowledge for one who lacks asceticism.
Just as food combined with honey, or honey combined with food,
so too are austerity and knowledge together a great medicine.

One does not incur sin by reciting [the Veda] even to a Brāhmaṇa who is constantly engaged in evil deeds, provided that he is endowed with knowledge and austerity and is devoted to the silent recitation of the sacred texts.
Now, Manu [12.104]:
"Austerity and knowledge are the supreme means for a Brahmin to attain the highest good.
Through austerity he destroys sin; through knowledge he partakes of immortality."
Devala said:
Knowledge, wealth, and austerity—these are the three splendors of embodied beings;
by means of these three, that which is beneficial both in this world and the next is accomplished.
Through knowledge, stainless light is attained; through the acquisition of wealth, the dawning of happiness;
and through austerity, pure prosperity is achieved—thus this triad is obtained by these three means respectively.
Now, regarding those who are to be instructed, Bṛhaspati [Saṃskāra 222] says:
"Having thus consecrated his son with the staff and other rites, the father..."
One should teach the Veda to one who is tranquil, as well as the Shastras such as those of Manu and others.
Yama says:
If a teacher does not impart knowledge to a student who has resided with him for a year,
the teacher shall take upon himself the evil deeds of that student.

Regarding service and obedience toward the teacher, Āpastamba [1.8.24–28] states: "In that regard, this is the conduct toward the teacher: desiring him as one would a son, and not concealing anything in all matters of dharma, he should diligently cause him to grasp the knowledge. And he should not, except in times of distress, obstruct him from his own purposes by creating obstacles to his study. A pupil who fails to apply himself skillfully toward his teacher ceases to be a pupil, even if he has been formally initiated. Likewise, a teacher who neglects what he has heard ceases to be a teacher."

"In that" one who serves the teacher, "conduct" is now described. "Him," the one who serves; "desiring," seeking after; "in all duties," even those difficult to perform; "not concealing," not deceiving; "well-yoked," not having a distracted mind; "with self surrendered," having offered his self to the teacher in various ways—even when there are many teachers for a single branch of knowledge. Manu [2.109]:
The son of the teacher, one who is service-minded, a giver of knowledge, righteous, and pure;
One who is trustworthy, capable, a giver of wealth, virtuous, and one's own kinsman—these ten are to be taught according to the Dharma.

A "giver of knowledge" (*jñānada*) is one who bestows other branches of learning. A "capable" (*śakta*) person is one who possesses the ability for comprehension and retention. "One's own" (*sva*) refers to kinsmen, sons, and so forth.
Yājñavalkya [1.28] states:
"Those who are grateful, non-malicious, intelligent, pure, and indicative of auspiciousness..."
Those who are virtuous, capable, trustworthy, wise, and givers of wealth should be taught according to the Dharma.

“Indicating auspiciousness” means possessing favorable characteristics. “Capable” refers to being competent in this regard—namely, in receiving instruction. “Bestowing wealth” means one who provides wealth for the purpose of maintaining the student, since teaching for wages is listed among the minor offenses (*upapātaka*) [in Yājñavalkya-smṛti 3.237]. Gautama [10.4] states: “The transmission of the Veda by a Brahmin occurs under the supervision of the teacher, kinsmen, friends, elders, wealth, or learning; otherwise, it is as previously described.”

The chapter titled “The Regulation of Wealth and Knowledge. Regarding the term “of Brahman,” it refers to the Veda. The phrase “other than as previously stated” means that, apart from those such as a student (*śuśrūṣaka*), these [rules apply] only to these [specific cases].
Viṣṇu [29.3–4]: One should not officiate at a sacrifice for someone who has not been examined, nor should one teach him.

Āpastamba [2.6.1–2]: When there is doubt regarding one’s caste or conduct, one should kindle a fire for the sake of determining the dharma and inquire about the person’s caste and conduct. If he declares his integrity, [the teacher] should say: “Agni is the witness, Vāyu is the listener, Āditya is the observer; he declares his integrity. May integrity be his lot; this man is false in his sin. Having said this, he should proceed to instruct him. “Having kindled the fire” means according to the procedure prescribed in one’s own Gṛhya-sūtra.
Manu and Yama [Manu 2.110]: One should not speak to anyone unless asked, nor to one who asks improperly;
for even though he knows, a wise man should behave like one who is dull-witted in the world.
A teacher of the Veda should rather die along with his knowledge at his will;
even in times of terrible distress, he must never sow it upon barren soil.
Knowledge approached a Brahmin and said: "I am your treasure; protect me.
Do not give me to one who is envious, so that I may remain most powerful."
But to that brahmin whom you know to be pure, disciplined in his student life, capable of receiving instruction, and free from negligence— to him speak of me.
“Śevadhiḥ” means a treasure. “Iriṇe” means in barren soil. Hārīta says:
“He who is indeed wise, desirous of learning, and whose conduct is that of a student...”
To one in whom there is no grief, no agitation, and no violation of dharma—
to him I shall impart knowledge with faith;
not to one who is inwardly corrupt, a chatterer, or of a miserable disposition.
“Vyathet” means “should move. Thus, having taught [the rules], now follows the instruction for the disciples.

Yama: "The instruction of a pupil shall be without corporal punishment; if that is impossible, it may be done with a thin rope or a split bamboo cane. One who strikes him with anything else shall be punished by the king.
A wife, a son, a slave, a servant, and a uterine brother—
when they have committed an offense, they may be beaten with a rope or a split bamboo cane.
The back, however, is never considered a superior limb of the body;
for striking it otherwise, one would incur the guilt of a thief.
Now follows the procedure for commencing study.
Regarding this, Manu states (2.70–75):
"One who is about to study, having sipped water according to the scriptures, facing north,"
With palms joined in the *brahmāñjali* gesture, wearing light-colored garments, and having conquered his senses, he should be taught.
At the beginning and at the end of the recitation of the Veda, one should always grasp the feet of the teacher;
having joined the hands together, one should study, for that is known as the *brahmāñjali*.
The clasping of the teacher's feet should be performed with crossed hands:
the left foot is to be touched with the left hand, and the right foot with the right hand.
When the student is about to begin his studies, the teacher, always free from sloth, should say, "Recite, sir! and he should conclude with, "May there be a pause."
One should always place the *praṇava* at the beginning and at the end of the *brahman*.
That which is not preceded by the *oṃ* slips away, and that which is not followed by it falls apart.
Seated upon grass-blades pointing eastward, purified by means of purifiers,
and cleansed by three breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas), he then becomes worthy of the syllable Om.

“Prākkūlān” means those with their tips pointing eastward. Since mantras such as the *Pavitra* and *Āpādaka-Pāvamānya*, which bring about purification, are not available at the time of commencing Vedic study, the purification by means of *darbha* grass is the contact of the sense organs mentioned by Gautama.
Likewise [Gautama 2.76–77]:
Prajāpati [created] the syllable ‘A’, the syllable ‘U’, and the syllable ‘M’.
From the three Vedas, he milked forth the syllables "bhūḥ," "bhuvaḥ," and "svar."
From the three Vedas alone, Parameṣṭhin Prajāpati milked out foot by foot that [first] quarter of this Sāvitrī verse beginning with "tat."
Gautama [1.52–62] |

Having grasped the left hand of the teacher with his own hand, excluding the thumb, he should address the teacher, saying: "Recite, sir! Therein, he should fix his eyes and mind [on the teacher]. He should touch his vital breaths (*prāṇa*) with *darbha* grass. He should perform three breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāma*), each consisting of fifteen *mātrās*. His seat should be upon [grass] whose points are directed toward the east. The five *vyāhṛtis*, preceded by the syllable *oṃ* and ending with the word "Truth" (*satya*), [are to be recited]. In the morning, he should clasp the feet of the teacher; likewise at the beginning and end of the recitation of the *brahman* (the Veda). Having been permitted, the disciple should sit down to the right of the teacher, facing either the east or the north. At the commencement of the acquisition of the *brahman*, the *Sāvitrī* is to be recited first. The syllable *oṃ* is used even elsewhere.

"With the right hand" means with his own right hand; "having placed the left hand" means having positioned both hands so as to form the *brahmāñjali* (the hollowed cup of the hands). "There" means one whose mind and eyes are fixed upon the teacher—that is, "one whose sight and mind are directed there. "Prāṇas" refers to the sense organs. "Mātrās" refers to the durations of short syllables. "Ending with *satya*" refers to those formulas such as *bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ puruṣaḥ satyam*. They are designated as "ending with *satya*" because they are recited by others ending with the word *puruṣa*. Furthermore, at the beginning—meaning at the commencement—the *Sāvitrī* must also be spoken.
Āpastamba [1.10.15–16]:
In the presence of the teacher, one should study after having said, "Recite, sir! Or one may teach.
Śaṅkha and Likhita: [246]

When summoned to study, with his hands joined in a pure *añjali* and holding the sacred grass (*pavitra*), and having caused the teacher to recite the *Gāyatrī* while he himself holds the *pavitra*, he should recite the *svādhyāya* facing the teacher. Yama says:
"With palms joined in reverence, he should say to the teacher: 'O Blessed One, I shall study.'"
With senses subdued, dressed in white garments, with palms joined in the *brahmāñjali* gesture, and remaining steady.

“*Brahmāñjalikṛtaḥ*” means having formed the *brahmāñjali* (the reverential gesture). Because the class beginning with *āhitāgni* is an *ākṛtigaṇa*, the word *kṛta* is placed at the end [of the compound]. Having first uttered the syllable *Oṃ*, one should then proceed with the *brahman*.
And having uttered the syllable *Oṃ*, one should touch the ground and then pause.
"Otherwise, that Brahman would become perverted; of this there is no doubt. Paiṭhīnasi says:

"Engaging in the daily recitation of the Veda, having covered his ears and muttered the five syllables, he should touch the teacher's feet with his head and offer salutation. He should not do so for the wife of the teacher without first touching [her feet]."
“The five syllables” are these: *bhūr*, *bhuvaḥ*, *svar*. Saṃvarta says:
Having joined the hands well together, they should be held positioned above the knees.
One should imitate the teacher while studying; one should not have any other thought.
Āpastamba [1.13.6–8]:

The syllable *oṃ* is the gate to heaven; therefore, one who is about to study the Veda should begin with this. Moreover, by engaging in other idle talk, the Veda is turned away from by means of worldly speech. And in sacrifices, these [mantras] beginning with *oṃ* are the invocations.

“Having engaged in other idle talk (*vikathā*)”: idle talk is discourse of a different genus from that of Vedic study. “This and so forth” refers to the *oṃ* syllable and the like. Thus, it is said: “By means of worldly speech, one turns away from the Brahman. This means that the Veda, having become mixed with worldly speech through discourse of a different genus, is again turned away [from such mixing] during the recitation of the Veda preceded by the *praṇava*. The sense is that it becomes thus purified from worldly speech. — Hārīta.

Now we shall define the defects (*upasarga*) pertaining to the duties and occupations of a Brahmin. Regarding *Vedic study* (*adhyayana*), the defects are: teaching to everyone indiscriminately; speculating on the Brahman; giving instruction [without formal initiation]; failing to follow the rules regarding the Vedic meters; revealing secret doctrines to one who is not a teacher or a student; and the interrogation of those who merely memorize texts. Also included are: studying without observing vows; studying without self-restraint; studying without service to the teacher; studying by means of purchase; and showing hatred toward the teacher. Regarding the *student* (*adhyāpya*), the defects are: studying with those of mixed or impure lineage with whom one should not associate; and studying for a fee (*bhṛtaka-adhyayana*). Regarding the *recitation of prayers* (*japya*), the defects are: reciting while following the breath (too fast); reciting in a disordered manner; reciting too slowly; being deficient in phonemes, letters, words, or word-halves; reciting in reverse order; reciting what has not been formally transmitted; reciting without proper pauses; reciting incompletely; and reciting without a firm foundation. When the Veda is defiled by these defects of the Brahman, it becomes powerless, lusterless, unaccomplished, fails to achieve its purpose, does not grant long life, is not divine, does not lead to heaven, and yields no fruit. Therefore, one should maintain these rules while studying, teaching, or reciting. Thus, studying the Vedas free from the defects of the Brahman, he indeed becomes purified, achieves his purpose, and attains all desires.
Whatever sacrifice a twice-born man studies who is liberated from calamities,
by that very act this [result] comes to pass, according to the word of Prajāpati.

“*Brāhmaṇakarmadharmavṛttiḥ*”: this is a *karmadhāraya* compound meaning that both his duties (*karman*) and his modes of livelihood (*vṛtti*) are like those of a Brāhmaṇa. Therein, *dharma* refers to study; *vṛtti* refers to the teaching of one’s own Veda (*svādhyāya*). “*Upasargāḥ*” means calamities. “*Sarvaśrāvaṇam*” means letting everyone, including Śūdras and others, hear it. “*Brahmatarkaṇam*” means fallacious reasoning (*kutarkana*), which results in establishing the lack of authority of the Veda. “*Ādeśanam*” refers to this being directed toward those who have not approached for instruction. “*Anuyogaḥ*” here means questioning at an inappropriate time. These are the calamities for those who preserve the texts. “*Vratāni*” are observances such as the practice of yoga and so forth, intended for the purpose of Vedic study. “*Niyamāḥ*” are rules such as staying in the forest for the sake of study. “*Krayādhyayanam*” is study according to the regulation: “for this much wealth, one shall recite this much. “*Saṃkaraḥ*” is one born of an unmarried woman. “*Saṃkīrṇaḥ*” is one defiled by sin. “*Saṃvyavahāraḥ*” is preoccupation with worldly social standing. “*Sarveṣām*” refers to all those who preserve, study, and teach the texts. “*Prakīrṇam*” is excessively slow. “*Adrutam*” is loud and without haste. “*Akṣarāṇi*” are the vowels such as *e*, etc. “*Varṇāḥ*” are the consonants such as *ka*, etc. “*Viparyastam*” is confused. “*Anāmnātam*” is studied without having heard it from a teacher. “*Avicchinnam*” is devoid of the proper pauses for the three accents (*traisvarya*) and half-verses (*ardharca*), etc. “*Asamāptam*” is due to excessive haste, lacking the proper phonemes (*jāti-varṇa*) and other markers. “*Apratiṣṭhitam*” is uncounted. “*Japyasya*” refers to the mantra to be recited. “*Ete*” are the calamities.
On the days when study is forbidden, according to Gautama [16.22–50].

Thunderbolts, earthquakes, eclipses, and meteors are immediate causes for impurity; as are thunder, rain, and lightning during a fire that has been kindled. During the day, this applies to the rainy season; during the night, it applies to lightning until the latter part of the night. If these phenomena begin after the third watch, the entire day is affected. Some say a meteor is the same as lightning. Thunder during the afternoon, or even at dusk, renders the entire night impure until midnight. Even during the day, if there is still light, the same rule applies. When a king residing within one's territory dies, or when one returns from a journey to meet another, one is impure for a day and night. Likewise, during a tumult, the offering of a *vaitāna* sacrifice, the completion of the Vedas, vomiting, a *śrāddha*, or at a meal offered by a human sacrifice (*manuṣyayajña*), one is impure for a day and night. This also applies on the new moon day, or for two days. The full moon days of Kārttika, Phālguna, and Āṣāḍha, and the three *aṣṭakā* days, require a three-night period of impurity; some say only the last *aṣṭakā*. On both sides of the rainy season, if there is a simultaneous occurrence of rain, lightning, and thunder, the entire period is affected. If they occur together while it is raining, the impurity lasts for three nights. After a festive meal, or for one who has begun Vedic study, the impurity lasts for four *muhūrtas* at night. Some say this applies permanently in a city. One is also impure through mental thought. For those performing a *śrāddha*, the impurity lasts until the end of the day. Also when one is in contact with those who have not prepared food for a *śrāddha*. And regarding each specific science, one should follow what the traditional authorities prescribe.

“*Ahaḥ*” (day) is an indication for the four *praharas* (eighths of a day). “*Ṛtau*” (in the rainy season): when clouds and rain are seen at the time the sacred fires have been kindled, there is no study during the day. By this, it is stated that the previously mentioned rule regarding the suspension of study (*akālika*) applies to seasons other than the rains. “*Vidyuti*” (during lightning): when lightning is seen at the time of the evening twilight (*sāyaṃsaṃdhyā*) during the rains, there is no study at night. That [night suspension] begins from the third part of the afternoon; when lightning occurs at the time of the evening or morning twilight, there is no study during the day until the end of the afternoon, and at night until the end of the night. Because of the word “*ca*” (and), it is implied that when lightning occurs at the time of the morning twilight, there is no study during the day until the end of the afternoon. Regarding “*tribhāgādi*” (starting from the third part): Jayasvāmin holds that when lightning persists from the third part of either night or day until the evening or morning twilights, there is no study for the entire night or the entire day until those times. “*Ulkā*” (a meteor): according to some, there is no study during a meteor just as during lightning. “*Stanayitnuḥ*” (thunder): this refers to a cloud; occurring in the afternoon, it causes a suspension of study similar to that of lightning. “*Api pradoṣe*” (even at dusk): thunder occurring even at dusk causes a suspension of study arising from lightning. “*Ahaś cit*” (if it lasts during the day): if the cloud persists before the end of the afternoon, then there is no study until the end of the day. “*Viṣayasthe*” (when the ruler of the region has died): there is no study when the king of the country where the student resides has died, not if he is in another country. “*Viproṣya ca*” (and after returning from travel): this refers to the absence of the teacher and the student, since the suspension of study lasting until the same time [the next day] was introduced previously. “*Saṃkule*” (in a crowded place); “*upāhite*” (during a fire-accident). By the mention of *śrāddha*, the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite is also included; the prior mention of the *ekoddiṣṭa* is for the purpose of indicating specific faults, like specific penances, referring to annual rites (*ābdika*) and so forth. “*Yajñabhojane*” (at a sacrifice meal): when eating as a guest. “*Dvyahaṃ vā*” (or two days): this is for the purpose of including the first day. “*Kārttikīpaurṇamāsī*” (the full moon of Kārttika): although a suspension of study is already established, this is repeated again to state an excess of fault. “*Tisro ’ṣṭakāḥ*” (the three *aṣṭakā* festivals): these are after the *Āgrahāyaṇī* full moon. “*Antyām eke*” (some say the last one): some hold that there is a three-night suspension of study on the final *aṣṭakā*. This refers to those for whom the *aṣṭikā-karma* ritual is performed on a single *aṣṭakā*. “*Prasyandini*” (other than the rains). “*Prādhīnasya*” (of one who has begun to study): the connection is that there is no study after eating for one who has just started his lessons. “*Pratividyam*” (regarding each branch of knowledge): one should not study even those specific suspensions of study which are traditionally remembered in succession, such as the non-study of the chapter called *prakṛta* in the Ṛgveda after eating.
Paiṭhīnasi [states]:
"Upon the appearance of the blue-and-red [Indra's bow].

Since this was already mentioned previously in the rule "having seen Indra’s bow at night," here, upon the appearance of the blue-and-red Indra’s bow during the day, there is a suspension of study for a full day and night.
Furthermore, Paiṭhīnasi states:
"On the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight, on all eighth days, and again at night, there is no study, with the exception of the Aṣṭakās.
Baudhāyana [1.21.6] says:
There is a suspension of study for one day and night upon the arrival of the ruler of the land, a *śrotriya*, or a person belonging to the same sacred ford (*tīrtha*).

The term “ruler of the land” refers to a military commander and the like, since Yājñavalkya specifies a three-night suspension of study when it concerns the king. A “*śrotriya*” is one devoted to the recitation of a Vedic branch other than one’s own. Therefore, the mention of a three-night suspension in another *smṛti* regarding a *śrotriya* pertains to one who studies his own Vedic branch, according to Yājñavalkya’s statement: “Likewise, when [the ruler or a *śrotriya*] belongs to one’s own Vedic branch.
Furthermore, Baudhāyana [states]: (1.21.17–18).
And for as long as one hears or sees a Śūdra or an outcast (apapātra), one should not study. At night, when a jackal howls, one should not study until the end of sleep.
An "outcast" refers to those who have fallen from their caste, Cāṇḍālas, and so forth.
Again, Baudhāyana [1.11.22]:
On other occasions of miraculous portents, there is a suspension of study for a day and night, except for mental recitation.
Gautama [16.47] states: "Even mental recitation is [forbidden] when one is impure."
Paiṭhīnasi:

Having eaten on the eleventh day after a birth or death, or having seen a rainbow at night, or following a lightning strike, the death of a teacher, a fall of Indra’s bolt, an eclipse of the sun or moon, the appearance of a comet, a thunderclap, or an earthquake—one must observe a three-night period of impurity for each of these occurrences.
Āpastamba [1.9.4–12]:

One should avoid studying in market-towns. Or one may study in a place smeared with a ball of cow-dung from an ox. One should not study within the range of a *śamyā*-throw in every direction around a cremation ground; however, there is no prohibition of study in a village or a field that has been settled by a community. But while that [cremation ground] is still being recognized, one should not study in that very location. A *śūdra* and an outcast (*patita*) are like a cremation ground; according to some, this applies when they are in the same house. In the case of a *śūdra* woman, however, there is a suspension of study only during mutual looking at one another. Likewise, there is a suspension upon sexual intercourse with any other woman who belongs to a different caste.

“Nigamas” are crossroads. “Śamyā” is a particular sacrificial implement. “Prāsa” means throwing. “Sarvataḥ” means in all directions. “When settled by a village or by a field” means when it has attained the status of a village or a field. “When it is known” means when its nature as a cremation ground is recognized. “Looking at one another” means mutual gazing. The meaning of the passage beginning with “likewise in another” is as follows: when a woman of a lower caste has engaged in sexual intercourse, there is a suspension of Vedic study upon their mutual gazing. Again, Āpastamba [1.9.14–16]:
[There is no study] when a corpse is inside [the village], or when a *caṇḍāla* is inside. However, there is no study on the boundary (*sīman*) once [the corpse] has been carried out.
Even if these same *caṇḍāla*s and others, having come [into the village], depart outside the village boundary, there is no study for that day.
Again, Āpastamba [says]: [1.9.22]

[At dawn] or at such a time when one can distinguish a black or red cow from the distance of a *śamyā*-throw, if lightning flashes, that day along with the following night is a period of non-study (*anadhyāya*). At such a time as it takes for a black or red cow to be recognized from the distance of a *śamyā*-throw in an open space, if lightning is perceived, the day together with the first watch of the night is a period of non-study.
— Hārīta.

Standing at the gates of villages or cities, on the roads or crossroads, during the three periods of twilight, or while being impure and unclean, one should not study. During a dense mass of clouds, continuous thunder, lightning, or the sound of a crash; during cold weather; during hailstorms or rain; and during times of great alarm, battle, the death of a city-dweller, a cow, or a Brahmin, the presence of a corpse, or when *cāṇḍālas*, *pulkasas*, or *mauṣṭikas* are present—there is no study at those times.

In the phrase “villages, cities, gates, streets, crossroads, and the three junctions of the day,” there is a collective singular compound (*dvandvaikavadbhāva*). Here, the phrase “one should avoid studying” (*adhītiṃ varjayet*) is understood to carry over from the previous context. A “multitude” (*samūha*) is a gathering of people of various castes. The word “continuous” (*saṃtata*) refers to uninterruptedness. The word “continuous” is connected individually with each term beginning with “thundering” (*stanita*) and ending with “rain. “Resounding” (*abhiśrava*) is the long, drawn-out sound of jackals and other animals gathered together. Cold weather and so forth, when continuous, are causes for not studying outside the prescribed seasons. “Great commotion” (*mahāsaṃbhrama*) is the agitation of people caused by village fires and the like. Wherever there are corpses within and so forth; a *puṣkasa* is a particular kind of barbarian (*mleccha*); a *mauṣṭika* is a wrestler. “At that time” (*tatkālam*) means for that duration of time.

Furthermore, Hārīta states: In the event of rainless winds, earthquakes, meteor showers, whirlwinds, conflagrations, or rains of dust, blood, flesh, bones, hair, curds, water, or charcoal; upon the occurrence of rites for peace (*śānti*) or prosperity (*svastyayana*); during the rising or setting of the sun; when there is vomiting or spilling [of offerings]; upon seeing a naked person or having a bad dream; and during periods of impurity (*sūtaka*) following a *ekoddiṣṭa* rite—one must first perform the initial expiation (*prāyaścitta*). During these circumstances, there is a suspension of study (*anadhyāya*) lasting until the completion of the rites for peace, prosperity, and so forth.

Regarding the term *abhyudita*: that question (or meal) at which the sun rises is called *abhyudita*; and that question (or meal) at which it sets is called *abhinirmukta*. *Vānta* means one who has vomited after eating. *Skanna* means one whose semen has been discharged. *Ādya* means having eaten facing [the food] with primary importance. Here, although the suffix *lyap* would normally follow the root *ad* preceded by the prefix *ā*, the substitute *jagdhi* does not occur due to the rule “*bahulaṃ chandasi*” (there is great diversity in Vedic usage). And this constitutes a suspension of study (*anadhyāya*) when these occasions—such as the *abhyudita*—occur and no expiation (*prāyaścitta*) is performed. Again, Hārīta says:

The first days of the months of Caitra, Śrāvaṇa, and Mārgaśīrṣa are constant [as days of non-study]. By "first days" is meant the first days of the bright fortnights (*śuklapakṣa*). By the word "constant," it is indicated that on other first days, the suspension of study (*anadhyāya*) is optional (*kāmya*).
Hārīta states this in connection with the recurring injunction "one should study."
There is no study during the great festivals of the *bali* and *śrāddha*, as if it were a falling meteor.

[255] “*Bali*” refers to an offering to the deities. Since no specific limit is mentioned regarding this period of non-study (*anadhyāya*), the remainder of the day—that is, the rest of the day—is a time for not studying.
Furthermore, Āpastamba [1.9.23–26]:

During the early part of the night and during the latter part of the night, as well as after midnight—according to some authorities; also when cows are being penned in; and for those who are to be executed, until they are actually killed.

"In the latter part of the night" means in the third division of the night; "in the early part" (dahre) also refers here to the time of dusk; this is to be connected with the rule that "the day is a period of non-study. "By thunder" means by the occurrence of a cloud accompanied by sound. "In the penning in" refers to the forceful confinement [of cattle]. For those "to be executed," the period of non-study lasts until the execution of the condemned. Again, Āpastamba [1.10.2–4]:

The three-day periods of suspension are: on the day of completing the study (*vairamaṇa*), when the teachers have passed away, and on the occasion of the *āṣṭakā* sacrifice (*aupākaraṇa*). Likewise, among one's relatives and kinsmen. There are twelve-day periods of suspension for the death of a mother, a father, or a teacher (*ācārya*). Regarding "on the day of completing the study" (*vairamaṇe*): it refers to the day the study is finished. Regarding "when the teachers have passed away" (*guruṣu saṃsthiteṣu*): this refers to their death. Regarding "on the occasion of the *āṣṭakā*" (*āṣṭakye*): this is the *āṣṭakā* festival; and this constitutes a twelve-day period of non-study. Regarding "mother" (*mātari*): one's own mother. Regarding "father" (*pitari*): one's own progenitor. Regarding "teacher" (*ācārye*): one who, having performed the initiation (*upanayana*), has taught the Veda along with its auxiliary sciences (*sāṅga*) and secret portions (*sarahasya*). However, the rule concerning the teacher’s death resulting in a single day of non-study applies specifically to the context of secondary teachers (*gauṇācārya*). Furthermore, Āpastamba states [1.10.20–23]:

And there is a suspension of study for the *Sāmans* in another *Śākhā*. And in all cases involving vocal actions, where they might become mixed; likewise after vomiting, until one has fallen asleep, or after consuming clarified butter.
The phrase "in another *Śākhā*" implies that it is to be recited [there]. Regarding the words "and in all," the meaning is when sounds such as rhythmic clapping (*tāla*) and singing are combined.
[256] Again, Āpastamba [1.10.27]:

And when both hands are wet. Again, Āpastamba [1.11.1–7]: At the commencement of a *kāṇḍa*, for one whose mother is alive; at the completion of a *kāṇḍa*, for one whose father is alive. Some say that after eating at a sacrifice to deities who have humans as their prototypes, there is no study. There is no study with stale rice, nor with raw meat. Likewise with herbs, trees, roots, and fruits. On the day they commence a *kāṇḍa*, one should recite its invitatory verse (*anuvākya*), but one should not study that particular section on that day. And at the commencement and completion of the *pārāyaṇa* of a specific branch of knowledge (*vidyā*).

"At the commencement of a *kāṇḍa*" means at the beginning of a section. Regarding "those whose nature is human": this refers to those who, being humans by birth, have attained divinity through their actions, such as Nandīśvara and others; the meaning is that there is no study after eating at a sacrifice performed for them. Regarding "with stale rice": the mention of rice is illustrative. Therefore, the meaning is that there is no study when rice and other grains, or meat, have been eaten at sacrifices for deities who were once human on another day. Regarding "the commencement" (*upākaraṇa*) and so forth: "reciting the whole" (*pārāyaṇa*) is the recitation of the science of sacrifice from the beginning until its conclusion, accompanied by specific observances for the sake of a transcendental result (*adṛṣṭa*). One should not study that very [science] at its commencement or at its completion.
Furthermore, Āpastamba [1.11.10–12] states:
"And during voluntary acts, such as washing the feet, massaging, and anointing; for that duration of time, one should neither study nor teach.
"Voluntary acts" (*svairikarma*) refers to actions performed according to one's own will. "Massaging" (*utsādana*) refers to rubbing with unguents.

[257] Again, Āpastamba [1.11.28–34]: During a moment when the wind has ceased; during the howling of a female jackal or the cry of a *ekasṛk* bird, until one falls asleep; at night in the forest, or when there is no fire or gold present; one should not study the Veda if it has not been previously learned, nor out of season, nor at the onset of evening. This is the rule for all times. Other matters have been stated as before regarding assemblies.

"Ananūktam" means that which has not been studied previously. "Apartau" means when the time for Vedic study has passed, that is, prior to the *upākaraṇa* ceremony. "Salāvṛkī" is a female jackal (*gṛdhra-vāsinī*). "Ekasṛkaḥ" is a solitary wandering jackal, according to Kapardin. Upon hearing these two sounds, there is a suspension of study until one falls asleep. Furthermore, Āpastamba [1.32.12–14] states: There is no study at night, except for the instruction of pupils in the Dharma; or one may study it mentally by oneself. Teaching may take place after midnight.
“Anadhyāyaḥ” means non-study. “In the night” means during the dead of night. Regarding the phrase “or mentally,” mental study should be performed from midnight onwards.
Following the recurrence of the term “anadhyāya,” Vasiṣṭha [13.35] states:
“In the case of rainbows, mountains, idols, waterfalls, or showers of stones, blood, and dust, the suspension lasts until the same time the next day.”
"Arcā" means an image.
Regarding the term "one should study," Śaṅkha and Likhita state in their continuation [of the rule]:
"Not at city crossroads, highways, or bridges."
Likewise:
there is no [inauspiciousness] for kings or great men when they are born under their own [natal] asterism.
A "great man" (*mahāpuruṣa*) is a person of excellent conduct.
Likewise:
"Not when the spiritual friend has passed away.
Likewise.
There were no sacrificial grounds for the final ablution (avabhṛtha). They were not heard of.

Land set aside for the purpose of sacrifice is called a "sacrificial ground" (yajñavāṭi). "They were not heard of" means that there was no great crowding among one another; otherwise, there would have been disorder.
And so it was.
Not in the case of *kaumudī*. The term *sarvarātrā* refers to the *kaumudī*, which is the full moon day of the month of Āśvayuja.
Likewise.
Not from seeing a rainbow.
Likewise:
[30.19–21] Not one who has vomited; not one who is dispassionate; not one who has indigestion.
Aṅgiras says:
"The Ṛgveda and Yajurveda should not be recited when the sound of the Sāmaveda is present. How then [should they be recited] at a sacrifice?
Because they are auxiliary parts of it."

Manu [4.99]: One should not recite the Veda without having touched water, nor should one recite it in the presence of a Śūdra. Nor, being exhausted at the end of the night, should one go back to sleep after having recited the Veda.
In the *Devīpurāṇa*, following the word "study" (*adhyayana*), it is said:
"One should not study where people are intermingled, nor in the presence of thieves,
nor where there are beards, red objects, or places crowded with weapons and the like."
"In a place crowded with people" means in a region where many people are gathered. "A barber" (*śmaśrukara*) refers to a hair-cutter. "An owl" (*karavādi*) refers to the *ulūka* bird.

One should not [recite] while eating at a *śrāddha*, nor when fatigued, nor when suffering from indigestion, nor when sexually aroused; nor during the festival of Indra, nor in an ill-fated place, nor at the time of a solar transit (*saṃkrānti*), nor in a marketplace.
In the Narasiṃha Purāṇa: "On the Mahānavamī, on the twelfth lunar day, on the Bharaṇī asterism,
and likewise on the Akṣaya Tṛtīyā, a wise man should not cause his disciples to study."
One should avoid [sexual intercourse] on the seventh day of the month of Māgha, as well as on the day known as Rathasaptamī;
likewise, one should avoid it at the marketplace, when anointed with oil, and at the time of bathing.
O best of the twice-born, having seen a corpse being carried along the ground,

or [on the occasion of] the "Dvādaśī"— that is, the Dvādaśī of the commencement or conclusion of the [rainy season] sleep— or on the "Bharaṇī," that is, the Bharaṇī of Indra’s fall, or on the day called "Ratha," that is, the seventh lunar day— one should not study; thus continues the rule of Śaṅkha.
Near a temple, an anthill, a cremation ground, or a corpse;
and when jackals, camels, elephants, and horses are crying out.
The wise declare that the days unfit for study are the vulnerabilities of the twice-born;
through these vulnerabilities, the sacred knowledge (brahman) acquired by a Brahmin flows away.
Whatever man-eaters there are, they remain specifically in the vulnerabilities;
staying there, O Brahman, they destroy whatever has been acquired by the Brahmins.
Likewise:
"Longevity, progeny, cattle, intelligence, and well-performed deeds—
these are lost by one who recites the Veda during forbidden times or speaks it aloud."
The eighth day destroys the teacher, the fourteenth destroys the pupil, and the fifteenth destroys intelligence; therefore, one should avoid these sacred festival days (parvan).
For Prajāpati resides within all branches of knowledge and their intervals;
therefore, one should not indeed proclaim these [mantras] on the sacred festival days (parvan) when seeking dharma, artha, and kāma.

Regarding the continuation of the *brahmayajña*—which is designated as the "daily recitation"—Āpastamba states [1.11.17–20]: "The rule for that is as follows: having gone to the edge of water before eating the morning meal, being self-restrained and pure, one should study it according to the lesson in a clean place, either by voice or mentally, except during times when study is forbidden. Manu [2.104–107] states:
Restrained and established in the daily rite near water,
