he should go to the forest with a concentrated mind and recite even the Sāvitrī.
There is no restriction regarding days unsuitable for study (anadhyāya) with respect to the auxiliary sciences of the Veda, the daily private recitation (svādhyāya),
and indeed the mantras used for burnt offerings (homa).

“Vedic auxiliaries” refers to grammar and so forth. The mention of *mantras* for the *homa* is intended to illustrate those *mantras* in the form of *stotras*, *śastras*, and the like, which are employed at the time of performing ritual acts (*karman*), because of the statement of Āpastamba: “A suspension of study (*anadhyāya*) is prescribed with respect to sacred knowledge (*vidyā*), but not regarding the application of *mantras* in ritual acts.
“In daily rites there is no suspension of study, for that is remembered as the ‘Brahma-sacrifice’ (*brahmasatra*).
It is meritorious, offered with the oblation of the Veda (*brahmāhuti*), and consecrated by the *vaṣaṭ*-call even during times when study is suspended.”
For that twice-born man who, being self-restrained, studies his own Veda according to the rule for a year,
this [sacrifice] constantly yields milk, curd, clarified butter, and honey.
Thus ends the section on the suspension of Vedic study [262].
Now, regarding what is to be studied, Bṛhaspati [at Saṃskāra 226] states:
"The Brahmins have traditionally held that the Veda and the Smṛti are equally the root of Dharma."
And likewise, these three should always be understood as pertaining to right conduct.
Śaṅkha and Likhita state: "One should not render a scripture fruitless. Without having studied the Veda, one should not study another science, except for the Vedāṅgas and the Smṛtis.
Whatever scriptures are outside the Veda, and whatever false views there may be—
all these are declared to be fruitless, for they are remembered as being grounded in darkness.
Whatever other things besides these arise and pass away,
they are fruitless and false because they belong to a limited, temporal duration.

“Vedic scriptures outside [the Veda]” refers to practices such as the veneration of *caityas* and the like; “false views” refers to erroneous doctrines, namely the treatises of the Buddhists and others.
Likewise [2.168]:
“The twice-born who, without having studied the Veda, exerts himself in another field...”
While still alive, he quickly falls to the status of a Śūdra, along with his lineage.
“With his lineage” means on all sides.
Now, regarding the limit of the period for the life of celibacy,
Devala says:
From this point forward, one should undertake the Vedic student’s life (*vedacaryā*) for forty-eight years. If one is unable, then for one year, twenty-four years, or twelve years.

Baudhāyana [1.2.1–6]: The ancient Vedic student’s life lasts forty-eight years; or twenty-four or twelve years per Veda; or half a year per section (*kāṇḍa*); or until the mastery of the text, because life is uncertain. This is in accordance with the Śruti: “One whose hair is still black should establish the sacred fires.”

“Ancient” (*paurāṇam*) means that which was practiced by the ancients, such as Manu and others. “Or half a year for each section” (*kāṇḍa*) means half a year for every individual section. Regarding the phrase “until its acquisition,” the reason given for the rule that studenthood (*brahmacarya*) lasts “until its acquisition” is “because life is unstable. Yājñavalkya [1.36] states: “Studenthood for each Veda shall last twelve years or five.”
Some say it lasts until the initiation; and the tonsure ceremony is performed in the sixteenth year.
Manu [2.65]: "The tonsure ceremony (keśānta) is prescribed for a Brāhmaṇa in the sixteenth year;
for a member of the royal class (rājanyabandhu) in the twenty-second; and for a Vaiśya two years after that."
In the *Brahma Purāṇa*: "Prolonged celibacy, the carrying of a water-pot (*kamaṇḍalu*),
marriage with a woman from one's own lineage or from the maternal sapinda-lineage, and likewise the killing of a cow [are forbidden]."
In the Kali age, human sacrifice, horse sacrifice, and liquor must be avoided by the twice-born.
Now, in the absence of a teacher, there is an alternative procedure.
Āpastamba [1.7.12–13] states:

"The teachers of that knowledge which one acquires from a guru are also his teachers who belong to that guru's lineage; furthermore, those others whom he sees and would otherwise greet by clasping their feet—these are the ones to be greeted at that time."

"The knowledge"—in the form of the *Ṛgveda* and so forth—"which he acquires from the teacher," meaning that the student (*brahmacārī*) should attend upon the preceptor (*ācārya*) and obtain it from his presence; "of this" knowledge, those who are the teachers of the preceptor and their descendants are also the teachers "of him," the student. Regarding the word "whom": while "he," the student, "is looking on," those others whom the teacher should "greet by clasping the feet," "at that time"—that is, at such a moment—"these" are to be greeted. — Paiṭhīnasi.

If the preceptor dies before the completion of the period of studentship (*brahmacarya*), the son should observe the entire conduct due to a teacher. In the absence of a son, he should live with a brother.
Thus, in the *Kṛtyakalpataru* composed by Śrī Lakṣmīdhara, son of the Minister of Peace and War, Bhaṭṭa Śrī Hṛdayadhara.
In the section on the student life within the treatise known as the Ācāra, [the topic of] the Upakurvāṇaka [is concluded].
Now, regarding the establishment of the four stages of life (*cāturāśramya*), Vasiṣṭha states [at 7.1–17]:

There are four stages of life (*āśrama*): the student (*brahmacārin*), the householder (*gṛhastha*), the forest-dweller (*vānaprastha*), and the wandering mendicant (*parivrājaka*). Having thoroughly studied one Veda, two Vedas, or all the Vedas, and having remained steadfast in his vow of celibacy (*brahmacarya*), he may enter whichever [stage] he desires. The student shall serve his teacher until the liberation of the body [from death]. When the teacher has passed away, he shall serve the sacred fire; for it is known that "the teacher is indeed the fire. He must restrain his speech. He shall eat at the fourth, sixth, or eighth meal-time of the day, subsisting on alms. He is dependent upon his teacher. He shall wear matted hair, or have a single lock of matted hair on the crown of his head. He shall follow the teacher when he walks; if the teacher is seated, he shall stand; if the teacher is lying down, he shall sit near him. He shall study only when summoned. Having announced everything he has obtained, he shall eat with the teacher’s permission. With the exception of sleeping on a bed, cleaning the teeth, applying collyrium, and anointing the body, he shall habitually remain standing during the day and sitting at night, and he shall approach water three times a day.

“Of unbroken celibacy” means one whose celibacy is not violated. “Restrained in speech” means silent. “Eating at the fourth, sixth, and eighth meal-times”: this refers to the number of times of eating, such as the fourth and so on, in relation to the total amount of food normally consumed. “Three times a day he should approach water” means that he should perform the three daily ablutions (*triṣavaṇa-snāna*). [266] Baudhāyana.

Practicing celibacy, they exhaust themselves by completely devoting themselves to the teacher’s household; some attend the ritual pressings, touching water at each and offering oblations into the single fire with various materials; others, having renounced all ritual acts, remain without fires or fixed dwellings, wearing only a loincloth and a garment, staying in one place during the rains, performing their needs with water collected on the ground, and dressed in ochre robes. They should beg for alms when the pestle has been laid aside, the embers extinguished, and the removal of the dishes has ceased. They should be free from malice toward living beings through the restraints of speech, mind, and action. They should carry a purifier for the sake of purification and perform their duties with drawn-up water. Having cast aside Vedic rituals, they say, "Severed from both sides, we shall cling to the middle state."

The connection [of the words] is as follows: "celibates" (*brahmacāriṇaḥ*), meaning lifelong students (*naiṣṭhikāḥ*), "having restrained" (*upasaṃgṛhya*)—that is, having fully controlled—"themselves" (*ātmānam*), meaning the body, "exert themselves" (*śrāmyanti*) in the teacher's household. "Exert themselves" means they perform austerities (*tapas*). "Some" (*eke*) refers to forest-dwellers (*vānaprasthāḥ*). "At the libations" (*savaneṣu*), meaning at dawn and so forth. "Sprinkling themselves" (*upaspṛśantaḥ*) means bathing. "With forest-grown food" (*vanyena*) such as wild rice (*nīvāra*) and the like. "Some" (*eke*) refers to renunciants (*saṃnyāsinaḥ*) established in yoga. "Rites" (*karmāṇi*) are those accomplished by means of the sacred fires. "Having renounced" (*saṃnyasya*) means having become wandering mendicants (*parivrāj*). "A loincloth" (*kaupīnam*) refers to the genitals; those whose clothing consists of only that much are "those clothed in a loincloth" (*kaupīnācchādanāḥ*). "Dwelling in one place" (*ekasthāḥ*) means living in a single location. "With filtered water" (*pariśrutābhiḥ*) means with water strained through a water-purifier (*pavitra*). "Vedic rites" (*karmāṇi*) include recitation, study of the Vedas (*svādhyāya*), and so forth. "Having cast aside" (*apavidhya*) and being "cut off on both sides" (*ubhayataḥ pricchinnāḥ*) means having turned away from the pairs of opposites (*dvandva*) such as pleasure and pain, honor and dishonor. "The middle station" (*madhyamaṃ padam*) refers to that which resembles neither pleasure nor pain—the divine station situated between *prakṛti* and *puruṣa*, known as Brahman—saying this, they exert themselves; such is the connection.
Laghuvyāsa states: Whether one is a lifelong student, a forest hermit, or even a wandering mendicant,
in whichever stage of life one chooses to dwell, there one should remain self-controlled.
Śaṅkha and Likhita state:

Some desire that the life of a wandering mendicant (pārivrājya) belongs only to those who have sublimated their sexual energy (ūrdhvaretas), and not to householders or forest-dwellers. Because the former stage is not cut off, because both sets of duties are applicable, and because the latter stage does not require dependence on the former, there is only one stage of life (aikāśramya).

The reason for the statement "only those whose vital energy is drawn upward" is given by the words "of the former," and so forth. Because that state of being one whose vital energy is drawn upward—preceded by [the stage of] the teacher—is not interrupted even in the life of a wandering mendicant (*pārivrājya*), there is "the occurrence of the duties of both"; that is, because the duties such as restraints (*yama*) and observances (*niyama*) which belong to both—the first and the fourth stages of life—are possible and attainable. Furthermore, because the "latter," namely the householder's stage, is no longer required once one's passions have matured and subsided, there is "unity of the single stage of life" (*aikāśramya*), meaning the same form for the first and the final stages of life.
Again, Śaṅkha and Likhita [state]:

The period of celibacy (*brahmacarya*) is either twenty-four or forty-eight years; that must be dedicated to the teacher. It is lifelong (*naiṣṭhika*) and centered on the knowledge of the Self. Because there is no further undertaking [of worldly life], there is a single realization regarding both the former and the latter stages. "One who is exhausted by the teacher’s service attains purity as a controller," so it is said: "Those whose selves are purified by austerity, who are devoted to truth and dharma, and who are perfected through Brahman itself—such Brāhmaṇas belong to the world of Brahman."
Those who practice with their vital energy drawn upward, being pure and consisting of the austerity of dharma, do not fall from that state; their worlds are composed of light.

“Twenty-fourfold” means measured at twenty-four. Likewise, “forty-eightfold. “To the guru” means for the sake of propitiating the guru. “To be practiced” means to be performed. “Established in self-knowledge” means grounded in the knowledge of the Self. “Of the first and last” means of the first and fourth [periods]. “Single knowledge” means knowing [them] as one. “Because of the absence of undertaking” means because of the absence of being intent upon sacrifices undertaken by priests (ṛtvij). [268] “Yantrī” means one who possesses restraints (yantra); the restraints (yantra) are the disciplines (yama), such as eating only at the fourth meal-time and so forth. —Hārīta.

Those who practice their conduct in all the stages of life (*āśrama*) attain the worlds of merit. This is the ladder of the stages of life by which the gods and their ancestors attained immortality. One who is first meritorious, a student (*brahmacārin*), and steadfast in studentship, attains the perfection of Brahman. One who is doubly meritorious, steadfast in the householder stage (*gṛhāśrama*), attains the even greater majesty of the world of Brahman (*brahmaloka*). Or, one who follows the sequence of the stages, a forest-dweller (*vānaprastha*), attains the established majesty of both stages in the world of Brahman. A mendicant (*bhikṣu*) who proceeds from stage to stage quickly finds perfection. Among students, the lifelong student (*naiṣṭhika*) is the most excellent; among householders, the wandering ascetic (*yāyāvara*); among forest-dwellers, the forest-dweller who follows the sequence (*ānuprasthika*); and among ascetics, the one perfected through the four stages of life (*cāturāśramyasiddha*).
“Possessing two merits” (*dvipuṇyaḥ*) means one for whom there are two meritorious duties belonging to the two stages of life (*āśrama*). “Perfection” (*siddhiḥ*) is the attainment of Brahman.
Manu [6.89–91]: “The student (*brahmacārī*), the householder (*gṛhastha*), the forest-dweller (*vānaprastha*), and likewise the ascetic (*yati*).”
These four distinct stages of life originate from the householder.
All these sacrifices, when practiced according to the sacrificial treatises,
lead a Brahmin who acts as prescribed to the supreme goal.
And among all these [orders], according to the injunctions of the Vedas and Smṛtis,
the householder is said to be the best, for he supports these other three.
(Viṣṇupurāṇa 3.10.13–15)
O King, having mastered the Veda and having given the teacher’s fee to the guru,
one who desires the life of a householder should take a wife.
[269] Or he may pass away while practicing celibacy according to his resolve;
or he should perform service to his teacher, or likewise to the teacher’s son or others.

"Or he may become a *vaikhānasa* (forest-dweller), or a wandering mendicant (*parivrāj*) according to his wish. Thus [it is stated] in Hārīta’s work following the passage beginning with "Prajāpati. He, having divided himself fourfold, exerted himself through celibacy, Vedic sacrifices, austerity, and meditation; those became the stages of life (*āśramas*).
Harita says:
"The man who belongs to no stage of life, he who has abandoned his stage, the one who observes a stage in vain,
and he who falsely assumes a stage— all such men go to hell."

"One who has fallen away from the stages of life" (*anāśramī vyapetaḥ*) refers to one who, being without a stage of life, has strayed from it. "One who is useless" (*nirarthakaḥ*) is one devoid of the performance of duties prescribed for his own stage, wearing only the external marks. "One who falsely observes a stage of life" (*mithyāśramī*) is one who practices the duties of a stage of life for the sake of hypocrisy.
Likewise, celibacy (*brahmacarya*) is said for all [stages] to consist in the retention of semen.
For householders, [approaching] the wife during the fertile period is constant, or alternatively, avoiding the sacred festival days.
The meaning is that for householders, approaching [one's wife] only during the fertile period (*ṛtukāla*) is called celibacy (*brahmacarya*). Likewise:
"The wise call the path of sacrifice the conjunction of mantra, substance, and fire."
But for mendicants, the sacrifice to the self is established in the self alone.
Vows, fasting, and the use of yantras are always recommended for those two;
however, the wise declare that for monks, [the practice] purified by the Three Truths is what is prescribed.

"Self-sacrifice" (*ātmayajña*) is the knowledge of the Self itself, which is called a sacrifice because it performs the function of a sacrifice characterized by spiritual prosperity (*abhyudaya*). "Vow" (*vrata*) refers to the kindling of the sacred fire and so forth according to the scriptures. "Restraint" (*yama*) is as follows: for students (*brahmacārins*), it is the discipline of kindling the fire and so forth; for householders, it is the five great sacrifices (*pañcamahāyajña*) and so forth; for forest-dwellers, it is the practice of subsisting on forest produce and so forth; and for mendicants, it is the abandonment of egoism and possessions, breath control (*prāṇāyāma*), and penances such as the *kṛcchra*, or the renunciation of harming others through speech, mind, and action via the three truths, even when acting for the sake of deities and the like. For one intent on acquisition, it consists of begging and so forth performed without violence (*ahiṃsā*).

“By non-violence” means by not causing pain. Therefore, after first honoring the deities and rising above the three types of labor performed since beginningless time, it is proper for a mendicant to avoid the fourfold violence.
Likewise: “One should place one’s foot down purified by sight; one should drink water purified by a cloth.”
One should speak words purified by truth; one should act with a mind that is pure.
"Indeed, he who serves the stages of life according to this rule,
having conquered all worlds, is fit for the world of Brahmā. Thus says Dakṣa.
He who, having entered the householder stage of life, becomes a celibate student again—
neither an ascetic nor a householder— is one who has abandoned all stages of life.
A twice-born man should not remain even for a single day without belonging to an āśrama;
remaining without an āśrama, a twice-born man becomes liable to penance.
One who is always devoted to recitation, fire-offerings, charity, and self-study,
yet has fallen from his stage of life (āśrama), does not obtain the fruit even while performing these acts.
There may be a movement in accordance with the three [higher castes], but a movement in reverse order does not exist;
for one who moves in reverse order goes downward, and there is no sinner more wicked than he.

“*Ānulomyam*” (the natural order) refers to this sequence: the student (*brahmacārī*), the householder (*gṛhastha*), the forest-dweller (*vānaprastha*), and the ascetic (*yati*). “*Prātilomyam*” (the inverse order) is the reverse of what has been stated.
Now, regarding the lifelong practice (naiṣṭhika-kriyā), Hārīta says:

The student of sacred knowledge (*brahmacārī*) is of two kinds: the temporary student (*upakurvāṇaka*) and the lifelong student (*naiṣṭhika*). Of these two, the temporary student has been explained. If he should reach the final goal, he should attend upon his teacher until the fall of his body; in the absence of the teacher, upon the teacher’s wife; in her absence, upon the teacher’s son. In the absence of the teacher’s son, he should tend the sacred fire alone. Having brought sacrificial fuel-sticks, he should tend the fire with acts such as sweeping, smearing, kindling, gathering, igniting, encircling with fire, circumambulation, standing in attendance, offering oblations, chanting hymns, and prostrating. He must not step over the fire, nor drag it with his feet, nor blow upon it with his mouth. He must not hold water and fire simultaneously. He must not add fuel while still digesting food or while impure from eating. He must not add fuel while stepping across it, nor spit upon it. Day by day, he should kindle the fire with various offerings of cooked rice and oblations dedicated to Agni. When departing, he should take leave; having returned, he should report his arrival. With his mind fixed on that [teacher], at the end of the dissolution of the body, the *brāhmaṇa* attains union (*sāyujya*). Or, having renounced, he may practice the thirteen-fold vow of celibacy. Some say the vow of celibacy consists of eight limbs. Those devoted to Viṣṇu attain the supreme, immovable state; others become [liberated].
For he who practices the life of celibacy according to this rule,
having completely conquered all worlds, is fit for the world of Brahmā.
They drink milk, they drink honey,
and indeed they drink Soma together with Aṣṭa;
before death, they become immortal.
Those Brahmins who practice the holy life.

One who dwells near the guru, performing the essential purpose of *svādhyāya* (Vedic study) until the comprehension of its meaning, is called an *upakurvāṇaka*. “Kindling” (*udbodhana*) is the manifestation of the fire. “Sweeping” (*samūhana*) is the gathering together of scattered fire. “Igniting” (*samindhana*) is setting it ablaze. “Circumambulation” (*parikramaṇa*) is moving clockwise around it. “Attendance” (*upasthāna*) is remaining in its vicinity with speech and mind directed toward it. The word “etcetera” (*ādi*) implies the employment of such expressions as “Victory! Victory! and so forth. “One who has not digested his meal” (*ajīrṇabhukta*) refers to one for whom what was eaten yesterday has not yet been digested. “He should add fuel” (*abhyādadhyāt*) means he should perform the placing of sacrificial wood (*samid*) preceded by the recitation of mantras. “*Caru*” is food cooked over steam that has not been formally consecrated with the *āśrāvita* call. “Offerings” (*havīṃṣi*) include clarified butter, parched grain flour, curd-mixture (*āmikṣā*), and so on, provided they are free from pungent salt; these should be cast into the fire according to the prescribed injunctions. By this same method, the act of igniting the fire is also accomplished. “He should depart after taking leave” means he should go only after asking permission from the teacher. “With mind fixed on him” (*tanmanāḥ*) means having the heart centered on the guru. “Thirteen qualities [to avoid]”: these thirteen qualities consist of—dwelling with women, entering where women are, physical contact, touching their limbs, looking at them, meeting them, gazing at them, looking askance at them, conversing with them, questioning them, listening to their words, watching them from afar, wandering near them, and hearing pleasant words concerning them. These are the thirteen qualities.
Devala said:

The duty of the religious student (*brahmacārin*) consists of celibacy (*brahmacarya*), the study of the Vedas, the performance of obligatory rites, and the wearing of the sacred thread (*brahmasūtra*), a rosary (*akṣamālā*), a staff (*daṇḍa*), a loincloth (*kaupīna*), a water-pot (*kuṇḍikā*), and a girdle of muñja grass (*mekhalā*). He should eat only once a day, bathe frequently, perform the fire-sacrifice (*agnihotra*) at both twilights, and attend upon the *saṃdhyā* prayers. He must not have his hair, nails, or skin cut, nor should he use perfumes, garlands, oils, ointments, cosmetics, ornaments, umbrellas, shoes, or vehicles; nor should he engage in jumping, swimming, running, medical treatment, astrology, palmistry, architecture, or the arts of auspicious, nourishing, or pacifying rites (*māṅgalya-pauṣṭika-śānti-karma*); nor should he practice music, join guilds, enter into contracts, or engage in crafts, writing, manual labor, house-building, field-work, the management of goods, grain, or wealth; nor should he indulge in weapons, gambling, legal disputes, commands, idle pastimes, joking, intimacy, deception, wonder-working, mockery, quarrels, arrogance, lamentation, weeping, or the application of oil to the bladder, nose, or feet, or the rubbing of them with powders. He must rise before his teacher and go to sleep after him, carry out whatever tasks are assigned to him according to the rules, serve him with devotion, and worship him constantly. He should honor him. In the absence of the teacher, this same conduct of obedience should be maintained toward his son or his wife until death.

“Kuṇḍikā” means a water-pot (*kamaṇḍalu*). “Luptaṃ” means cut or severed. “Veṣaḥ” means adornment. “Plavanaṃ” means leaping up. “Lakṣaṇavāstuvidyā” refers to that science [of marks] belonging to Śūdras. “Saṅghaḥ” means a multitude. “Samayaḥ” means a convention; “bandhanaṃ” is the binding rule thereof. “Kāravaḥ” refers to cooks and the like. “Bhāvaḥ” is a mental modification that is the source of sentiments such as the erotic (*śṛṅgāra*). “Utsekaḥ” means pride. “Vastiḥ” refers to enemas and the like. By “nasta,” nasal medication (*nasya*) is indicated. “Pramāṇasaṃdiṣṭakaraṇaṃ” means performing what has been instructed according to the authoritative measure, not service for one’s own desired ends through delusion and so forth. “Apacitiḥ” means worship.

Śaṅkha and Likhita state: "Or, in this very [state], there is the study of the Veda at will. One who looks toward a purpose—being devoted to the *gāyatrī*, the *rudrakalpa*, and the *upaniṣads*; performing ablutions at the [three] *savanas*; and practicing what has been prescribed as the remaining mode of livelihood; delighting in the Self, being established in the teacher’s household, or established in the Self—he attains immortality. The phrase "one who looks toward a purpose" refers to the teacher. The "rudrakalpa" is the ritual procedure for the *śatarudriya*. "One who performs ablutions at the *savanas*" means one who bathes three times a day.
[274] Manu [3.242–244]: A disciple seeking the highest goal should not dwell for life with a non-Brāhmaṇa teacher, nor even with a Brāhmaṇa who has not studied the Vedas.
But if he should desire to dwell permanently in the family of his teacher,
he should attend upon him with devotion until the liberation of the body.
That Brahmin who serves his teacher until the completion of his body goes straight to the eternal abode of Brahmā.

Likewise [3.247–249]: "But when the teacher has indeed passed away, one should behave toward the teacher’s son who is endowed with good qualities, or toward the teacher’s wife, or toward a sapinda relative, just as toward the teacher."
But when these are not available, one who is capable of standing, sitting,
and moving about should perfect his own body by performing service to the sacred fires.
The Brahmin who thus practices the unimpaired vow of celibacy goes to the supreme abode and is not born here again.
Viṣṇu states, under the continuation of the rule "in the case of the death of a teacher, there is a period of impurity" (*anubandha*),
that this applies to the wives of the guru who are of the same caste (*savarṇa*).
Bṛhaspati [Saṃskāra 259–262] says:
This vow has been prescribed by me for the student who returns home;
now I shall explain briefly that of the lifelong student.
The twilight rites, the fire-ritual, Vedic study, living on alms, sleeping on the ground, self-restraint,
abandoning what was previously forbidden, and doing what is beneficial for the teacher— this is the way of life arising from the mind.
In the absence of a guru, however, the lifelong student (naiṣṭhika), by serving his [the guru's] wife, son, kinsmen, and sacred fire until death,
shall attain the world of Brahmā.
Now, regarding the ceremonial bath upon the payment of the teacher’s fee (*gurudakṣiṇā*), Vyāsa states:
"Having duly obtained knowledge through service to the teacher, the twice-born [student]..."
Having given him a cow as a sacrificial fee, he should bathe with the permission of his teacher.
Yājñavalkya [1.51]: Having given a gift to the teacher, he should bathe with his permission;
or, having brought the Vedic observances (*vedavrata*) to completion, or indeed both.
“Vara” refers to cattle and so forth.
Manu [2.245–246] states:
One who knows the Dharma should not provide anything to the teacher beforehand.
But when he is commanded by his teacher to bathe, he should provide for the teacher's needs according to his ability.
Bringing satisfaction to his teacher, he offered a field, gold, a cow, a horse, an umbrella, sandals, grain, vegetables, and garments.

"Prītim" means what is pleasing. Āpastamba [1.7.19–25]: Having acquired as much learning as he is able, he should offer a teacher’s fee according to dharma and according to his capacity. But if the teacher has fallen into distress, he may obtain it from a fierce person or from a Śūdra. Some say that obtaining the teacher’s requirements from a Śūdra or a fierce person at all times is dharma. Or, having given [the fee], he should not speak of it; and having performed [the service], he should not dwell upon it. He should avoid self-praise and the disparagement of others.

“*Yāvatīm vidyām śaknuyāt*” means having mastered as much of the Veda or Vedas as one is able. “*Vedadakṣiṇām*” means a fee corresponding to the meaning of the Veda. “*Ugraḥ*” is one born of a Kṣatriya father and a Śūdra mother; according to Kapardin, he is so called because he possesses the character of a Kṣatriya while being born of a Brāhmaṇa woman. “*Iti*” (thus) indicates the reason why the giving of one’s own fee would be for the sake of praise, and the giving of another’s fee for the sake of censure, as well as for the purpose of recounting or remembering them. The meaning is that one should avoid either praise or censure. — Vasiṣṭha and Baudhāyana [Bau 4.4.10].
The sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) consists of a thousand [cows] with a bull as the eleventh, or it may be the favor of the Guru.

Regarding the word "thousand," it refers to cows. Regarding the phrase "with a bull as the eleventh," Bhartṛyajña states that this applies when one is unable to give a thousand. Thus says Laghuhārīta.
If a teacher should impart even a single syllable to a disciple,
there is no wealth on earth that, by giving it, he would become free from debt.

Having heard the knowledge of the meaning here, Laghuvyāsa stated immediately thereafter: "He who, having completed his studies according to his ability and in accordance with the rules, knows their meaning and has properly observed the vows, is worthy of the *samāvartana* ceremony."
Having completed the period of studentship (*brahmacarya*), that bath performed with mantras using fragrant substances and so forth is called "returning" (*samāvartana*). Hārīta says:

There are three types of *snātaka*s: the one who has bathed after knowledge (*vidyā-snātaka*), the one who has bathed after vows (*vrata-snātaka*), and the one who has bathed after both knowledge and vows (*vidyā-vrata-snātaka*). He who returns home having completed the Veda but not the vows is a *vidyā-snātaka*. He who returns home having completed the vows but not the Veda is a *vrata-snātaka*. He who returns home having completed both is a *vidyā-vrata-snātaka*. Thus, one who has bathed after knowledge may take up ornaments and the like; he should wear garments according to his purpose. "According to his purpose" means according to necessity. Āpastamba [1.30.1–4].

"By means of sacred knowledge one bathes," say some; likewise, by means of a vow (*vrata*) of forty-eight years' duration. Others say it is by means of both sacred knowledge and the vow. In all these cases, the conduct is that of a *snātaka*. Again, Āpastamba [2.18.4]:

"Covering himself below the navel and above the knees, touching water at the three times of day (*triṣavaṇa*), subsisting on food not cooked over fire, not seeking shelter, and remaining either standing or sitting, he should observe this vow for a year. This, they declare, is equivalent to the forty-eight-year vow."
Having stated the mantras for cleaning the teeth and so forth, Pāraskara says:
"The cleaning of the teeth and such acts are also [performed] daily; however, if the garment, umbrella, and sandals are new, they are accompanied by a mantra.
Baudhāyana says: [1.5.1–6]...

He should wear an inner garment (*antarvāsa*) and an upper garment (*uttarīya*). He should carry a bamboo staff and a water-pot containing water. He should wear two sacred threads (*yajñopavīta*). He should also have a turban, an upper garment of deerskin (*ajina*), sandals, and an umbrella.

The term “*antarvāsa*” refers to the lower garment. The term “*uttarīya*” refers to the upper garment. An upper garment of deerskin is optional in conjunction with a cloth garment, according to the Vedic scripture: “Either a deerskin or a cloth, worn over the right shoulder as a sacred thread. (Manu 4.35).
Having trimmed his hair, nails, and beard, self-controlled, wearing white garments, and pure,
he should be constantly engaged in the private recitation of the Veda and in what is beneficial for the self.
“Kḷptam” means cut. Likewise [4.36]:
the sacred thread, the Veda, and two auspicious golden earrings.
“Veda” means a handful of *darbha* grass. “In golden” means in gold.
Vasiṣṭha [12.39]: “One should not break a garland outside.”
Hārīta says:
One should not wear a garland that is odorless or red, except for golden lotuses and blue water-lilies;
"kuvalaya" refers to the *utpala* (blue water-lily).
Āpastamba: He should wear beautiful garlands and be anointed with fragrant unguents.
Jābāli: [279]
The householder, together with his wife, should observe the vows, remaining constantly pure, fragrant, wearing white garments, and patient, while being devoted to his own religious duties.

Gautama [9.1–7]: Having bathed according to the prescribed rule and taken a wife, the *snātaka* who practices the duties of a householder as they have been described should observe these following vows: he should always be pure, fragrant, and habituated to bathing; if he has the means, he should not wear worn-out or dirty clothes; he should not wear dyed, gaudy, or clothes previously worn by another, nor garlands or sandals (unless they belong to him); he may wear washed clothes if he lacks the means; and he should not let his beard grow unless there is a specific reason—the meaning is that he should not have a long beard except for a particular cause.
Manu [4.66]: One should not wear shoes, clothing,
a sacred thread, an ornament, a garland, or even a water-pot that have been worn by others.
“*Karaka*” means a water-pot (*kamaṇḍalu*). [Thus ends the section on the Teacher’s Fee and the Bathing Ceremony in the *Brahmacārikāṇḍa* of the *Kṛtyakalpataru*.
